abgaal: The Abgaal belong to the Mudulood, one of the divisions of the Hiraab, with the Habar Gidir, Sheekhaal and Duduble. The clan is regarded as relatively young, its founder dating from the 1500s. A tradition recorded by the Italian scholar Enrico Cerulli makes the founder, Ali Isman, the son of Osman Darandolle of the Hiraab and of Faduma Sarjeele, a woman of the Gareen house that headed the Ajuran Sultanate.

According to the story, Faduma's father was warned that the boy's descendants would drive out his own and tried to poison him, but the mother drank the poison by mistake. The boy hid behind a camel and called the camels his grandfather, whence the name Abgaal, camel-grandfather. Cerulli read the story as a memory of fighting between Abgaal pastoral nomads coming from the north and the Ajuran.

Clan traditions say that the Abgaal Darandoolle began to arrive in the hinterland of Mogadishu in the sixteenth century, while the Muzaffar dynasty ruled the town, and manuscripts from Mogadishu record Abgaal nomads in the interior at about the same time. Towards the end of the seventeenth century an imam of Abgaal descent settled in the Shangaani quarter. His lineage, the Yaaquub, intermarried with merchant families of Yemeni origin and became known in the trade between the coast and the interior, and by the 1700s it ruled most of the town.

Traditions of the fall of the Ajuran speak of heavy taxes and of a quarrel over watering rights, after which the Darandoolle killed the Ajuran imam at a well called Ceel Cawl. According to oral tradition as reported by Lee Cassanelli, the Hiraab Imamate that followed was an alliance of related groups that ruled from the Shabelle valley to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. Mogadishu was its capital, and the port of Hobyo its commercial centre.

The Abgaal are divided into three main branches: the Harti, the eldest, the Wacbudhan and the Waceysle, the youngest. The imam of the Mudulood and of the Hiraab traditionally comes from the Abgaal, from the Owbakar sub-clan, while the ugaas of the Mudulood comes from the Reer Ugaas sub-clan. Mogadishu is regarded as Abgaal territory, and they form the majority of its population. Three presidents of Somalia, Ali Mahdi Muhammad, Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, have been Abgaal, as was Daud Abdulle Hirsi, the first commander-in-chief of the Somali National Army.
abu-tahir-al-jannabi: Abu Tahir Sulayman was an Arabized Persian, born in June or July 906 at Ganaveh on the coast of Fars. His father, Abu Sa'id, a tribal leader taught by Hamdan Qarmat of Kufa, had begun the militarization of the Qarmatians.

Most Arabic sources agree that Abu Sa'id named his eldest son, Abu'l-Qasim Sa'id, as heir and that Abu Tahir revolted against him and usurped power. Another tradition, reported by the Kufan anti-Isma'ili polemicist Ibn Rizam, holds that Sa'id was only a regent and handed over power in 917/918, when his brother was barely ten. It is likely that power was nominally shared among all the sons, with Abu Tahir dominant. Abu'l-Qasim was not executed and lived until 972.

In 926 he led his army as far north as Kufa and made the Abbasids pay large sums for him to leave. On his return he built palaces at Ahsa and declared it his permanent capital. In 928 Caliph al-Muqtadir sent against him the generals Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Mu'nis al-Muzaffar and Harun, who were beaten and driven back to Baghdad.

At Mecca in 930 he was at first refused entry, invoked the right of all Muslims to enter and swore that he came in peace. Once inside, his men rode into the Masjid al-Haram, massacred the pilgrims, set fire to the Kaaba and threw bodies into the Zamzam Well. The attack was believed to be meant to prompt the appearance of the Mahdi and followed millenarian excitement over the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in 928.

The Mahdi he recognised in 931, Abu'l-Fadl al-Isfahani, a prisoner who claimed descent from the Sasanian kings, restored the veneration of fire, burned religious books and had members of Bahrayn's notable families executed. In one account Abu Tahir's mother exposed him and his brother Sa'id killed him after eighty days; in others Abu Tahir denounced him as a false Mahdi and had him executed.

Abu Tahir took back control of the state and resumed his attacks on pilgrims crossing Arabia. He rejected the attempts of both the Abbasids and the Fatimids to persuade him to return the Black Stone. He died of smallpox in 944, aged about 38, and was succeeded by his three surviving sons and his nephews. According to the historian al-Juwayni the stone came back in 951, thrown in a sack into the Great Mosque of Kufa with a note: "By command we took it, and by command we have brought it back." Its removal had broken it into seven pieces.
akim-oda: Akim Oda lies in the south of Ghana, surrounded by rain forest, in the basin of the Birim River, which flows through the town and is rich in gold and diamonds. The climate is semi-equatorial and wet. Rain falls heavily from April to June and again from September to November, and a dry season, with markedly lower temperatures, lasts from December to February. The town is the capital of the Birim Central Municipal District and had 60,604 residents as of 2013.

Cocoa is grown on formal and informal plantations, sometimes along the roads; the harvested beans are dried and kept in warehouses until they are shipped. North of the Birim there are palm oil plantations covering roughly 6,000 hectares, most of them small and independently owned, and bamboo is also cultivated. Local miners take gold and diamonds from the river bank by traditional methods, often with simple tools.

The forests near the town are cut for timber. Ghana's forest cover shrank from 8.2 million hectares in 1900 to 1.6 million in 2000, and forest plantations are being established near Akim Oda under the National Forest Plantation Development Program. Visitors are shown a tree described as the largest in West Africa, 12 metres in circumference and 66.5 metres high, and may see the mining from dug-out boats and ceremonies with Akan drumming.

The Akim Oda Government Hospital serves the Kotoku traditional area and takes referrals from nearby communities in the Akyem states; private hospitals in the town also serve Akyem Bosome and part of the Abuakwa traditional area. The public sector has more than fifteen primary and junior high schools and three senior high schools, and four radio stations broadcast from the town.
ali-adil-shah-ii: Ali Adil Shah II was the eighth sultan of Bijapur. He came to the throne on the death of Mohammed Adil Shah on 4 November 1656, through the efforts of the prime minister Khan Muhammad and of the queen Badi Sahiba, a sister of the Qutb Shah of Golkonda. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, who wished to annex Bijapur, found a pretext in doubts about Ali's parentage and, at the plea of his son Aurangzeb, sanctioned an invasion, although Bijapur was an independent ally of the Mughals and not their vassal. Aurangzeb had to raise the siege and hurry north for the war of succession to the Mughal throne.

With the accession of a young ruler, disorder began in the Karnataka, where the Nayaks tried to recover their former lands; Bangalore was Bijapur's administrative headquarters for controlling these feudatories. At court the struggle of factions for supremacy reached its height, and Aurangzeb intrigued with the Bijapur nobles and won over most of them. Shivaji meanwhile took more and more Bijapur territory, and his diplomacy prevented any coalition of the Mughals and Bijapur against him.

Through the sixteen years of his reign Ali fought both the Mughals and the Marathas, and he three times repulsed Mughal invasions. The reign was also marked by developments in Persian and Deccani literature and the fine arts. Beside the poet laureate Nusrati, the historian Nurullah wrote under his patronage a history known as the Tarikh-i Ali Adil Shah.

Ali died on 24 November 1672. By then the kingdom had lost most of its important territories, shrinking as Shivaji's kingdom grew, and the reign is seen as marking the decline of Bijapur. He was buried in Ali Ka Rouza, the monument at Bijapur known as the Bara Kaman.
altan-khan: Altan was the second son of Bars Bolud Jinong and a grandson of Dayan Khan. After Dayan Khan the Mongols formed six tümen divided into a Left Wing under the Great Khan and a Right Wing under Altan's father, who held the office of jinong, or vice-regent. Altan ruled the Tümed, whose pastures lay north of the border with Shanxi. When his elder brother Gün Bilig died in 1542, Altan became the effective leader of the Right Wing. After the death of Bodi Alagh Khan in 1547 he forced the new khagan, Darayisung Küdeng Khan, to flee eastward, and in 1551 Darayisung compromised by granting him the title Gegeen Khan.

Altan wanted to trade horses for Chinese farm produce and textiles, but the Ming court, suspicious of him, repeatedly refused and sometimes killed his envoys. He raided northern China in 1529, 1530 and 1542, and in 1550 crossed gaps in the Great Wall and besieged Beijing, setting its suburbs on fire. He strengthened his Tümed base by settling Chinese refugees there and kept a network of Ming conspirators led by Zhao Quan, a disciple of the White Lotus. In 1552 he gained control of the remains of Karakorum.

In 1570 his grandson Daičing Ejei Taiji defected to the Ming after a family quarrel. Ministers of the Longqing Emperor proposed that Altan accept a Ming title and hand over Zhao Quan in return for his grandson and trading rights. Altan agreed; Zhao and his fellow conspirators were executed, Altan was made Shunyi prince and his capital was renamed Guihua. The American Orientalist Owen Lattimore writes that the Mongols were nominally vassals, but that the Ming was eager to please them and the arrangement was more or less of benefit to both.

Altan first invited Sonam Gyatso in 1569; the lama accepted a second invitation in 1577, and Altan later had Thegchen Chonkhor, Mongolia's first monastery, built where they met. Sonam Gyatso declared Altan a reincarnation of Kublai Khan. One reason for adopting Buddhism was a fear among the Mongol elite that the peace of 1571 would spread Chinese cultural influence. Laws set out by Sonam Gyatso and instituted by Altan forbade blood sacrifices and the burning of widows. Altan died on 13 January 1582, aged 74 or 75, and his son Sengge Düüreng succeeded him as Shunyi prince. His great-grandson Yonten Gyatso was chosen as the 4th Dalai Lama in 1601.
andhra-mahabharatam: Nannaya began the translation from Sanskrit at the request of the king, and his part marks the earliest known beginning of a written literary tradition in Telugu. It is composed in the Champu style and is so polished that several scholars think it probable that literary works existed in Telugu before him. No such writings have been found, apart from references to songs and poems and some verses in inscriptions, and Telugu tradition honours him as the Adi Kavi, the first poet.

Tikkana, who lived from 1205 to 1288, was born into a Niyogi Brahmin family and was a minister of the Nellore Chola ruler Manumasiddhi II. Errana, also called Yerrapragada, was a poet at the court of King Prolaya Vema Reddy, who reigned from 1325 to 1353 and founded the Reddy dynasty; he bore the titles Prabandha-parameshvara and Shambhudasudu, servant of Shiva.

The work is not a stanza-by-stanza translation but a Telugu rendering that keeps the core narrative of the Mahabharata. Nannaya wrote the Adi Parvam, the Sabha Parvam and part of the Aranya Parvam, the Book of the Forest. Tikkana wrote the fifteen books from the Virata Parvam to the Svargarohana Parvam but did not touch the half-finished third book, because it was considered inauspicious to take up what Nannaya had left incomplete. It remained unfinished for more than a century until Errana completed it. He began his portion in the style of Nannaya and ended it in the style of Tikkana, as a bridge between the two.

The Sanskrit epic is reckoned at 100 parvas and 100,000 verses. In Telugu Nannaya arranged it in eighteen parvas, divided into chapters called ashvasas, without the subdivision into upaparvas, and left out the Harivamsa; Tikkana followed his arrangement, and Errana wrote the Harivamsa as a separate work.

The three poets are revered by later Telugu poets as the Kavitrayam, the trinity of poets, and became models for all who followed. Though written by three hands over about two and a half centuries, the work is read as a single book, as if one poet had composed it in one period. Errana went on to translate the Ramayana from Sanskrit and to write an independent work, the Nrusimhapuranamu.
argead-dynasty: The dynasty, also called Temenid, had King Caranus as its mythical founder. Herodotus tells in The Histories that three brothers of the lineage of Temenus, named Gauanes, Aeropus and Perdiccas, fled from Argos to the Illyrians and then to a town called Lebaea in Upper Macedonia, where they served the king. Dismissed by him because of an omen that something great would happen to Perdiccas, they settled near the garden of Midas below Mount Bermio and slowly formed a kingdom of their own. A Greek inscription relating to the belief in descent from Heracles was found by Manolis Andronikos in the royal palace of Aigai, near modern Vergina.

According to Thucydides, in the History of the Peloponnesian War, the Argeads came down from the highlands to Lower Macedonia, expelled the Pierians from Pieria, gained a narrow strip along the river Axios reaching to Pella and the sea, and added Mygdonia by driving out the Edoni, Eordians and Almopians. Another theory, held by the Greek historian Miltiades Hatzopoulos following the ancient author Appian, is that the dynasty came from Argos Orestikon rather than from the Peloponnese, its people completing their wandering from Orestis to Lower Macedonia in the 7th century BCE.

The Argeads were at first rulers of the tribe of the same name, which prevailed in early Emathia, later Lower Macedonia, with its capital at Aigai. Herodotus relates that when Alexander I of Macedon entered the Olympic Games, in 504 or 500 BCE, other competitors objected that he was not Greek; the judges, the Hellanodikai, examined his Argead claim and allowed him to take part. By the time of Philip II of Macedon the kingdom, now governed from Pella, included all the states of Upper Macedonia.

The death of a king almost invariably set off disputes among members of the family, and often a war of succession. A six-year interregnum from 399 to 393 BCE followed the death of King Archelaus, and wars of succession followed the deaths of Pausanias, Amyntas III and Perdiccas III, the last of which brought Philip II to power in 360 to 359 BCE after he deposed Amyntas IV. An established king could also face rebellion by a relative, as Perdiccas II did from his brother Philip. Modern historians disagree on a number of details of the family's genealogy.
asaf-ud-daula: Born on 23 September 1748, Asaf-ud-Daula was the son of Shuja-ud-Daula and of Umat-ul-Zohra, better known as Bahu Begum. He became nawab at the age of 26 on his father's death in January 1775, with the aid of the British East India Company. His younger brother Saadat Ali led a mutiny in the army, which the British Colonel John Parker defeated decisively. Asaf's first chief minister, Mukhtar-ud-Daula, was assassinated in the revolt. His position as Nawab wazir was ratified by the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.

After the revolt he restructured the government, appointing nobles favourable to him and British officers to his army. Hasan Riza Khan became chief minister, ably assisted by Haydar Beg Khan, and Tikayt Ray finance minister. His mother remained a challenge to his rule: she controlled much of the treasury, held her own jagirs and armed forces, and at one point sought the Company's help in appointing ministers opposed to him.

Shuja-ud-Daula had left two million pounds sterling in the vaults of the zenana, which his widow and his mother claimed under a will that was never produced. When Warren Hastings pressed the nawab for the debt due to the Company, Asaf obtained from his mother a loan of 26 lakh rupees against a jagir of four times the value, and later 30 lakh more in return for a full acquittal and the Company's recognition of her jagirs for life. The jagirs were afterwards confiscated on the ground of her complicity in the rising of Chait Singh.

The Bara Imambara, or Asafi Imambara, was begun as a charitable project to give employment in the famine of 1784, in which even nobles were reduced to penury. It is said that over 20,000 people worked on it, and that nobles were paid to pull down part of the work in secret at night so that their dignity was kept. The Rumi Darwaza, sixty feet tall, was modelled in 1784 on the Sublime Porte in Istanbul.

He died in Lucknow on 21 September 1797 and is buried at the Bara Imambara. A saying still known in the city records his generosity: to whom even God does not give, Asaf-ud-Daula gives. The painter Johann Zoffany portrayed him several times, and the Urdu poet Mir Taqi Mir was at his court.
az-zahir-ghazi: Al-Malik az-Zahir Ghiyath ud-din Ghazi was the third son of Saladin. In 1186, when he was 15, his father appointed him governor of Aleppo, Mosul and the neighbouring areas recently taken from the Zengids, lands that had been under the control of Saladin's brother al-Adil. His two older brothers received Syria (al-Afdal) and Egypt (al-Aziz) at the same time. When he inherited in 1193 he was to owe suzerainty to al-Afdal in Damascus, but he conducted his affairs independently and for a while stayed out of his brothers' quarrels with their uncle.

In 1193 he called on al-Adil for troops to put down the revolt of the Zengid Izz al-Din in Mosul. The next year he received Latakia and Jableh in a settlement by which he recognised al-Afdal's authority, but in 1196 he joined al-Aziz and al-Adil in deposing and exiling that brother. In October 1197, with Bohemond III of Antioch threatening Latakia and Jableh, he destroyed the two ports; Bohemond took them, found them of no use and withdrew, and az-Zahir reoccupied them and rebuilt the fortress at Latakia. He kept many of his father's advisers and appointed Baha ad-Din as a judge in Aleppo.

After al-Aziz died in 1198, az-Zahir allied with al-Afdal, and with most of the other Ayyubid princes they besieged Damascus. The city held out for months, and he withdrew his troops. Al-Adil, having conquered Egypt, returned, reduced az-Zahir's territories to the area around Aleppo and forced him to recognise his suzerainty. In his last decade az-Zahir skirmished with crusaders and lent his army to other Ayyubid princes. King Leo of Cilicia defeated his forces at the Battle of Amq in 1206 but gained no lasting advantage against Aleppo, and in 1207 his troops lifted a siege of Homs.

In 1212 az-Zahir married Dayfa Khatun, the daughter of his old rival al-Adil, a match that ended the rivalry between the two branches of the family. Before his death he appointed his younger son al-Aziz Muhammad, born in 1213, to succeed him. He died on 8 October 1216. His lands had included northern Syria and a small part of Mesopotamia.
b-j-habibie: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie was born on 25 June 1936 in Parepare, South Sulawesi, the son of Alwi Abdul Jalil Habibie, an agriculturist of Bugis-Gorontalese descent, and R. A. Tuti Marini Puspowardojo, a Javanese noblewoman from Yogyakarta. He began to study aviation at Delft in the Netherlands but, because of the dispute between the two countries over West New Guinea, moved to the Technische Hochschule Aachen in Germany, where he took an engineer's degree in 1960 and a doctorate in aerospace engineering in 1965. In 1962 he married Hasri Ainun Besari, a medical doctor.

He joined Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm in Hamburg, where he worked on the Airbus A-300B and reached a middle management post in 1974. That year President Suharto recruited him to return as part of a drive to industrialise Indonesia. Two years later he became head of the new state aircraft maker, known as IPTN, which built Puma helicopters and CASA planes and in 1995 produced a small passenger aircraft, the N-250, a commercial failure.

From 1978 he was state minister of research and technology. By 1991 he oversaw ten state-owned industries, among them shipbuilding, steel, arms and energy; an estimate of 1993 put their cost at nearly 2 billion dollars a year in state funds. In 1990 he was elected the first chair of the Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals, a modernist organisation that gave him a political base. When Suharto signalled in January 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, that he wanted him as vice-president, the rupiah fell.

As president he also forbade the official use of the terms pribumi and non-pribumi, lifted restrictions on the teaching of Mandarin Chinese and passed laws giving autonomy to regencies and cities. He had opposed independence for East Timor and offered special autonomy; the armed forces' leaders were not consulted on his decision to hold a referendum. After the vote of 30 August 1999 pro-Indonesian militias killed and displaced large numbers of people, and on 12 September he accepted a peacekeeping force mandated by the United Nations.

A leaked telephone call with his attorney general raised doubts about the investigation of Suharto. The Bank Bali scandal of 1999, in which bank funds reached members of his re-election team, damaged him further. In October 1999 the assembly known as the MPR rejected his accountability speech by 355 votes to 322, and he withdrew his candidacy; Abdurrahman Wahid succeeded him. He died in the Gatot Soebroto Army Hospital on 11 September 2019 and was buried at the Kalibata Heroes' Cemetery beside his wife.
bahadur-shah-of-gujarat: Born Bahadur Khan into the Muzaffarid dynasty, he was the son of Prince Khalil Khan, who became sultan in 1511 as Muzaffar Shah II, and of Rani Lakshmi Bai, daughter of a Gohel Rajput. His grandfather, Sultan Mahmud Begada, kept him at court. When his elder brother Sikandar Shah was named heir, Bahadur Khan feared for his life and fled, first to Chittor and then to Ibrahim Lodi; he was present at the Battle of Panipat without taking part in the fighting.

Muzaffar Shah II died in 1526. Sikandar Shah was murdered after a few weeks on the instructions of his slave Imad-ul-Mulk Khush Kadam, who put an infant brother on the throne as Mahmud Shah II. Bahadur Khan returned, the nobles joined him, and he marched on Champaner, executed Imad-ul-Mulk and had the child poisoned.

Bahadur Shah campaigned in the Deccan in 1528 and 1529, taking the fort of Ahmednagar and forcing the rulers of Ahmadnagar and Berar to sign a humiliating treaty. The fortress of Mandu fell on 28 March 1531, when Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Malwa and his seven sons were captured; they were later put to death by their guards during a rescue attempt. In 1532 he raised a siege of Chittor in return for an enormous ransom. Until his defeat by Humayun the power of Gujarat was at its height, with the rulers of Ahmednagar and Burhanpur acknowledging him as overlord.

The quarrel with Humayun began because Bahadur Shah had sheltered the Mughal prince Muhammad Zaman Mirza. The rout near Mandasur is usually explained by the treachery of Rumi Khan, the Turkish head of the Gujarat artillery. Bahadur Shah fled to Mandu, Champaner and finally Diu. When Humayun left to face the revolt of Sher Shah Suri, the country rose, and Bahadur Shah defeated the Mughals at Kanij and expelled them from Gujarat.

The Treaty of Bassein was signed on 23 December 1534 aboard the galleon St. Mattheus. Having recovered his kingdom, Bahadur Shah regretted the alliance. In February 1537 he visited the Portuguese viceroy's ship off Diu and was attacked and killed on his way back, on 13 February; his body was thrown into the sea. According to the Mirat-i-Sikandari, the viceroy had intercepted his message inviting the Deccan sultans to ally against the Portuguese. He left no son, and after his chosen heir, his nephew Miran Muhammad Shah of Khandesh, died on the way to Gujarat, the nobles chose Mahmud Shah III, son of his brother Latif Khan.
banabhatta: What is known of Bana's ancestry and early life is reconstructed from his own words: the introductory verses attached to the Kadambari and the first two chapters, or ucchvasas, of the Harshacharita. He was born to Chitrabhanu and Rajadevi in the village of Pritikuta, in a Kanyakubja Brahmin family. His mother died early and left him in the care of his father, who married again and had two more sons.

His father died when Bana was fourteen. For a time he led a colourful, wandering life with his half-brothers, and afterwards he came back to his native village. There, on a summer day, he received a letter from Krishna, a cousin of Harsha, and went to meet the king, who was camping near the town of Manitara. Harsha received him at first with mock signs of anger and then showed him much favour. Bana became the court poet during Harsha's reign at Kanyakubja.

The Harshacharita, whose title means the deeds of Harsha, was Bana's first composition; its third chapter describes the circumstances in which he came to write it. It is considered the first Indian work that may be regarded as a historical biography and the beginning of historical poetic writing in Sanskrit, and it gives a vivid picture of life in the Indian countryside.

Bana died before he could finish the Kadambari, and his son Bhushanabhatta completed it. Two further works are attributed to him, the Chandikashataka and a drama, the Parvatiparinaya. A Sanskrit saying, Banochhistam jagatsarvam, holds that Bana described everything in the world and left nothing out. The Harshacharita was translated into English by E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas for the Royal Asiatic Society in 1897.
battle-of-albulena: Skanderbeg had fought the Ottoman Empire since 1444, and after more than a decade of war his resources were worn out. His siege of Berat in 1455 ended in catastrophe when an Ottoman counterattack fell on the Albanians during his temporary absence. Afterwards some of his most trusted officers deserted. Moisi Golemi returned in May 1456 at the head of an Ottoman force, was defeated at the Battle of Oranik and was taken back without punishment.

A graver loss was his nephew Hamza Kastrioti, one of his most important officers, who had grown dissatisfied with Skanderbeg's increasing power and was promised control of much of Albania once it was conquered. Relations with Venice were at their lowest point. Alfonso V of Aragon and Pope Calixtus III, his allies, could not provide for him fully, and a fleet the pope promised in 1457 did not arrive.

By the end of May 1457 an Ottoman army of between 50,000 and 80,000 men approached, against which Skanderbeg had between 8,000 and 10,000. He stalled the akıncı vanguard marching through Dibër, then withdrew before the main force. Since both Ottoman commanders knew his usual ambushes, he split his army into several groups and ordered them to march through the forests and mountains in different directions, supplied by the local people and by depots, and not to assemble or attack without his word.

The Ottomans pillaged the Mat valley and camped at Albulena, north of Mount Tumenishta and south of modern Laç. Through July and August Skanderbeg stayed out of sight, and rumours spread that he had fled. On 2 September his reassembled army attacked the camp in three groups with a great noise of clashing metal. The Ottomans, believing the attackers more numerous than they were, panicked. Their dead may have been as many as 30,000, though it is unlikely that more than 15,000 were killed; 15,000 were taken prisoner and twenty-four standards were captured.

Hamza Kastrioti was captured and sent as a prisoner to Naples. An Ottoman envoy came to ransom the standard bearers and forty distinguished prisoners and proposed a truce, which Skanderbeg would accept only if Svetigrad and Berat were restored to him. In 1460 Sultan Mehmed II and Skanderbeg signed an armistice that lasted three years, giving Skanderbeg the opportunity to cross to Italy and help Ferdinand I of Naples. The historian Franz Babinger called the battle Skanderbeg's most brilliant victory. Desertions from his army became rare afterwards, but the war continued until the fall of Krujë in 1478.
battle-of-bir-hakeim: Bir Hakeim was a fortress built by the Ottomans at the crossing of two Bedouin paths. It stood at the southern end of the Gazala line, a series of brigade-sized defensive boxes that the British Eighth Army held west of Tobruk. On 14 February 1942 the 1st Free French Brigade took over the box, which was surrounded by 50,000 mines. The brigade had a fighting strength of 3,000 men, with the 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion as its backbone, and by mid-May it had dug 1,200 entrenchments, foxholes and gun emplacements. The Axis plan sent the armour around the box while the Italian 132nd Armoured Division Ariete neutralised it.

On the morning of 27 May an Italian tank battalion of the Ariete Division, with 60 tanks, charged the minefield and wire. It lost 31 tanks and a self-propelled gun, and ten tanks that got through were knocked out by 75 mm anti-tank guns. From 2 June the position was shelled and bombed, and Stuka dive-bombers raided it more than twenty times, but the well-built positions were almost invulnerable. On 6 June the 90th Light Division attacked with pioneers, who cleared passages through the minefields.

From 8 June Rommel directed attacks from the north with part of the 15th Panzer Division, and the perimeter was forced back. On 10 June, with ammunition almost gone, the fort took the largest air raid of the siege, by 100 Stukas. After dark sappers cleared a narrow passage through the mines on the western face. Kœnig left at the head of the column in a car driven by Susan Travers, an Englishwoman serving with the Foreign Legion, and most of the brigade broke through troops of the 90th Light Division to reach lorries and ambulances sent by the British 7th Motor Brigade.

Thomas Buell and Ken Ford give the French losses as 141 dead, 229 wounded and 814 taken prisoner, with 53 guns and 50 vehicles; the Axis lost 3,300 dead or wounded and 227 captured, with 164 vehicles destroyed and 49 aircraft shot down. The defence had lengthened the Axis supply route around the Gazala line and gave the British time to recover from their defeat in the Cauldron, and the delay influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta. Tobruk still fell ten days later. Both sides used the battle for propaganda, and Winston Churchill declared the Free French to be the Fighting French.
battle-of-koppam: From his accession Rajadhiraja Chola I sought to subdue the Chalukyas, who ruled parts of northern Karnataka and the south of present-day Maharashtra, and to add their lands to the Chola Empire. His first invasion, in 1047–48, had failed. On the second expedition he led a large army north and plundered the province of Rattamandalam, with his brother and heir-apparent Rajendra Chola II following in the rear.

According to the Chola sources and the Thiruvalandur copper plate, Rajadhiraja had personally led the attack on Kalyanapura, also called Kalyani, the modern Basavakalyan. Someshvara I fled when the city was attacked, returned with an army and was beaten again, and the Chola king then withdrew towards Kollapura. The copper plate says that Someshvara gathered a huge army and called out for battle as the Chola withdrew, and that the Chola turned to meet him at the place called Koppam.

The copper plate describes columns of foot soldiers, horses and elephants engaging their counterparts, with Rajadhiraja fighting from his elephant until a downpour of Chalukya arrows killed him. The Chola troops, who had been holding the upper hand, panicked and began to retreat. Rajendra II, commanding the reserve, took over the army, rallied it and inflicted heavy losses, forcing Someshvara to flee. Chola sources record that the elephants, horses and camels of the Chalukyas, a large booty and the queens of Someshvara fell into Chola hands. Rajendra is reported to have set up a victory pillar at Kolhapur before returning to his country.

The battle is known chiefly from the Chola side: an inscription dated to 1054 and Rajendra Chola II's Manimangalam record of 1055. The latter gives the victory to Rajendra and says that Ahavamalla, as it calls the Chalukya king, became afraid, incurred disgrace and ran away. The year is given as 1054, or as 1052 by the historian Sen. The site is also uncertain. The Manimangalam inscription places Koppam on the bank of the great river; the scholar Fleet identified it with Khidrapur, 30 miles south-east of Kolhapur, taking the river to be the Krishna, while other historians have put it near Maski.
bodleian-library: The first purpose-built library known at Oxford was founded in the 14th century under the will of Thomas Cobham, Bishop of Worcester (d. 1327): a small collection of chained books kept above the north side of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin. When Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, gave a great collection of manuscripts between 1435 and 1437 a larger room was needed, and one was built above the Divinity School and completed in 1488; it is still known as Duke Humfrey's Library.

In the later 16th century the library declined. Its furniture was sold, and only three of Duke Humphrey's original books remained. In 1598 Thomas Bodley, a former fellow of Merton College, wrote to the Vice Chancellor offering to restore it at his own cost. The room was refitted, Bodley gave some of his own books, and the library was formally reopened on 8 November 1602 with around 2,000 books.

In 1610 Bodley made an agreement with the Stationers' Company, suggested by the first librarian, Thomas James, that a copy of every book registered with the company would be placed in the library. The collection grew so fast that the building was extended between 1610 and 1612, and the Schools Quadrangle was built between 1613 and 1619. By 1620 there were 16,000 items. John Selden left his books and manuscripts to the library in 1654. Until the establishment of the British Museum in 1753 the Bodleian was effectively the national library of England.

The library took over the neighbouring Radcliffe Camera in 1860, and the Copyright Act of 1911 continued the Stationers' agreement by making it a library of legal deposit. Its holdings passed one million books in 1914. The New Bodleian, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, was completed in 1940; rebuilt behind its original façade, it reopened as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.

The Bodleian works principally as a reference library, and documents may not be taken from the reading rooms. New readers must agree to a formal declaration not to remove, mark or damage anything in the library, nor to bring fire or flame into it. Its head is known as Bodley's Librarian; 25 people have held the office. Since 2000 it has been the largest member of a group of Oxford libraries, called the Bodleian Libraries since 2010. With over 13 million printed items it is the second-largest library in Britain after the British Library, and its principal store is at South Marston.
brihatkatha: The date of the work is uncertain. Gunadhya may have flourished under a Satavahana king of Pratishthana, the modern Paithan in Maharashtra; according to D. C. Sircar he probably lived between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE. Another account, in the Nepala Mahatmya of the Skanda Purana, makes him a native of Mathura and court poet of King Madana of Ujjain, a tradition Sircar calls less authentic. Paishachi, the language he used, is a little-known Prakrit, described as the speech of the common people of the border regions of northwest India.

The earliest surviving reference seems to be that of Subandhu in his Vasavadatta, and Banabhatta refers to the work in the Harshacharita and the Kadambari. Dandin, in the Kavyadarsha, calls it marvellous and says it was composed in the vernacular of the bhutas, though his information appears to be second-hand. A Cambodian inscription of about 875 names Gunadhya, and the Kannada Kavirajamarga of about 850 mentions a Sanskrit version, now lost, by Durvinita. A romantic work by Gunadhya can safely be assumed to have existed before 600 CE.

The adaptations differ too much for the original to be reconstructed whole, but what they share allows strong inferences. The life of Udayana of Kaushambi served as a prelude: his upbringing in a hermitage after a monstrous bird carried off his pregnant mother, his captivity under Pradyota, king of Ujjayini, his elopement with Pradyota's daughter Vasavadatta, and his second marriage to Padmavati, arranged by ministers who made him believe Vasavadatta dead. The central story was that of their son Naravahanadatta, born as a boon of Kubera and fated to become emperor of the Vidyadharas. Kshemendra's version is in eighteen books called lambakas, as the original is thought to have been.

Besides the two Kashmiri versions, the story is known from the Sanskrit Brihatkathashlokasamgraha of Budhasvamin, of which the complete text has not been found, and from the Perunkatai and the Vasudevahimdi in vernacular languages. Dandin states that the original was in prose, not in the verse of the Kashmiri recensions. Scholars compare Gunadhya with Vyasa and Valmiki, and the disappearance of his text is counted a very great loss to Indian literature.
chagatai-khan: Chagatai was born in late 1183 or 1184 to Börte, of the Onggirat tribe, and Temüjin, the later Genghis Khan. Because Börte had been kidnapped by the Merkit tribe before the birth of her elder son Jochi, whose paternity was never known, Chagatai was the first son definitively fathered by Temüjin. When Genghis divided his new nation after the assembly of 1206, Chagatai received territories near the Altai Mountains and either 4,000 or 8,000 subjects. He was known for his knowledge of Mongol law and custom, and chroniclers such as Juzjani noted the harshness of his temperament.

With his brothers Jochi and Ögedei he commanded the right wing in the invasion of the Jin dynasty in 1211. In the invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219 he was charged with building bridges and maintaining roads. He and Ögedei besieged Otrar, which fell in February 1220; the Mongols killed or enslaved its entire population. At the Siege of Gurganj, which fell in April 1221, the usual narrative has Chagatai and Jochi quarrel over how to conduct it until Genghis placed Ögedei over both; the historian Christopher Atwood argues that this account was a later invention meant to support Ögedei's right to rule.

Genghis thought Chagatai too strict and narrow-minded for a ruler and was troubled by his hatred of Jochi, and excluded him from the succession. After Genghis died in 1227, Chagatai held to his father's will, prevented any usurpation before the accession of Ögedei in 1229, and presided over the coronation with Tolui and their uncle Temüge. In Central Asia his capital and summer pastures were at Almaliq. He disputed jurisdiction with the imperial official Mahmud Yalavach, and when Bukhara revolted against tax demands in 1238 he left its suppression to Ögedei's armies.

After Ögedei died in December 1241, Chagatai's support made Töregene regent. He died in 1242; his wife Yesülün accused a steward named Vajir of poisoning him and had him executed. His grandson Qara Hülegü succeeded him but was displaced by Chagatai's son Yesü-Möngke between 1246 and 1250.

Chagatai upheld traditional Mongol law, which forbade elements of Islamic practice, and gained a reputation for being anti-Muslim; one contemporary Muslim writer claimed that he urged Ögedei to kill every Muslim in the empire. The historians Michael Hope and Peter Jackson think this far from the truth, pointing to the powerful Muslim officials at his court. His descendants were nonetheless far slower to convert to Islam than the rulers of the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate.
chand-dynasty: The traditional genealogical lists of the Chand kings, the vamshavalis, were compiled in the mid-19th century and are not completely reliable. They place Som Chand in the 7th century, and a British report of 1849 accordingly dated the start of Chand rule to 685 CE. Historians dispute this, because the Katyuri kingdom is known to have ruled Kumaon until the third quarter of the 10th century.

Tradition makes Som Chand an immigrant from Jhusi and a relative of the king of Kannauj. The historian Krishna Pal Singh suggests that he came to Kumaon during the upheaval of the Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj in 1018–1019, and dates the beginning of Chand rule to 1019–1021. By the early 13th century the Chands appear to have ruled as feudatories: the Baleshwar Temple inscription of 1223, set up by Krachalla Deva, a conqueror from present-day Nepal, lists men whose names suggest that they belonged to the family.

Rudra Chand (1565–1597) seized Sira in 1581 and made the first of several attacks on the Garhwal Kingdom, all of which were repulsed. In 1587 he visited the Mughal emperor Akbar at Lahore as a mark of obeisance, and the Ain-e-Akbari lists a Sarkar of Kumaon. Baz Bahadur Chand (1638–78), one of the most powerful of the line, joined Shahjahan in an attack on Garhwal in 1655 that captured the Terai region including Dehradun, and extended his territory east to the Karnali river. In 1672 he began a poll tax whose revenue was sent to Delhi as tribute.

In 1744 the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan sent a force that took Almora against weak resistance. The Rohillas stayed seven months and left after a payment of three lakh rupees; a second attack was defeated at Barakheri. Hill troops under Dip Chand later fought beside the Rohillas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Internal strife over the following thirty years cost the kings most of the land they had held in the plains.

The Gurkhas invaded early in 1790, crossing the Kali River, and the Chands were driven to the Bhabhar and finally expelled. Nepalese rule lasted twenty-four years. During the Anglo-Nepalese War Harak Deo Joshi, minister of the last Chand raja, sided with the British, who captured Almora on 26 April 1815; with the Treaty of Sugauli, ratified on 4 March 1816, Kumaon passed to British rule. Champawat, the first capital, keeps a medieval fort and the Baleshwar and Nagnath temples, and Chand kings also built temples at Bageshwar, Bhimtal and Almora.
chavundaraya: In his own writing Chavundaraya claims descent from the Brahmakshatriya line, Brahmins who had taken Kshatriya status. The 10th-century Algodu and Arani inscriptions name him as the grandson of Govindamayya and the son of Mabalayya, a subordinate of King Marasimha II; the family's political position under that king is believed to have led to its gradual adoption of Kshatriya status. He was a devotee of the Jain teachers Nemichandra and Ajitasena Bhattaraka, and a eulogy of him is inscribed on the Tyagada Brahmadeva Pillar at Shravanabelagola, whose base shows him with his guru Nemichandra.

The Western Gangas were feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, and as their commander Chavundaraya fought many battles for those overlords, beginning in the days of the Rashtrakuta king Khottiga Amoghavarsha. In the last years of Rashtrakuta rule the Gangas were threatened by civil war and by invasions of the Chola dynasty. When civil war broke out in 975 he supported Prince Rachamalla IV and installed him on the throne.

In the same year he suppressed a rebellion by Panchaldeva Mahasamanta, and in the battle of Bageyur he killed Mudurachayya, avenging the death of his own brother Nagavarma. His exploits earned him titles such as Samara Parashurama and Vira Martanda. He remained influential into the reign of Rachamalla V, who ruled from 986 to 999.

The Chavundaraya Purana, also known as the Trishashtishalaka Mahapurana, is the second oldest existing prose work in Kannada. It is based on two Sanskrit works, the Adipurana of Jinasena and the Uttarapurana of Gunabhadra, and tells the legends of sixty-three figures of Jain tradition: twenty-four tirthankaras, twelve chakravartis, nine balabhadras, nine narayanas and nine pratinarayanas. It was meant mainly for ordinary readers and avoided the complicated elements of Jain doctrine. He also wrote the Charitrasara in Sanskrit, and he patronised the Kannada grammarians Gunavarma and Nagavarma I and the poet Ranna.

The statue of Bahubali that he commissioned stands on the Indragiri hill, also called Vindhyagiri. Carved from fine-grained white granite, it is 60 feet tall, with a face measuring 6.5 feet, and has no support up to the thighs. The Chavundaraya basadi on the Chandragiri hill is credited to him by some scholars and to his son Jinadevana by others; another view holds that it was consecrated in the 11th century in his memory.
chinvat-bridge: The Avestan name, Cinvatô Peretûm, is rendered as bridge of judgement or as beam-shaped bridge; other forms of the name are Chinwad, Cinvat, Chinvar and Chinavat. How the bridge appears depends on the asha, the righteousness, of the soul that comes to it. Three divinities are thought to be its guardians: Sraosha, who stands for conscience, Mithra, for covenant, and Rashnu, for justice. Believers hold that the souls that cross successfully are united with Ahura Mazda. The Yasna describes the bridge in its 71st chapter and the Vendidad in its nineteenth fargard.

The bridge has often been identified with the rainbow or with the Milky Way, as in C. P. Tiele's History of Religion. Other scholars, among them C. F. Keary and Ferdinand Justi, reject this reading, citing descriptions of the bridge as rising straight upward and not in a curve.

Cyrus Niknam, a mobad and writer on ancient Iranian culture, denies that Zoroaster taught a bridge at all. In his reading the phrase in the hymns means a passage concerned with how to live, a questioning of the conscience, with no material crossing for the soul. He holds that the priests of the Sasanian era adapted beliefs about heaven, hell and the afterlife from other cultures that had reached Iran, and that the picture of a bridge wide for the righteous and thin as a hair for sinners belongs to that later development, as does the Book of Arda Viraf, and not to the Gathas.

The most notable of the Sogdian depictions is on the east wall of the funerary couch of the sabao Wirkak, excavated at Xi'an; a fragmentary one is on the couch in the Miho Museum. As-Sirat in Islam is a similar idea. In Yazidism the Silat Bridge at Lalish leads to the holiest Yazidi shrine, marks the passage from the profane world to the sacred, and is held to play a part at the end of times as well. In modern literature Charles Olson refers to the bridge in The Maximus Poems, and Dimitris Lyacos alludes to it in With the People from the Bridge.
chutia-people: The origin of the name Chutia is not known; the chronicles written in the Ahom language called the kingdom Tiora, while those in Assamese used Chutia. The historic Chutias are thought to have had some Shan admixture, and their ruling families are estimated to have been originally matrilineal or not entirely patrilineal. They worshipped a primordial male deity and a primordial female deity, Kechaikhati, whose worship was conducted by a priestly section identified today as the Deori people. The settlement of Brahmins in the kingdom led to the Hinduisation of its rulers, and inscriptions of the late 14th century suggest that the kings then followed the Vaishnava tradition.

After the annexation the capital region became a frontier province of the Ahom kingdom under an officer called the Sadiya-khowa Gohain, and the Chutia nobles were widely dispersed in Upper Assam. Those Chutias who had not been Hinduised were initiated in the 17th century into the Ekasarana dharma under the Mayamara Satra by Aniruddhadev. After the fall of the kingdom a new Hindu lineage was constructed, tracing the Chutias to the legendary King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha.

The community divided into several groups. The Hindu Chutias were a large section. The Ahom Chutias intermarried with the Ahoms, held high offices in the Ahom administration and were mostly absorbed. The Borahi Chutias had religious rites of their own, and the Miri Chutias fled to the Miri hills and intermarried with the Mishing. According to one chronicle, the Ahom court adopted muga silk by employing a thousand producers and weavers from the Chutia community.

Most Chutias live in Upper Assam, mostly in the interior on the banks of rivers, in villages of about 60 to 140 families. They generally live in joint families headed by the father, which at times exceeded one hundred members. Their original Tibeto-Burman language has disappeared; a British colonial officer of the 19th century wrongly identified it with the Deori language, but the Deori community is not related to the Chutias ethnically or linguistically.

Their rituals have a tribal and tantric base influenced by Hinduism and Vaishnavism. Those called Kesa-ponthi accept restrictions on meat and alcohol in their rites, while the Poka-ponthi keep the older customs. The Government of India recognises the Chutias as an Other Backward Class, and there is a political movement to include them in the list of scheduled tribes.
cudjoe: The name Cudjoe corresponds to the Akan day name Kojo or Kwadwo, given to a boy born on a Monday. The Leeward Maroons most likely emerged in 1690, when a Coromantee rebellion broke out on Sutton's estate in western Jamaica and most of the enslaved Africans there ran away into the mountainous interior. Cudjoe was probably the son of one of the leaders of that revolt. The oral history of the Accompong Town Maroons, as told by Milton McFarlane, holds that he was the freeborn son of Naquan, who led those who fled from the estate.

According to contemporary white enslavers, Cudjoe challenged a Madagascan for the leadership of the Leeward Maroons in 1720, and by defeating and killing him became their undisputed leader. His community was known as Cudjoe's Town, or Trelawny Town. For about half a century, until the treaties of 1739 and 1740, the Maroons operated outside direct British control.

During the First Maroon War of the 1730s the English colonial forces failed to win any significant victory over Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons. The agreement of 1739 recognised them as a semi-autonomous entity and freed their land from taxes. In the 1740s some Leeward Maroons who opposed the treaty rose in revolt, and Cudjoe crushed these risings.

Two descriptions of him survive from colonial writers. The physician R. C. Dallas, writing half a century after Cudjoe lived, claimed that he was short and stout, with a large lump of flesh on his back. The slaver Thomas Thistlewood, who met him in 1750, noted in his diary that he wore a feathered hat, with a sword at his side and a gun on his shoulder, barefoot and with "somewhat a Majestic look".

One source claims that Cudjoe died in 1744, but Edward Long and Thistlewood wrote of meeting him in the 1750s and 1760s. Long described him leading his Maroons in a martial performance at Montego Bay for Governor Sir William Lyttleton in 1764, and in the same year Thistlewood heard that he had been dead for some time. The treaty had named Accompong as his successor, but Governor Roger Hope Elletson had the Trelawny Town badge of authority given instead to a Maroon officer named Lewis, leaving Accompong authority over Accompong Town only. Cudjoe Day is celebrated in Jamaica on the first Monday in January.
dabhol: Dabhol, also written Dabul, is a small seaport town in the Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra. It lies on the northern and southern sides of the Vashishti River, which also flows by the town of Chiplun. Under the Bahmani dynasty the port was known as Mustafabad and later as Hamjabad before it took its present name. From the 14th to the 16th century it was the principal port of the southern Konkan, trading with ports of the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

The Russian traveller Afanasy Nikitin, who visited India from 1468 to 1474, found Dabhol a large town and extensive seaport, to which horses from Mysore, Arabia and Khorasan were brought for sale, and which had links with all the major ports from India to Ethiopia. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was an opulent Muslim trading centre, first under the Bahmani sultans and later under those of Bijapur. It was the port with the most convenient access to the Bahmani capital at Bidar, and its fortunes rose with that dynasty; at its height it was arguably the most important port between Chaul and Goa.

That prominence made it a target. In December 1508 a Portuguese expeditionary force under Francisco de Almeida bombarded, sacked and razed the town in the Battle of Dabul, a prelude to the Battle of Diu, though the fort was not taken. The Portuguese tried several more times over the following decades to destroy it; at the last recorded attack, in 1571, the governor was Khwaja Ali Shirazi, and 150 men were killed at Dabhol.

The break-up of the Bahmani state into smaller Deccan sultanates hastened the port's decline. As new capitals were built its position was no longer so favourable, and during the 16th century much commerce moved south to the rising port of Rajapur. Shivaji conquered Dabhol around 1660 and annexed it to the new Maratha kingdom. It passed to Sambhaji, who gave it to Khando Ballal Chitnis as a reward for saving him from drowning in a river in Goa.

The Dabhol vatan is still claimed by descendants of the Chitnis family of Satara, although some descendants of the Shirke family argue that it should be theirs. On the southern side of the town, between the villages of Veldur and Ranavi, stands the Dabhol LNG power plant, which was set up by the company Enron.
dakshinapatha: The name joins two Sanskrit words, dakshina, south, and patha, road. The later Vedic texts divide the Indian subcontinent into three parts: Aryavarta in the north, Madhya Desha in the centre and Dakshinapatha in the south. The Aitareya Brahmana, of the first half of the first millennium BCE, names peoples of the south of Vindhyan and north Deccan origin, among them the Satvants, Vidarbha, Andhra, Nishadas and Kuntis. The grammarian Panini, about 500 BCE, mentions the Asmaka Kingdom in connection with the south and with Kalinga.

The term has carried three meanings. It can denote the ancient south of the subcontinent below Uttarapatha, usually the Deccan and sometimes Tamilakam and Ceylon as well. It can mean the great southern highway, running from Magadha to Pratishthana. It has also been used for a kingdom on the Godavari River. The Junagarh rock inscription of 150 CE, set up by an Indo-Scythian king, records that he twice defeated Satakarni, the lord of Dakshinapatha, in fair fight and did not destroy him because of the nearness of their connection.

The southern road was one of two great highways that have linked the parts of the subcontinent since the Iron Age. The other, the Uttarapatha or great northern road, ran from Taxila through the Punjab to the Yamuna and followed that river south to Mathura; from there a route went on to Ujjain in Malwa and to Broach on the western coast. According to the writer Sanjeev Sanyal, the course of the northern road has stayed roughly the same since before the Mauryas, while the southern road appears to have drifted.

The route of Rama into exile in the epic may reflect an early version of it. By the time of the Buddha it started at Varanasi and ran through Vidisha in central India to Pratishthana, now Paithan, and it probably extended to the Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms of the far south. By the Mauryan period there would have been a branch from Ujjain to the ports of Gujarat, which made Ujjain a major city by the Gupta era. The modern highway that roughly corresponds to it runs much further east than the old road but still meets the northern road at Varanasi.
dara-shikoh: Muhammad Dara Shikoh was born at Ajmer on 20 March 1615, the first son and third child of Prince Khurram, the later Shah Jahan, and Mumtaz Mahal. He studied the Quran, history, Persian poetry and calligraphy, and beside his native Persian learned Hindi, Arabic and later Sanskrit. He and his elder sister Jahanara Begum were their father's favourite children.

On 1 February 1633 he married his half-cousin Nadira Banu Begum at Agra, and he contracted no other marriage. In the same year he was appointed heir apparent, which Shah Jahan formally confirmed on 10 September 1642 with the title Shahzada-e-Buland Iqbal, Prince of High Fortune. He was made governor of Allahabad in 1645 and of Gujarat in 1648.

Dara followed the Qadiri Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore, to whom Mullah Shah Badakhshi introduced him, and the mystic Sarmad Kashani, and he formed a friendship with the seventh Sikh Guru, Guru Har Rai. The treatise known as Majma-ul-Bahrain was written in Persian in 1654–55. His Persian version of fifty Upanishads, completed in 1657 and often called Sirr-i-Akbar, proposes in its introduction that the hidden book named in the Quran is the Upanishads. Annemarie Schimmel notes that he remained committed to the fundamentals of Islam and repeatedly called himself a Hanafi Qadiri.

He was a patron of painting, music and dancing, tastes that Aurangzeb frowned upon. The album of paintings and calligraphy that bears his name was presented to his wife in 1641–42; after her death the inscriptions linking it to him were deliberately erased.

After Samugarh he retreated by Delhi, Lahore, Multan and Thatta to Kathiawar, where Shah Nawaz Khan, governor of Gujarat, helped him raise a new army. After the rout at Deorai on 11 March 1659 he sought refuge in Sindh with the Afghan chieftain Malik Jeevan, whose life he had saved more than once, but Malik Jeevan seized him and informed Aurangzeb, whose army took him on 10 June 1659.

In Delhi he was paraded through the streets in chains on an elephant. A convocation of nobles and clergy called by Aurangzeb declared him a threat to the public peace and an apostate from Islam, and he was killed in front of his son on the night of 30 August 1659. He was buried in an unidentified grave in Humayun's tomb. In 2020 Sanjeev Kumar Singh, a municipal engineer, identified one of three unmarked cenotaphs beneath the dome as his, relying on the Alamgirnama; several historians and archaeologists have accepted the identification.
dean-barrow: Dean Oliver Barrow was born on 2 March 1951 in Belize City, then in British Honduras, where he grew up. He attended St. Michael's College in Belize, took a law degree at the University of the West Indies at Cave Hill in Barbados in 1973 and a Certificate of Legal Education at the Norman Manley Law School in Jamaica in 1975, and later studied at the University of Miami.

He entered the legal profession in 1974, working with his maternal uncle Dean Lindo, and became a partner in Lindo's firm in 1977. He later founded his own firm, Barrow and Williams, with Rodwell Williams. Among its more controversial clients were Lord Ashcroft and his associated businesses, including Belize Bank and Belize Telemedia Limited.

Barrow entered electoral politics in December 1983, winning a seat on the Belize City council as one of a slate of nine. In 1984 he stood for the newly created Queen's Square constituency, defeated Ralph Fonseca of the People's United Party and joined the first cabinet of Manuel Esquivel as attorney-general and minister of foreign affairs. He held his seat in 1989, when his party lost power, and became deputy leader in 1990 after the death of Curl Thompson. Back in government in 1993, he added the ministry of national security to his former posts; his detractors called him Minister of Everything.

In the heavy defeat of 1998 he was one of only three party candidates to win, and he replaced the defeated Esquivel as party leader and Leader of the Opposition. The general election of 7 February 2008 gave his party 25 of 31 seats, and he was sworn in the next day as the country's first black prime minister, serving also as minister of finance. He won a reduced majority in 2012 and a third consecutive victory in November 2015, which he said would be his last election as leader.

Citing his health, he at first intended to step down by the end of 2019, but on 18 November 2018 his cabinet urged him to stay until the general election of 2020, and he agreed. He did not contest Queen's Square in that election and endorsed his sister, Denise Barrow, to succeed him. He has returned to private practice as head of litigation at Barrow and Williams. His eldest son, Moses Michael Levi Barrow, a former rapper under the name Shyne, was elected to the House of Representatives in 2020 and later became leader of the party and of the opposition.
deeg: Deeg lies in the Deeg district of eastern Rajasthan, about 32 km from the city of Bharatpur, at an average elevation of 174 m. Its nearness to Agra gave it a part in the politics of the region. Deeg Fort is square in plan and stands on slightly raised ground; its walls of rubble and mud are strengthened by twelve towers, the largest of which, the Lakha-Burj, is at the north-west corner. The towers carried cannon. A wide, shallow moat surrounds the fort, crossed by a bridge on the northern side that leads to the only gate.

After acquiring the throne, the Jat ruler Maharaja Badan Singh chose Deeg as his stronghold and capital and began the building of a palace there, so that Deeg became the first capital of the Jats of Bharatpur. The town was almost constantly under threat of Mughal invasion, and his son Maharaja Suraj Mal ordered a fortress built to protect the palace. In 1804 both the Battle of Deeg and the Siege of Deeg set the British East India Company against Bharatpur's Jat rulers and their Maratha allies.

The palace complex served the Jat Maharajas as a summer retreat. It consists of several palaces called Bhawans set among charbaghs and water gardens, among them the Gopal Bhawan, the Kishan Bhawan, the Nand Bhawan, the Keshav Bhawan, the Hardev Bhawan, the Suraj Bhawan and the twin pavilions of Sawan and Bhadon.

The palace was in use until the early 1970s and now holds a museum. Its 900 fountains are run twice a year, at the Braj Holi festival in February or March and at a festival in September, and a fair named after Maharaja Jawahar Singh is held each year around September. Inside the fort a partly ruined palace, or haveli, of red sandstone is the principal building; parts of it were rebuilt in the 20th century. The 2011 Indian census counted 44,999 inhabitants.
diego-silang: Diego Silang y Andaya was born on 16 December 1730 in Aringay, then part of Pangasinan and now in La Union. His father was Pangasinense and his mother Ilocano. He was baptised on 7 January 1731 in Vigan, in the then undivided province of Ilocos, where as a boy he worked as a messenger for a local Castilian priest. Fluent in Spanish, he carried correspondence from the Ilocos to Manila, journeys on which he first saw the injustices of colonial rule.

Spain was allied with France in the Seven Years' War, and the British seizure of Manila in October 1762 inspired risings in the far north of Luzon. Silang at first wanted to replace Spanish functionaries in the Ilocos with native-born officials and offered to lead Ilocano forces on the Spanish side. The Spanish administrators instead transferred their powers to the Catholic Bishop of Nueva Segovia, who rejected the offer. The revolt drew on grievances over Spanish taxation and abuses and on Silang's belief that church and government in the Ilocos should be led by trained Ilocano officials.

Joaquín Martínez de Zúñiga, writing in 1805, gave a hostile account. He called Silang very quick and artful and said he persuaded the chiefs and many commoners, especially those of Vigan, that to keep the Catholic faith they must arm against the Spaniards and deliver them to the English. Armed men demanded that the alcalde give up his staff of government to the vicar-general; he did so and escaped from the province. The rebels then demanded of the bishop-elect, a Dominican named Ustariz, an exemption from the tribute, while Silang gathered troops for wider operations.

Silang was killed on 28 May 1763, aged 32, by a friend, a Spanish-Ilocano mestizo named Miguel Vicos, whom church authorities had paid and who was helped by Pedro Becbec. Gabriela Silang was forced to retreat to what is now Abra, led her troops towards Vigan and was driven back; she and her men were hanged on 20 September 1763, she last of all. The Philippine Navy has named two frigates after Diego Silang, one in service from 1976 to 1990 and one that entered service in 2025.
du-yuesheng: Du was born on 22 August 1888 in Gaoqiao, and his family moved to Shanghai the next year. By the age of nine he had lost his immediate family: his mother died in childbirth, his sister was sold into slavery, his father died and his stepmother vanished. He returned to Shanghai in 1902, worked at a fruit stall in the French Concession until he was dismissed for theft, and became a bodyguard in a brothel, and joined the Green Gang at 16. A friend introduced him to Huang Jinrong, the highest-ranking Chinese detective in the French Concession Police, for whom he became an enforcer in gambling and opium.

His rise came after Huang's arrest in 1924 for beating the son of Lu Yongxiang, the tuchun then ruling Shanghai: Du's diplomacy and money freed his mentor, and Du, Huang and Zhang Xiaolin became sworn brothers, known as the Three Tycoons of Shanghai. In April 1927 the three formed with Chiang Kai-shek the Chinese Progress Association. On the night of 11 April Du's lieutenant Wan Molin killed the labour leader Wang Shouhua at Du's house, and gang members wearing armbands marked Labor attacked workers and left-wing activists. Chiang rewarded him with the rank of major general and advisory posts.

From 1928 he moved into finance, founding the Zhonghui Bank and becoming a director of the Bank of China and the Bank of Communications. In 1931 he opened a temple to his ancestors; within months its private wings housed a heroin factory. When war with Japan broke out in 1937 he refused to cooperate with the Japanese, unlike Zhang Xiaolin, and went to Hong Kong, while Green Gang men working with Chiang's intelligence chief Dai Li smuggled weapons and goods to the Nationalist forces.

After the war he returned to Shanghai and founded the newspaper Shang Pao. He hoped to become mayor but gave way under pressure from Chiang, and in 1948 his son Du Weiping was sentenced to six months in an anti-corruption campaign led by Chiang Ching-kuo. In April 1949 he moved to Hong Kong, declining approaches from both the Kuomintang and the Communists. His health failed through asthma, and he died on 16 August 1951. He was buried in Xizhi in Taiwan, where the authorities raised a statue of him, though some doubt that the tomb holds his body.
durrani-empire: Ahmad Khan, of the Sadozai lineage of the Abdali tribe, was the son of Muhammad Zaman Khan, who had served as governor of Herat, and a commander under Nader Shah. After Nader Shah's death in June 1747 a loya jirga, or grand council, met near Kandahar for nine days. The two chief contestants were Hajji Jamal Khan of the Mohammadzai and Ahmad Khan. A holy man, Mohammad Sabir Khan, spoke for Ahmad Khan, reputedly placed sheaves of wheat or barley in his turban and crowned him with the title Durr-i-Durran, Pearl of the Pearls, from which the tribe took the name Durrani.

Ahmad Shah took Qalati Ghilji and Ghazni from the Ghilji and Kabul and Peshawar from the Mughal governor Nasir Khan. In 1749 the Mughal emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur ceded Sindh and the Punjab to save his capital, and Ahmad Shah then took Mashhad from Shahrukh Afshar and subdued the peoples north of the Hindu Kush. He sacked Delhi in 1757. In 1762 his forces killed thousands of Sikhs in the Punjab, in what Sikhs call the Vaḍḍā Ghallūghārā, and destroyed the Golden Temple at Amritsar, yet the Sikhs rebuilt it and he never subdued them. He died east of Kandahar in 1772.

His son Timur Shah Durrani took the throne in November 1772 and made Kabul the capital. Timur's sons fought one another: Zaman Shah, who succeeded in 1793, was blinded and replaced by Mahmud Shah in 1801, and Shuja Shah ruled from 1803 to 1809. On 7 June 1809 Shuja signed with the British East India Company the first Afghan pact with a European power. By 1818 the Sadozai rulers held little more than Kabul and the land within 160 kilometres of it. Kashmir was lost to the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Shopian in 1819, and Ayub Shah was deposed in 1823.

The army was based on cavalry armed with flintlocks, who made hit-and-run attacks. Its core was 10,000 mounted ghulams, or slave-soldiers, carrying blunderbusses; a third of them were Qizilbash who had served Nader Shah. The bulk of the army was irregular Afghan tribal cavalry armed with lance and broadsword, and infantry played a very small part. Ahmad Shah balanced tribal alliances and hostilities, a balance his successors upset when they tried to rule without the other Durrani chiefs. The Barakzai under Dost Muhammad Khan later displaced the dynasty at Kabul, and the empire is regarded as the foundation of the modern Afghan state.
east-indies: European exploration of the region began in the last three years of the 15th century and continued into the 16th, led by Portuguese explorers after the Cape Route had been found. The Portuguese called the whole region they reached the Indies. Christopher Columbus, who had grossly underestimated the westward distance from Europe to Asia, at first took the New World for the easternmost part of the Indies. To avoid confusion the Americas came to be called the West Indies, also the New Indies or Little Indies, and the original Indies the East Indies, also the Old Indies or Great Indies.

The term has had a broad and a narrow sense. In the Age of Discovery it covered the coasts of the Indian subcontinent and the Indochinese Peninsula together with the Malay Archipelago. In the narrow sense it meant the Malay Archipelago alone, which today comprises the Indonesian Archipelago, New Guinea and the Philippine Archipelago. The former Dutch New Guinea, however, is geographically counted as part of Melanesia and is not included.

Parts of the region are sometimes named after the colonial empire that held them. The Spanish East Indies, the Philippines, were Spanish territory for 333 years before the American conquest and later independence. The Dutch East Indies kept that name for about 300 years until Indonesian independence, and British East Indies refers to Malaysia. The term may also take in the former French Indochina, the former British territories of Brunei, Hong Kong and Singapore, and the former Portuguese Macau and Timor.

The peoples of the region are culturally very diverse and do not consider themselves a single ethnic group. Most are Austronesians, whose ancestors first expanded from the island of Taiwan. In the early modern period Han Chinese began to migrate south and became known as the Peranakans or Straits Chinese. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism are the most widespread religions.

After the founding of European trading companies in the 17th century, among them the British East India Company and the Dutch East India Company, the Indies were important sources of trade goods, particularly cotton, indigo and spices. The name East Indian was once applied to people of all the East Indies, to keep them apart from the indigenous peoples of the Americas, who were then simply called Indians. In colonial times South-East Asians who were not from India were also called Indians. Today the inhabitants of the region are not called East Indians.
east-karelia: East Karelia, also called Eastern or Russian Karelia, is the part of Karelia beyond the eastern border of Finland which, since the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, has remained Eastern Orthodox and a part of Russia. It is distinguished from the western part, Finnish Karelia, which before 1808 was Swedish Karelia. It consists mainly of two old historical regions, Viena or White Karelia and Aunus or Olonets Karelia.

The Fennomans, ethnic nationalists of the 19th century, saw East Karelia as the ancient home of Finnic culture, untouched by Scandinavians or Slavs. In its sparsely populated backwoods, mainly in White Karelia, Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884) collected the folk tales that became the Kalevala, published from 1835 to 1849. The idea of joining the region to a Greater Finland had wide support in newly independent Finland after 1917.

When Finland and Soviet Russia divided Karelia between them in 1920, the Soviet authorities promised far-reaching cultural rights to the Finnic peoples who made up most of East Karelia's population. Within the Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic these rights were never realised, and under Stalin ethnic Finns were persecuted and an intensive programme of Russification began.

Annexation was most popular during the Continuation War of 1941–1944, when an expected German conquest of the Soviet Union made it seem feasible. Finnish forces occupied most of East Karelia from 1941 to 1944, and the war brought hardship to the local ethnic Russian civilians, including forced labour and internment in prison camps as enemy aliens. After the Moscow Armistice of September 1944 calls for annexation virtually disappeared.

Most of East Karelia is now part of the Republic of Karelia within the Russian Federation. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Finnic culture in the region has experienced a revival. In Finnish the region is called Itä-Karjala or Venäjän Karjala, and in Karelian Idä-Karjala.
ecomog: The members of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) agreed a Protocol on Mutual Defence Assistance at Freetown on 29 May 1981, which provided for an allied armed force when needed. ECOMOG itself was created by the Standing Mediation Committee at its meeting in Banjul on 6 and 7 August 1990. The Nigerian scholar Adekeye Adebajo has written that this body stood on shaky legal foundations, that the guidelines of the defence protocol were not followed, and that the force was justified largely on humanitarian grounds.

It was the English-speaking members of ECOWAS that acted, intervening in the Liberian civil war that had begun in 1989. Several French-speaking members strongly opposed the deployment, and the leaders of Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire supported Charles Taylor in his attempt to depose Samuel Doe.

Unlike the usual United Nations mission of the time, the force had to fight its way into a many-sided civil war to hold the factions apart. Most of its men and resources came from the Nigerian Armed Forces, with smaller units from Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone, The Gambia and others. Its first commander was the Ghanaian Lieutenant General Arnold Quainoo; after Samuel Doe was killed by Prince Johnson's Independent National Patriotic Front of Liberia on 9 September 1990, Major General Joshua Dogonyaro took over, the first of an unbroken line of Nigerian commanders.

Senegal sent 1,500 soldiers with some financial support from the United States, but withdrew them all by mid-January 1993, after six were killed in a confrontation with Taylor's supporters at Vahun on 28 May 1992. Corruption and organised looting by its troops led some Liberians to read the acronym as Every Car or Movable Object Gone. After Taylor was elected president on 19 July 1997, the last field commander, General Timothy Shelpidi, withdrew the force fully by the end of 1998.

Within Africa the force was the first credible attempt at a regional security initiative since the Organisation of African Unity tried to send an Inter-African Force to Chad in 1981. A deployment of 1,700 men planned in 2001 for the border between Guinea and Liberia never took place, for lack of funds and because of fighting in Liberia. In 2003, under pressure from the United States, ECOWAS launched a similar mission, ECOMIL, to halt the rebel occupation of Monrovia during the Second Liberian Civil War; it was soon succeeded by the United Nations mission UNMIL.
esen-taishi: Esen was the son of Toghon, the Oirat taishi, of the Choros clan. The title, derived from a Chinese term, was the highest rank among the Mongols below that of khan, which Toghon could not hold because he was not of the lineage of Genghis Khan. In the 1420s Esen led three successful campaigns against Eastern Moghulistan, twice capturing its ruler Uwais Khan. In the 1430s he fought beside his father against the Khalkha taishi Arughtai, who died in 1434. Toghon then installed Taisun as a puppet Great Khan of the Northern Yuan and married him to Esen's elder sister.

After Toghon died in 1438 Esen inherited his title. In 1443 and again in 1445 Oirats attacked Hami, an oasis that acknowledged Ming suzerainty, and its prince came to the Oirat camp in 1448. In 1445 Esen forced the leaders of the Shazhou and Qizhin guards in western Gansu to accept Mongol titles. By 1447 he had conquered two of the three Uriankhai guards and driven the third to migrate, giving him control from present-day Xinjiang to Korea.

Oirat tributary missions to Beijing, in fact commercial, grew from around a hundred men to more than two thousand. In 1448 a mission falsely claimed over three thousand members and was granted one fifth of the gifts it demanded; the court then rejected a marriage between Esen's son and the imperial family that Chinese interpreters had promised without authority. In July 1449 Esen invaded. Emperor Yingzong of Ming led an army reportedly of half a million men, which was massacred at the Tumu postal station on 1 September. Esen besieged Beijing from 27 to 30 October but withdrew, and in September 1450 the emperor was taken back to China.

Esen and Taisun fell out over the choice of Taisun's successor. Taisun allied with the Ming and with Esen's subordinate Alag, but his brother Agbarjin defected to the Oirats in the winter of 1451. Esen defeated Taisun, who fled and was killed by a local chieftain in early 1452. Esen proclaimed Agbarjin khan and soon murdered him. In a letter of 1453 to the Ming court he styled himself Tian-sheng Khagan of the Great Yuan.

Chinese accounts attribute the revolt against him to his lavish living and heavy drinking. He had also refused the title of taishi to Alag, granting it to his own son Amasanj. Esen was defeated and was killed by a man named Bukun, whose father he had ordered put to death, and the Oirat state collapsed.
finnish-war: After concluding the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon in 1807, Emperor Alexander I of Russia wrote on 24 September 1807 to King Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden that peace between them depended on Sweden accepting the treaty's limits, which in practice meant cutting off trade with Britain. The king, who viewed Napoleon as the Antichrist, secured an alliance with Britain on 8 February 1808. In Saint Petersburg his stubbornness was seen as a convenient pretext for occupying Finland. Swedish plans assumed that war in winter was impossible, while Russian planners chose a winter offensive, when frozen seas would isolate Finland.
