On 21 February 1808, 24,000 Russian troops under Friedrich Wilhelm von Buxhoeveden crossed the border and took Loviisa; war was not declared until April. Helsinki fell on 2 March and Turku on 21 March, as the Swedish army under General Wilhelm Mauritz Klingspor withdrew northwards. Sveaborg, with a garrison of 6,000 men and over 700 cannons, surrendered on 6 May 1808 after prolonged negotiations, its commander Admiral Carl Olof Cronstedt believing resistance futile, and the Russians gained most of the Swedish archipelago fleet intact. Swedish counter-attacks at Siikajoki and Revolax halted the offensive for a time, and Finns rose in guerrilla fighting.

Reinforced to 55,000 men against an estimated 36,000, the Russians attacked again in August, and Count Nikolay Kamensky won the most important victory at Oravais on 14 September. By November 1808 Russian forces had overrun all of Finland, and the Convention of Olkijoki of 19 November obliged the Swedish army to leave. In March 1809 Russian columns crossed the frozen Gulf of Bothnia, occupying the Åland Islands and entering Umeå on 24 March. King Gustav IV, blamed for the loss of Finland, was dethroned by a coup in Stockholm on 13 March, and his uncle became Charles XIII of Sweden.

By the Treaty of Fredrikshamn of 17 September 1809 Sweden also gave up its domains east of the Torne river. The Grand Duchy of Finland kept the Gustavian constitution of 1772 with only slight modifications until 1919, and in 1812 Russia attached to it the areas it had gained from Sweden in the 18th century, known as Old Finland. In Sweden the war was followed by a new constitution and, in 1818, by the establishment of the House of Bernadotte. Two studies of 2015 by the political scientists Jan Teorell and Bo Rothstein argue that the defeat moved Swedish elites to reform the bureaucracy.
francisco-del-rosario-sanchez: Sánchez was born in Santo Domingo on 9 March 1817. His mother, Olaya del Rosario Belén, was a free woman of colour; his father, Narciso Sánchez Ramona, a descendant of slaves, worked in the cattle and meat trade. The parents married only in 1819, which is why he bore his mother's surname before his father's. He was taught first by his mother and then by the Peruvian priest Gaspar Hernández. Juan Pablo Duarte, a classmate, recruited him to La Trinitaria, founded in 1838.

When Duarte and others left the country on 2 August 1843 to escape Haitian persecution, Sánchez, who was ill, stayed behind in hiding and took over the leadership of the movement. On the night of 27 February 1844 his men took the Ozama Fortress, and at the Puerta del Conde, after Matías Ramón Mella fired his blunderbuss, he raised the flag. He presided over the Central Government Board, and assured freed people who had mutinied under Santiago Basora that slavery would not return.

Pedro Santana marched on Santo Domingo and on 12 July 1844 drove the Trinitarios from the board. On 22 August Duarte, Sánchez and Mella were declared traitors and deported for life. He lived as a teacher in Curaçao until an amnesty granted by President Manuel Jimenes in 1848. Back home, he sided with Buenaventura Báez against Santana, was exiled again to Curaçao, returned in August 1856 and became governor of the province of Santo Domingo, and in 1859 was banished a third time, to Saint Thomas.

In 1861 Sánchez formed the Dominican Revolutionary Board and obtained from the Haitian president Fabre Geffrard passage through Haitian territory and weapons for a force of 500 men. He entered through Hondo Valle on 1 June 1861. When Haiti withdrew its support under threat from a Spanish squadron at Port-au-Prince, the expedition turned back. On 20 June Sánchez was ambushed near Hondo Valle by Santiago de Óleo, a former ally, wounded in the leg and groin, and captured.

A war council at San Juan under General Domingo Lazala tried the prisoners; Sánchez, conducting his own defence, asked that he alone be condemned. He was shot at San Juan de la Maguana on 4 July 1861 with some twenty companions, some of whom were finished off with machetes and clubs. Spain withdrew from the country in 1865. Dominicans honour him with Duarte and Mella as a founder of the republic, and the Order of Merit of Duarte, Sánchez and Mella bears his name.
gadadhar-singha: Born Gadapani Konwar, and known by the Ahom name Supatphaa, he was the son of Gobar Roja, a descendant of the king Suhungmung. The minister Debera Borbarua made Gobar king in 1675; he reigned only twenty days and was executed after Debera's fall. In 1679 Laluk Sola Borphukan had the minister Atan Burhagohain murdered, installed Sulikphaa, called Lora Roja, as king and began to hunt down the Ahom princes eligible for the throne.

To escape, Gadapani became a fugitive in the Naga hills, perhaps near the present-day Mon district, among the Konyak Naga. During this time his wife Joymoti Konwari was tortured and killed by the henchmen of Sulikphaa and Laluk Sola Borphukan. Little is known of his two years in exile, though the hills are rich in lore and legend about him.

He was formally crowned in March 1682, and bound the leading nobles to himself by marrying their daughters. His first act was to equip an army against the Mughals at Guwahati: the forts at Bansbari and Kajali fell at the first assault, and a naval victory near the mouth of the Bar Nadi delivered the whole enemy fleet to the Ahoms. The campaign ended eighty years of Ahom–Mughal conflict. He also stopped Naga raids on the border villages, partly through marriage alliances with Naga chiefs.

He built roads, among them the Dhodar Ali, 211 km long from Kamargaon to Joypur, and two stone bridges, and had a number of tanks dug. The earliest known copper plates recording grants of land by Ahom kings to Brahmins or Hindu temples date from his reign. Having met the Mughal system of land measurement while hiding in Lower Assam, he brought surveyors from Koch Bihar and Bengal; the survey began in Sivasagar and was completed only after his death.

He died in February 1696 after a reign of fourteen and a half years, leaving two sons, Lai and Lechai. Lai succeeded him under the Hindu name Rudra Singha, and under him the Ahom kingdom reached its zenith; the Tungkhungia house ruled until the end of the kingdom in 1826. Gadadhar Singha was buried at Charaideo. The American Baptist missionary Nathan Brown, who saw the royal tombs there dug open, reckoned his about ninety feet high and so natural in appearance that a stranger would have taken it for an ordinary hill.
ganapati-kakatiya: Ganapati's father Mahadeva was killed in a conflict with the Seuna, or Yadava, kingdom in 1198–1199, and Ganapati himself was taken captive. During his captivity the kingdom suffered revolts and invasions, and the commander-in-chief Rudra of the Recherla Reddi family appears to have governed in his name. An inscription at Manthena dated 26 December 1199 calls Ganapati the establisher of all the kingdom, which suggests that he had been freed by then. Yadava inscriptions claim that their king Jaitrapala released him out of compassion; the Yadavas may rather have wanted a quiet eastern border while they fought the Hoysalas.

Helped by the decline of the Kalyani Chalukya and Chola empires, Ganapati first turned to coastal Andhra, which the Kakatiyas had lost. The Krishna delta was conquered by 1201, and his general Chaunda plundered the island of Divi, whose Ayya chiefs submitted; Ganapati married two daughters of their chief, and their brother Jayapa became his commander. The Velanati Choda ruler Prithvishvara probably died fighting the Kakatiyas about 1206, and by 1209 Vela-nadu and Kamma-nadu were annexed. At Nellore Ganapati installed the Telugu Choda chief Tikka on the throne.

Repeated campaigns in Kalinga and Vengi from 1212 against the Eastern Ganga kings Ananga Bhima III and Narasimha I had mixed results, and Kakatiya control was probably limited to the land south of the Godavari River. In 1250 an army under Samanta Bhoja won a decisive victory at Palaiyaru and restored Tikka's son Manuma-siddhi II at Nellore. Around 1257, however, the Pandya king Jatavarman Sundara I attacked; the Pandyas captured Nellore and killed Manuma-siddhi II at the Battle of Muttukuru in 1263.

Ganapati continued the removal of the capital from Anumakonda to Orugallu, where he built a fortification of 75 bastions, each protected by a nayaka, comprising a stone fort and a mud fort one within the other. He also subdued the petty chiefs who had been harassing foreign merchants at the port of Motupalli.

Ganapati apparently retired after his defeats by the Pandyas in the late 1250s. He had no male heir and two daughters, Rudrama-devi, married to the Vengi Chalukya prince Virabhadra, and Ganapama-devi. Rudrama began to rule as co-regent in 1259–1260 under the regnal name Rudra-deva Maharaja, though an inscription at Duggi shows that Ganapati was alive at least until 1269. The 17th-century Pratapa-charita says that two sons of his by junior queens, Hari-hara and Murari-deva, rebelled against her; no other source knows these sons. Inscriptions listing distant kings as his vassals follow literary convention and can be dismissed.
george-i-of-greece: He was born Prince William of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Glücksburg on 24 December 1845 at the Yellow Palace in Copenhagen, the second son of Prince Christian and Princess Louise of Hesse-Kassel. The family was relatively obscure until 1852, when his father was designated heir to the childless Frederick VII of Denmark. William entered the Royal Danish Navy as a cadet.

After the expulsion of Otto in October 1862 the Greeks held a plebiscite in which Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, a son of Queen Victoria, received over 95 per cent of the 240,000 votes; William received six. The ruling families of the great powers were barred from the Greek crown, and the choice fell on the Danish prince. The Greek National Assembly elected him unanimously on 30 March 1863.

George reached Athens on 30 October 1863, learned Greek quickly and was often seen informally in the streets. He sent home Danish advisers who had become unpopular, and in October 1864 pressed the Assembly to finish its work; on 28 November he swore to a constitution that created a single chamber, the Vouli, elected by direct, secret, universal male suffrage. Governments were short-lived: 21 between 1864 and 1874. After Charilaos Trikoupis blamed the king in a newspaper article for imposing minority governments, George declared in 1875 that the leader of the parliamentary majority would in future be appointed prime minister.

Trikoupis and Theodoros Deligiannis alternated in office between 1882 and 1897. In 1896 the king presided over the opening of the revived Olympic Games in Athens. A revolt in Crete led in 1897 to a war with the Ottoman Empire that was lost by the end of April; Greece paid an indemnity of 4 million Turkish pounds and Crete passed to international administration. George considered abdication, but regained esteem after he and his daughter Maria survived an attack by two riflemen on 27 February 1898.

In August 1909 a league of army officers demanded that the royal family lose their military commissions and attempted a coup. George gave way to calls for a revising assembly, and Eleftherios Venizelos became prime minister in 1910. King and minister agreed on rebuilding the army, which entered Thessaloniki on 9 November 1912 under Crown Prince Constantine. On 18 March 1913, walking near the White Tower without meaningful protection, George was shot in the back by Alexandros Schinas and died at once. Schinas fell to his death from a police station window six weeks later. The dynasty he founded reigned, with breaks, until the monarchy was abolished in 1973.
germania: Roman geographers placed Germania roughly between the Rhine in the west and the Vistula in the east, from the upper Danube northwards along the North and Baltic seas to the known parts of southern Scandinavia. The free lands are also called Magna Germania, and by modern scholars Germania Libera or the Germanic Barbaricum. The origin of the name Germani is uncertain. Tacitus wrote that the name had once belonged only to the Tungri, west of the Rhine, and was later extended to supposedly related peoples beyond it.

The country held many peoples with little unity among them, and river names suggest that another Indo-European group lived there, probably under Germanic domination. Archaeologically it corresponds, from the 1st to the 4th century CE, to the Roman Iron Age: largely agrarian, without cities or coinage of its own. Amber was a primary export, and Roman luxury goods were imported on a large scale and have been found as far away as Scandinavia and western Russia.

Julius Caesar met peoples from beyond the Rhine during the Gallic Wars and called their homeland Germania, a name the Romans appear to have borrowed from the Gauls. Augustus later carried Roman arms as far as the Elbe and in 7 BCE created a short-lived province, Germania Antiqua, before the victory of Arminius ended the attempt. The Rhine became the frontier. Germani such as the Ubii and Sicambri were settled on the Roman bank, which was heavily affected by the Revolt of the Batavi under Gaius Julius Civilis in 69–70 CE.

Under the Flavian dynasty the two provinces were organised, Germania Inferior with its headquarters at Colonia, the modern Cologne, and Germania Superior at Mogontiacum. The Romans also occupied the land between the Rhine, Main and Danube, known as the Agri Decumates. In the 3rd century confederations such as the Alemanni and Franks emerged and raided the provinces, and around 280 CE the Agri Decumates were evacuated and taken by the Alemanni. In 406 a large number of people fleeing the Huns crossed the Rhine, and Roman rule there eventually collapsed.

Much of Germania, including all the former Roman provinces, was eventually incorporated into the Frankish Empire and later East Francia. The name survived in learned use: it is attested in Old English translations of Bede and Orosius, and since the 17th century the usual English name of Germany has been derived from it, as are the names of that country in many other languages.
giovanni-giustiniani-longo: Giustiniani, born in 1418, belonged to the House of Giustiniani and was probably a native of Chios. That he lived as a mercenary suggests he was not the first-born son of his family. He left no testimony of his reasons for going to Constantinople. Reportedly Emperor Constantine XI promised him sovereignty over the island of Lemnos in case of victory.

Constantine XI gave him the rank of protostrator. Why he in particular was chosen is unclear; one explanation offered is that the emperor distrusted the city's large and discontented Venetian population and preferred a Genoese. Giustiniani trained the recruits, strengthened the fortifications and brought back men who had fled to monasteries to escape military duty. Drawing on the siege of 1422, he concentrated the defence on the outer walls. Some 8,000 to 9,000 people were available to defend the city, and his own post was at the lowest-lying section of the walls, between the gates of St. Romanos and Charisius.

After Sultan Mehmed II arrived on 6 April, Giustiniani led sorties that destroyed Ottoman troops, siege works and artillery, until their cost in lives caused them to be given up. Against the Ottoman guns, which included a cannon 6 metres long, he had the walls covered with soft surfaces and the breaches filled with debris, into which the cannonballs sank. On 18 April his men repelled the first assault, by Janissaries and archers at a narrow breach, after four hours.

In the final assault of 29 May two waves were beaten back before the Janissaries attacked a line held by no more than 3,000 exhausted troops. The accounts differ on his wound: a cannon shot or a crossbow bolt struck his arm, chest or leg. He was taken to his ship and sailed away with his men when the fall of the city became known. He died on 1 June and was buried in the church of San Domenico in the Castle of Chios. The tomb is lost, possibly destroyed in the earthquake of 1881, though descriptions of its inscription survive.

Sources hostile to the Genoese, above all the Venetian eyewitness Nicolò Barbaro, claim that he was lightly wounded or not at all and left his post out of fear. The charges of cowardice and treason spread so widely that the Republic of Genoa denied them in letters to the chanceries of England, France, the Duchy of Burgundy and others. The historians Marios Philippides and Walter Hanak rebut Barbaro, citing several other sources that record an injury.
gorgan: The present city of Gorgan is the capital of Golestan province and lies about 400 km north-east of Tehran and some 30 km from the Caspian Sea. North of it stretches the wide Dasht-e Gorgan, the Plain of Gorgan. The city has hot, humid summers and cool, wet winters, with about 584 millimetres of rain a year, while the Gorgan valley has a semi-arid climate. Some 150 km to the east is the Golestan National Park.

More than 50 archaeological sites lie on the Gorgan Plain, among them Tureng Tepe and Shah Tepe, with remains from the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods. According to the Greek historian Arrian, Zadracarta was the largest city of Hyrcania and the site of its royal palace. Hyrcania became part of the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great or his successor Cambyses. The Great Wall of Gorgan was built in the Parthian and Sasanian periods, and under the Sasanians the name Gurgan was used for a city, a provincial capital and a province.

The region kept its independence as a Zoroastrian state even after the Arab conquest of Persia in the 7th century. In 1210 the city was invaded and sacked by the army of the Kingdom of Georgia under the Mkhargrdzeli brothers. Old Gorgan was destroyed during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, and the centre of the region moved to Astarabad, which is the city now called Gorgan. Astarabad was an important political and religious city in the Qajar era.

The census of 2016 counted 350,676 people in the city, against 269,226 in 2006. It has several universities, among them Golestan University and Gorgan University. Among the people the city counts as its own are the 11th-century poet Fakhroddin Asaad Gorgani, composer of Vis and Ramin, the 11th-century grammarian Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, and Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, Shah of Iran from 1789 to 1797.
gortyn-code: The code, also called the Great Code, is known only from the inscription itself, cut on the circular wall of what may have been a bouleuterion or other public building in the agora of Gortyn. The building was 30 m in diameter; the twelve surviving columns of text are 10 m long and 1.5 m high and hold some 600 lines. It has been dated to the first half of the 5th century BCE.

It belongs to a tradition of Cretan law, the only substantial body of Greek law from antiquity found outside Athens. Earlier laws, of about 600 to 525 BCE, were inscribed on the steps and walls of the temple of Apollo Pythios, and the Great Code is one of a series written on walls in or near the agora between about 525 and 400 BCE.

The code distinguishes the free, the serf, the slave and the foreigner. Anyone bringing a suit is forbidden to seize the accused before trial, on pain of a fine that varies with the status of the person detained. Rape is punished by fines set largely by the difference in status between victim and accused. Adultery is treated similarly, with higher fines when it took place in the house of the woman's father, husband or brother; the fine falls on the man, and the code provides no punishment for the woman.

A divorced woman keeps the property she brought to the marriage and half of the income derived from it. A child conceived before a divorce and born after it belongs to the father and, if he does not accept it, to the mother. A widower holds his wife's property in trust and may not act on it without her children's consent; when a father dies, the land goes to the sons, and a childless widow is compelled to remarry. Adopted children inherit as natural children do, but women may not adopt.

The first fragment was discovered in 1857 by Georges Perrot and Louis Thenon. In 1884 the Italian archaeologist Federico Halbherr found four more columns while excavating near a local mill, and with Ernst Fabricius he uncovered eight further columns whose stones had been reused in the foundations of a Roman odeion of the 1st century BCE. The wall has since been partly reconstructed. All the Cretan legal texts are fragmentary and show continuous amendment, and from them scholars have traced the development of the law, notably the diminishing rights of women and the increasing rights of slaves.
harsha-of-kashmir: Harsha, also called Harshadeva, was born in 1059, the son of King Kalasha of Kashmir. Almost everything known of him comes from the Rajatarangini of Kalhana, whose father Champaka had been one of Harsha's ministers and who wrote in the time of Jayasimha, between 1127 and 1159. According to Kalhana he was built like a god and extremely handsome. He is said to have begun as a capable and noble king before his spending brought him into financial trouble.

Extravagant outlay on his troops and on pleasures left the king in grave difficulties. The historian Prithvi Nath Kaul Bamzai notes Kalhana's statement that even night soil was taxed. An accidental discovery of hoarded treasure at the Bhimasahi temple led him to despoil other temples and to melt down gold and silver images. Kalhana writes that not one temple kept its images, and that only two chief divine images were respected, Ranaswamin in the city and Martanda. Two colossal statues of the Buddha were saved by requests made one at Parihasapura by the singer Kanaka and one in the city by the monk Kusalsri.

Kalhana calls him that Turushka, and he bore the epithet raja-Turushka, Turk king. Turkish troops served him as mercenaries, and the chronicle says he continually supported Turushka captains-of-hundreds with money, while adding that he ate domesticated pigs until his death. According to the historian André Wink, Harsha in all likelihood took up the Muslim tradition of iconoclasm, as the epithet indicates. Kalhana also charges him with credulity towards parasites at court, who passed off slave girls as goddesses, and with incest with his sisters and violence against Naga, his father's sister's daughter.

Harsha died on 31 August 1101, the last ruler of the First Lohara dynasty. His conduct has remained a subject of discussion. The great Buddha of the capital outlived him: Kalhana records that when a fire reduced the city to a heap of earth in the reign of Sussala, the statue alone stood visible, blackened by smoke. The statue at Parihasapura had been made by Lalitaditya Muktapida, and Abul-Fazl states that the temples of that place were finally destroyed by Sikandar Butshikan, who ruled from 1389 to 1413.
hawiye: The Hawiye trace their lineage to Sheikh Ahmed bin Abdulrahman bin Uthman, known as Sheikh Hawiye. Oral tradition and Arabic hagiologies remember him as a saint called Hawi al-Ulum, conservator of knowledge, a name shortened in time to Hawiye, and carry his genealogy back to Aqeel bin Abu Talib. Some scholars regard such claims as historically untenable. The anthropologist Ioan Lewis held that traditions of descent from noble Arab families are most probably figurative expressions of the importance of Islam in Somali society. Tradition places his tomb at Qundhuro in the Haraghe region, where his eldest son Karanle is buried beside him.

The 12th-century writer Al-Idrisi placed the Hawiye on the coast between Ras Hafun and Merca and in the lower basin of the Shabelle river, the first documentary reference to a specific Somali group. Ibn Sa'id, who lived from 1214 to 1274, called Merca their capital.

In the 13th century the Hawiye, with the Rahanweyn, came under the Ajuran Empire, whose domain reached from Hobyo in the north to Qelafo in the west and Kismayo in the south. The Ajuran are themselves said to descend from the Jambelle branch of the Hawiye, and Lee Cassanelli describes Ajuran power as resting on spiritual pre-eminence and Hawiye kinship solidarity.

According to local oral tradition as Cassanelli reports it, the Hiraab Imamate was an alliance of closely related groups of the Gorgaarte division. Its founders rebelled because the Ajuran rulers had grown proud, neglected sharia law and imposed heavy taxes. With Mogadishu as its capital, the imamate ruled from the Shabelle valley and the Benadir to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. The explorer John Kirk, visiting in 1873, met Imam Mahmood at Mogadishu and saw about twenty large dhows there and at Merca loading grain, much of it for Zanzibar.

At independence in 1960 the first president, Aden Adde, the first prime minister, Abdullahi Issa, and the founder of the army, Daud Abdulle Hirsi, were all Hawiye. Hawiye leaders formed the United Somali Congress in opposition to President Siad Barre, whom General Mohamed Farrah Aidid, of the Habar Gidir, overthrew in 1991. From late 1991 Mogadishu was divided between the factions of Aidid and of President Ali Mahdi Muhammad, of the Abgaal. The stalemate lasted until 2006, when the Islamic Courts Union, a predominantly Hawiye organisation, ended the rule of the factional warlords, before an Ethiopian intervention overthrew it. The Hiraab hereditary leadership survives to this day.
hoelun: Most of what is known of Hö'elün comes from the Secret History of the Mongols, a mid-13th-century epic that is very favourable to her; its anonymous author probably had links to her. According to it she was born into the Olkhonud clan of the Onggirat tribe and was married at around fifteen, in about 1160 or 1161, to Chiledu, brother of the Merkit chief. On the journey to his lands the couple were ambushed by Mongols out hawking, led by Yesügei of the Borjigin clan. The kidnapping, omitted from most official chronicles, left a grudge among the Merkit that later became a blood feud.

Yesügei already had a wife, usually named Sochigel by historians, and a son, Behter, but Hö'elün became his primary wife. She bore him four sons, Temüjin, Qasar, Hachiun and Temüge, and a daughter, Temülen. The year of Temüjin's birth is disputed, with 1155, 1162 and 1167 each favoured by different historians.

Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars when Temüjin was about eight. The Tayichiud faction excluded Hö'elün from the ancestor ceremonies and abandoned her camp. The Secret History says the whole Borjigin clan followed, though other sources, such as the Persian historian Rashid al-Din, imply that Yesügei's brothers stood by her. When Temüjin and Qasar ambushed and killed Behter, the Secret History has her angrily reprimand them.

After Temüjin married Börte, the two women managed the economy of his camp, and he turned to them first for counsel when he split from Jamuqa. After his defeat at Dalan Balzhut in 1187, Hö'elün married Münglig, an old retainer of Yesügei, in her third and final marriage. In the following years she probably arranged marriages for her youngest children and maintained alliances while Temüjin was away. The Secret History says she raised numerous foundlings, but problems of chronology indicate that the best known, Shigi Qutuqu, was in fact raised by Börte.

At the assembly of 1206 Hö'elün was reportedly granted 10,000 followers jointly with Temüge, and felt that this undervalued her work; Münglig, by contrast, received the seat at the khan's right hand. When Münglig's son, the shaman Kokechu, divided Genghis Khan from his brothers, she defended Qasar and Temüge vigorously, and with Börte persuaded Genghis that Kokechu must be eliminated. The Secret History claims that she died soon after, worn out by her efforts, an account that some historians, such as Igor de Rachewiltz, have called poetical melodrama. By the time of the Yuan dynasty she had received the posthumous name Empress Xuanyi.
hussein-badreddin-al-houthi: Hussein al-Houthi was born on 20 August 1959 in the Marran area of northern Yemen, the ancestral home of the Houthi tribe; some sources give 1956 as the year. His father, Badreddin al-Houthi, was a prominent Zaydi cleric. According to a disciple, he lived for part of his life in Qom, in Iran, with his family, including his father and his younger brother Abdul-Malik; the same disciple claimed that he was close to Ali Khamenei, Supreme Leader of Iran, and to Hassan Nasrallah of Hezbollah.

He sat in the Yemeni parliament from 1993 to 1997 for Al-Haqq, the Party of Truth, a party of Zaydi and Shafi'i membership. When the party supported South Yemeni separatism it became a target of the government, and he fled, allegedly to Syria and then to Iran. After his return he broke with Al-Haqq. In 1990 or 1992 he founded the Believing Youth movement to teach young people about Zaydi Islam and its history and so to revive Zaydism in Saada Governorate.

The government of Ali Abdullah Saleh accused him of trying to set himself up as an imam, of opening unlicensed religious centres, of creating an armed group called Ansarallah and of staging violent protests against the United States and Israel. His followers held that the government was too closely allied with the United States.

On 18 June 2004 police arrested 640 of his followers who were demonstrating in front of the Great Mosque of Sanaa, and two days later the government offered a bounty of 55,000 US dollars for his capture and began an operation against him. In July the army killed 25 of his supporters and raised the bounty to 75,500 dollars. On 10 September the interior and defence ministries announced that he had been killed with 20 of his aides in Marran.

His father briefly took control of the movement after his death. The government buried him at the central prison of Sanaa so that his grave would not become a shrine. After Saleh stepped down, the new government handed his remains to his family on 28 December 2012, and on 5 June 2013 tens of thousands attended his reburial in Saada. His brothers Abdul-Malik, Yahia and Abdul-Karim are leaders of the movement.
isthmian-games: The games were reputed to have begun as funeral games for Melicertes, instituted by Sisyphus, the legendary king of Corinth, who found the body and buried it on the Isthmus. Another myth, probably later, held that Theseus, the legendary king of Athens, enlarged a closed night rite into athletic games dedicated to Poseidon and open to all Greeks. A further version credits Kypselos, tyrant of Corinth in the 7th century BCE, with restoring the games to their old splendour. According to Solinus they were constituted in the 49th Olympiad; 582 BCE is the date generally accepted, though one recent study places the first games in 581 BCE.

The festival was held in spring, in the second and fourth years of each Olympiad, the year before and the year after the Olympic Games, at the rural sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus of Corinth, a place easily reached by land and by sea. The contests were the same as at Olympia, among them wrestling, boxing, pankration and horse and chariot racing, and there were musical and poetical contests in which women were allowed to compete.

Until at least the 5th century BCE, the time of Pindar, the victor's wreath was of celery; later it was made of pine. A victor might also be honoured with a statue or an ode, and Athens paid its own victors 100 drachmas. Before the games Corinth declared a truce that gave athletes safe passage through Greece: in 412 BCE the Athenians were invited as usual although Athens and Corinth were at war. The games were especially popular with Athenians, while the Eleans boycotted them.

The festival served many as a forum for political propaganda, and from 228 or 229 BCE Romans were allowed to take part. Corinth, rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BCE, recovered the games shortly afterwards, but they were then held in the city itself and did not return to the Isthmus until 42 or 43 CE. Libanius mentions cult activity at the Isthmus into the middle of the 4th century, and the games probably continued at least until the end of that century. The circumstances of their end are unknown; imperial pressure against pagan rites grew at that time, though some polytheistic cult practices continued at Corinth into the 6th century.
jaswant-singh-of-marwar: Jaswant Singh was born on 26 December 1626 at Burhanpur, the youngest son of Maharaja Gaj Singh of Marwar. He succeeded on 6 May 1638 by special decree of Emperor Shah Jahan and was installed at Mehrangarh in Jodhpur on 25 May 1638. His father's favourite concubine, Anara Begum, who regarded him as her own son and was at odds with the heir apparent Amar Singh Rathore, had a part in his accession; Amar Singh was later given Nagore in compensation. He held in jagir the parganas of Jodhpur, Siwana, Merta, Sojat, Phalodi and Pokharan, and Shah Jahan granted him the personal title of Maharaja on 6 January 1654.

Shah Jahan sent him to stop the advance of the rebel princes Aurangzeb and Murad. The armies met at Dharmatpur, fifteen miles from Ujjain, on 15 April 1658. His advisers proposed a night raid on Aurangzeb's artillery and gunpowder, since the Rajput army was almost wholly light cavalry; he is quoted as answering that it was inconsistent with the manliness of the Rajputs to employ stratagems or make a night attack. He was defeated and lost 6,000 men, among them Ratan Singh Rathore of Ratlam and Mokand Das Hada of Kota.

Posted to the Deccan, he made Pune his headquarters. In 1664 he besieged Kondana without success, and he left for Delhi after Jai Singh was sent to the Deccan. He returned in 1667 with Prince Muazzam, the new viceroy, and acted as an intermediary between Shivaji and Aurangzeb. In 1670 he was posted at Burhanpur.

His son Prithviraj Singh died at Delhi on 8 May 1667; the khyats, the chronicles of Marwar, say that Aurangzeb had given him a poisoned robe. Jaswant Singh died at Jamrud, near Peshawar, on a date usually converted as 28 December 1678, though another scholar makes it 28 November 1678. Two of his wives were pregnant at his death and both bore sons, which led to a war over the installation of Ajit Singh Rathore as ruler of Marwar. He was also a man of letters, the author of the Siddhant-Bodh, the Anand Vilas and the Bhasha-Bhushan.
jayasimha-siddharaja: Jayasimha was the son of the Chaulukya king Karna and his Kadamba queen Mayanalladevi. The 14th-century author Merutunga has him seated on the throne at the age of three, on 7 January 1094, which would place his birth in 1091, but the story is absent from earlier writers and does not seem accurate. His courtier Hemachandra relates that Karna's nephew Devaprasada burned himself on Karna's funeral pyre. The historian A. K. Majumdar thinks this hides an unpleasant truth: that Devaprasada tried to usurp the throne from the young king and was killed by Mayanalladevi and her minister Santu, after which she ruled as regent.

Literary sources and inscriptions agree that he defeated Khangara, also called Navaghana, king of Saurashtra; his Dahod inscription boasts that he imprisoned that king. He appointed Sajjana governor at Girnar, which an inscription of 1120 corroborates, but he could not take all of Khangara's lands.

Inscriptions disagree on whether the Paramara king he defeated was Naravarman or his successor Yashovarman. Majumdar holds that the war began under the first and ended under the second, and dates the capture of the Paramara capital Dhara to 1135-1136; the title Avantinatha, Lord of Avanti, first appears in an inscription of 1137. The Shakambhari Chahamana king Arnoraja, whom several sources say he subdued and to whom he gave his daughter Kanchana in marriage, helped him in this war, as did Asharaja of Naddula. Chaulukya chronicles claim that he then subdued the Chandela king Madanavarman, while a Chandela inscription claims the reverse, which suggests an inconclusive war.

He was a Shaivite who tolerated other faiths. Jains held important posts under him, and the Muslim historian Muhammad Aufi records that he inquired in person at Khambhat after a mosque was destroyed and eighty Muslims killed, and paid for its rebuilding. He renovated or rebuilt the Rudra Mahalaya Temple at Siddhapura, completed in 1142. The Sahastralinga lake was a renovation of one built by his ancestor Durlabha, ringed by 1008 small shrines each holding a linga. The grammar he commissioned from Hemachandra, the Siddha Hema Shabdanushasana, carries his name in its title.

Jayasimha had no son. According to Hemachandra he learned by divination that his grand-nephew Kumarapala would succeed him; later Jain chronicles say that he hated Kumarapala and persecuted him. It is not known how long he held Malwa. Bohra and Satpanth traditions claim that he was converted to Islam, but there is no evidence that he ever gave up Shaivism.
jimena-diaz: Jimena, whose name is also spelled Ximena, was born before July 1046. She was the daughter of Diego Fernández, Count of Oviedo, himself the son of Count Fernando Flaínez, and of his wife Cristina, and she was a sister of Fernando Díaz, Count of Asturias. She married Rodrigo Díaz between July 1074 and 12 May 1076.

It is unclear whether she lived with her husband in the Taifa of Zaragoza during his first exile, from 1080 to 1086, when he led the army of its rulers, or whether she went to Asturias in those years. A legal action from Tol dated 1083 suggests that she kept a presence there even while the two were apart. At the start of his second exile, in 1089, she was imprisoned with her children Cristina, Diego and María by order of Alfonso VI. Nothing more is known of her until the end of 1094.

Rodrigo Díaz conquered Valencia on 17 June 1094 and secured it by his victory at the Battle of Cuarte on 21 October, after which Jimena rejoined him and stayed with him until his death. The principality he had founded was an independent state, and she succeeded him as its ruler. Their son Diego had been killed in 1097, fighting under Alfonso VI. A deed of gift that she made to the Cathedral of Valencia in 1101 survives with her signature. When the king judged the city impossible to defend, he escorted her back to Castile.

In 1103 she signed a document at the Monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña selling a monastery she owned to two canons of Burgos. This does not show that she spent her old age in the abbey, as the monastery maintained until the 18th century in the hagiographic texts known as the Legend of Cardeña; it is more likely that she lived her last years in or near Burgos. She died between 29 August 1113 and 1116, probably in 1116.

Through her daughters her descendants entered several ruling houses. Cristina married Ramiro Sánchez of Monzón and was the mother of King García Ramírez of Navarre, and María married first a prince of Aragon and then Ramon Berenguer III, Count of Barcelona. Jimena and her husband were buried at San Pedro de Cardeña. After the tombs were ransacked during the Napoleonic Wars the remains were reburied in Burgos, and they now lie in Burgos Cathedral.
jin-song-wars: The two powers began as allies. After Wanyan Aguda united the Jurchen tribes and in 1115 named himself emperor of the Jin, the Song emperor Huizong sought his help against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, hoping to recover the Sixteen Prefectures lost in 938. The Jin took the Liao capitals quickly, while Song attacks on Yanjing failed twice in 1122. By the treaty of 1123 the Song received only seven prefectures and agreed to pay the Jin 300,000 bolts of silk and 200,000 taels of silver a year.

The alliance soon broke down. Zhang Jue, a former Liao governor, turned his city over to the Song, though the treaty forbade harbouring defectors, and in 1124 Song officials asked for nine more prefectures. In November 1125 the Jin emperor Taizong ordered the attack.

Two Jin armies invaded. Kaifeng was first besieged on 31 January 1126, and after 33 days the new emperor Qinzong bought a withdrawal by ceding three prefectures; when he went back on the agreement the Jin returned and broke into the city on 9 January 1127. The Jin then tried to rule the north through puppet states, Da Chu in 1127 and Da Qi from 1130 to 1137. Gaozong, enthroned on 12 June 1127, was pursued as far as the sea in 1130, but the Song navy on the Yangtze and an insurgency in the north checked the invaders.

The peace of 1142 was broken twice. The Jin emperor Wanyan Liang invaded in 1161, was defeated at the Battle of Caishi in November and was assassinated by his own officers in December. Under the Song chancellor Han Tuozhou war was declared on 14 June 1206; the offensive failed, and the treaty of 2 November 1208 raised the tribute. Pressed by the Mongols, the Jin attacked the Song again from 1217 until a peace in 1224 ended the tribute. In 1233 the Song allied with the Mongols, and in 1234 their troops took Caizhou, where the Jin emperor Aizong killed himself.

Some two to three million Jurchens came to rule about 30 million Han Chinese in the north. Over half a million people fled south in 1126–1127. Lin'an, declared the capital in 1138, grew into a major commercial centre. The wars also spurred gunpowder weapons: the fire lance is first reported at the siege of De'an in 1132, and the iron-cased bombs the Jin used at Qizhou in 1221 are the first known hard-casing bombs. After the Jin fell the Mongols turned on the Song, which collapsed in 1279.
juan-gines-de-sepulveda: Sepúlveda was born at Pozoblanco in the province of Córdoba, of humble background; his parents were Ginés Sánchez Mellado, a craftsman, and María Ruiz. In 1510 he enrolled at the University of Alcalá de Henares, where he studied philosophy and Greek, and in 1513 he began theology at the College of San Antonio de Sigüenza. In February 1515 he obtained a letter of recommendation from Cardinal Cisneros to the Spanish College in Bologna, where he matriculated that September. There he studied under Pietro Pomponazzi and gained a lifelong expertise in the works of Aristotle, encouraged by his patron Alberto Pío, Prince of Carpi, and by Giulio de' Medici.

By 1523 Sepúlveda had earned doctorates in arts and theology and had taken religious vows as a Dominican priest. When Giulio de' Medici became Pope Clement VII in that year, he served at the papal curia in Rome, where he gained a reputation for scholarship and rhetorical skill. He translated several works of Aristotle from Greek into Latin, among them the Parva Naturalia in 1522 and De mundo in 1523.

He also wrote on the religious controversies of the day: De fato et libero arbitrio against Martin Luther in 1526, De ritu nuptiarum in 1531 against the divorce proceedings of Henry VIII, and the Antapologia against Erasmus in 1532. He despised Luther, but respected Erasmus and corresponded with him for many years. In 1529 he wrote Ad Carolum V, urging Emperor Charles V to unite Europe and fight the Turks.

In Democrates, of 1535, Sepúlveda defended the idea that a just war based on natural law was compatible with Christianity. His case for the conquest drew also on Saint Thomas Aquinas, on the Roman law of just war and the right of conquest, and on the Bible, which he used to justify forced conversion; his position differed from that of the School of Salamanca represented by Francisco de Vitoria. He had never been to America. He claimed that some, though not all, Amerindians were natural slaves as Aristotle defined them in Book I of the Politics, and compared them to children before parents.

Bartolomé de las Casas used the same sources in reply. He held that Christianity should be offered to the natives as an option, not imposed as an obligation, and that no Amerindians lacked the ability to rule themselves. Sepúlveda's later works include histories of the deeds of Charles V, of 1556, and of Philip II, of 1564, and De regno, of 1570. He died on 17 November 1573.
kakusthavarma: Kakusthavarma, also written Kakusthavarman, was a son of King Bhageerath, the third ruler of the Kadamba dynasty. When his father died the throne passed to his elder brother Raghu, and Kakusthavarma became Yuvaraja, or crown prince. As heir apparent he held a court of his own, perhaps at Palashika, the present-day Halasi, from where he is known to have issued land grants. In due course he succeeded his brother as king.

His reign is noted above all for its marriage alliances. The marriage of one daughter, read as a marriage into the imperial Gupta family, is counted the most important. It is also likely that another daughter married the Vakataka prince Narendrasena: Vakataka records describe Narendrasena's wife, Ajjhitabhattarika, as a princess of the Kuntala country, which probably corresponds to the Kadamba kingdom. Through such ties the Kadambas stood in close diplomatic relations with the great royal houses of India. The Talagunda and Halmidi inscriptions praise the king as a formidable warrior.

He appears also to have been a builder and a patron of both secular architecture and religious causes. He is described as owning numerous palaces adorned with gopuras. The Talagunda pillar inscription of his son Santivarma records that he had a great water tank made near a Shiva temple at which Satakarni and other kings of the past had worshipped. His own leanings seem to have been Jain: his grant at Halasi opens with an invocation to Jinendra, the lord of the Jinas, and he probably patronised a Jain temple there.

On his death the kingdom appears to have been divided among his descendants. One son, Santivarma, succeeded him at Banavasi and ruled the northern part of the realm. Another, Krishnavarma I, seems to have founded a junior branch of the dynasty at Triparvatha, in the south. The height of Kadamba power under Kakusthavarma was therefore followed by a kingdom held in two lines.
kathiawar: The peninsula covers about 61,000 square kilometres and faces the Arabian Sea on the south and south-west. From the heads of its two gulfs the Little Rann of Kutch and the waste tracts of Khambhat, half salt morass and half sandy desert, reach inland towards each other, so that only one narrow neck on the north-east joins Kathiawar to the mainland of Gujarat. Two belts of hill country cross it, and nine rivers drain it radially; they carry little water outside the monsoon months, and dams have been built on some of them. Most of the natural vegetation is dry scrub. The region has also been called Sorath.

The name Kathiawad seems to derive from the early settlements of the Kathis, who entered Gujarat from Sindh in the early centuries of the Common Era; Saurashtra comes from Sanskrit words meaning good nation. In the reign of Chandragupta Maurya the region was governed by Pushyagupta, and under Ashoka by the Yavana Tushaspa. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, of the first century CE, calls the coast Syrastrene and describes a fertile country yielding wheat, rice, sesame oil, clarified butter and cotton cloth, with many cattle. The Junagadh rock inscription attributed to Rudradaman I, dated to 150 CE, also mentions the region.

After Indian independence in 1947, 217 princely states of Kathiawar, among them the former Junagadh State, were merged on 15 February 1948 into the United State of Kathiawar, renamed Saurashtra State in November 1948. Vallabhbhai Patel spent much time persuading the princes; Maharaja Krishnakumar Sinhji of Bhavnagar State was the first to offer his state. Rajkot was the capital and Uchharangray Navalshankar Dhebar the first chief minister. On 1 November 1956 Saurashtra was merged into Bombay state, and when that state was divided along linguistic lines in 1960 it became part of Gujarat.

The region now comprises eleven districts of Gujarat, with part of Ahmedabad district; historically it also took in Diu. Gir National Park and its surroundings hold the last remaining population of Asiatic lions, and the peninsula has two further national parks, the Blackbuck National Park at Velavadar and the Marine National Park in the Gulf of Kutch. Severe droughts have repeatedly left farmers without crops or drinking water. A campaign to build check dams from the late 1990s raised water tables, but in 2019 a severe drought struck again and water had to be brought by tanker from the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River.
kigeli-iv-rwabugiri: Rwabugiri, whose birth name is given as Sezisoni Rwabugiri, was a Tutsi of the Nyiginya dynasty, which traced its line back to Gihanga, one of the first kings whose deeds are celebrated in Rwanda's oral chronicles. His year of birth is uncertain and is given as about 1840. He held authority from 1867 to 1895 and was among the last kings of his line.

Around 1870 Rwabugiri established a royal court at Rubengera that collected labour dues and tribute in food. It channelled food across the country and became a centre of commerce. The court managed production so as to keep a surplus as a provision against famine, and on the king's order this was distributed to the poorest in exchange for their labour; in times of shortage, however, the very rich Tutsi living at Rubengera could find food and livestock while most of the country suffered.

As he annexed new lands he placed appointed chiefs over them, drawn into a network that bound the regions to the court. These chiefs sometimes met local resistance: in the north-west the Balera challenged the Nduga whom the court had installed, a contest along lines of clan, since both groups were then counted as Tutsi. Several annexed districts, such as Bugoyi, Bwishaza and Kingogo, had been inhabited entirely by Hutu, and Tutsi moved into them in numbers afterwards. He also killed chiefs of his own Nyiginya lineage who had shown too much independence.

He was the first king of Rwanda to come into contact with Europeans. He built an army equipped with guns obtained from Germans and barred most foreigners, especially Arabs, from the kingdom, defending its borders against neighbouring kingdoms and slave traders. By the end of his rule the country was divided into provinces, districts, hills and neighbourhoods under a hierarchy of chiefs.

Rwanda had been assigned to the German Empire at a conference in Brussels in 1890, but no expedition came until that of Count Gustav Adolf von Götzen in 1894. Rwabugiri died in September 1895 on an expedition in what is now Congo. His son Rutarindwa was proclaimed king as Mibambwe IV, with Kanjogera of the Bega clan, another of Rwabugiri's wives, as queen mother. With her brother Kabare she carried out a coup at Rucunshu in which Rutarindwa was killed, and made her own son king as Yuhi V Musinga. The weakened state opened the way to direct German colonisation in 1897.
kobayakawa-clan: The Kobayakawa claimed descent from the Taira clan, through its Kanmu-Heishi branch, which traced itself to Emperor Kanmu, the 50th emperor of Japan. Nakamura Munehira, son of Taira no Tsunemune, founded the Nakamura clan of Sagami Province. His second son, Dohi Sanehira, who died in 1191, founded the Dohi clan, and Sanehira's second son, Kobayakawa Tohira, who died in 1237, founded the Kobayakawa. Two sons of the third head of the family, Kobayakawa Shigehira, who died in 1264, divided the clan: Masahira, his third son, made his base at Numata and began the Numata-Kobayakawa, and Masakage, his fourth son, settled at Takehara and began the Takehara-Kobayakawa.

The two branches continued side by side for some three centuries; the lists of their heads end with the same man, Kobayakawa Takakage, born in 1533, the third son of Mōri Motonari. Takakage was the uncle of Mōri Terumoto, and his brother headed the allied Kikkawa clan, so that the Kobayakawa held great power in the politics of western Japan. Toyotomi Hideyoshi regarded Takakage as one of the best statesmen and appointed him to the Council of Five Elders, but Takakage died in 1597, before Hideyoshi.

At the end of the 16th century the Kobayakawa fought beside the Kikkawa, Mōri, Toyotomi and Ōtomo clans against the Shimazu for control of Kyūshū, and after the defeat of the Shimazu they were awarded Chikuzen Province as their fief. Takakage's successor, Kobayakawa Hideaki, born in 1582, was a nephew of Hideyoshi.

A powerful clan of the Sengoku period, the Kobayakawa were disbanded in the Edo period, after the Battle of Sekigahara. In the Meiji period the Mōri clan restored the house, which was given the title of baron in the new nobility. The Kusai clan of Takehara, a branch of the Kobayakawa, was also granted noble rank.
kuntillet-ajrud: Kuntillet Ajrud, also known by the Hebrew name Horvat Teman, was one of the few water sources along the Darb el-Ghazza, the Gaza Road, which ran from the site of ancient Eilat or Ezion-Geber past Kuntillet Ajrud and Kadesh Barnea up to Gaza. Carbon-14 dating indicates that the site was occupied from 801 to 770 BCE.

The main building is fortress-like and divided into two rooms, one large and one small, both with low benches. Both rooms held paintings and inscriptions on the walls and on two large water jars, or pithoi, one found in each room.

What the site was for is disputed. It is frequently described as a shrine, though this is not certain. The excavator, Ze'ev Meshel, first argued for a religious function from the inscriptions and drawings with religious themes and from an unusual amount of linen, which he connected with the dress of priests. Other scholars point out that the site has no temple, shrine or cultic objects, and that similar textiles have since been found at Kadesh Barnea. Four inscriptions carry the military title Commander of the Fortress, three on storage jars and one on the plastered walls, which supports the view that it was a state-sponsored fortress or a caravanserai.

Although its position in the Sinai would normally point to the Kingdom of Judah, the occupants are usually taken to have come from the northern Kingdom of Israel. The evidence is the pottery, the personal names with the ending -yaw, the northern spelling of some inscriptions and the references to Yahweh of Samaria.

Edward Henry Palmer identified the place in 1869, when it was known as Contellet Garaiyeh, with the station Gypsaria on the Tabula Peutingeriana, and noted the remains of an ancient fort. Ze'ev Meshel of Tel Aviv University excavated it in 1975 and 1976, and the excavation report was published in 2012.

The paintings on the pithoi show animals, stylised trees and human figures. They appear to have been made over a considerable period by several artists and form no coherent scenes. Talley Ornan has argued that all the drawings have parallels in Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs and were preliminary sketches for wall paintings, and Schniedewind has read the inscriptions as scribal exercises of soldiers stationed at the fortress. Mordechai Gilula's theory that two figures on one jar represent Yahweh and the goddess Asherah has been almost abandoned: the scholars who have analysed the images in most detail hold that they are Bes or Bes-like figures.
lau-islands: The Lau Islands, also called the Lau Group or the Eastern Group, lie in the southern Pacific just east of the Koro Sea. About thirty of the islands and islets are inhabited. The group has a land area of 487 square kilometres and had a population of 10,683 at the census of 2007. Most of the northern islands are high and of volcanic origin, while those of the south are mostly low carbonate islands.

The islands lie between Melanesian Fiji and Polynesian Tonga and are a meeting point of the two cultural spheres. The south-east trade winds made it easy to sail from Tonga to Fiji and much harder to return. The culture of the islands became more Fijian than Polynesian from around 500 BCE, but Tongan influence remains in names, language, food and architecture: Lauan houses tend to have rounded ends, as in Tonga, where most Fijian houses are square-ended.

The British explorer James Cook reached Vatoa in 1774, and by 1820, when the Ono Group was sighted by Europeans, Lau was the most thoroughly mapped part of Fiji. The first missionaries arrived at Lakeba in 1830 but were expelled.

Political unity came late. The islands formed three territories. Northern Lau, as far south as Tuvuca, was under the overlordship of Taveuni and paid tribute to the Tui Cakau, paramount chief of Cakaudrove. Southern Lau, from Ono-i-Lau north to Cicia, was the traditional chiefdom of the Tui Nayau. The Moala Islands were closer to Bau Island and Lomaiviti. Around 1855 Enele Ma'afu, with the help of the Tui Nayau's army, conquered the region and set up a single administration, with Lomaloma on Vanua Balavu as his capital. The Tui Nayau gave him the title Tui Lau, King of Lau.

The title Tui Lau was vacant after the death of Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna in 1958. In 1963 the Vuanirewa clan bestowed it on Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara, who was also installed as Tui Nayau after his father, Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba II, died in 1966, so that the two titles came into personal union in 1969.

Lauan villages remain very traditional, and the islanders are known for wood carving and masi painting. Cricket, not rugby or football, is the most popular team sport, and Lauan players dominate Fiji's national cricket team. In July 2014 Tonga's lands minister, Lord Maʻafu Tukuiʻaulahi, proposed that Tonga give the disputed Minerva Reefs to Fiji in exchange for the Lau Group; the proposal had not then been discussed with the Lau Provincial Council.
legio-xii-fulminata: The legion was levied by Julius Caesar in 58 BCE and accompanied him through the Gallic Wars until 49 BCE. It fought in the battle against the Nervians and probably at the Siege of Alesia, and was at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE, when Caesar defeated Pompey. After the civil war it was named Victrix; in 43 BCE it was enlisted by Lepidus and Mark Antony, who led it, renamed XII Antiqua, on his campaign against the Parthian Empire. In the later part of the reign of Augustus it served in Syria, camped at Raphana.

In 62 CE the Twelfth joined Legio IV Scythica under Lucius Caesennius Paetus and both were defeated by the Parthians and Armenians at the battle of Rhandeia; after their surrender the legions were shamed and withdrawn from that theatre. In 66, sent with detachments of two other legions to restore Roman authority in Jerusalem, it was ambushed by Eleazar ben Simon at the Battle of Beth Horon during the withdrawal of Cestius Gallus and lost its eagle. It fought well in the later part of the First Jewish–Roman War and supported Vespasian's bid for the throne, after which it was posted to Melitene with Legio XVI Flavia Firma.

In 75 Vespasian sent it to the Caucasus to support the allied kingdoms of Iberia and Albania. It was probably in Armenia for Trajan's campaign of 114, and in 134 helped the governor Arrian defeat the Alans. Under Marcus Aurelius it campaigned against the Quadi, where the sources report a rain and lightning storm, held to be miraculous, that saved one of its units; a belief that the emperor then forbade the persecution of Christians seems to rest on a forgery. Its loyalty during the revolt of Avidius Cassius in 175 earned the title Certa Constans, surely constant.

After the death of Pertinax in 193 the legion backed Pescennius Niger against Septimius Severus, and when the frontier was moved from the Euphrates to the Tigris it stayed in reserve, possibly as a punishment. The country around Melitene was among the first where Christianity spread, and Polyeuctes, a martyr under Valerian, was a soldier of the Twelfth. In the 3rd century it was under the command of Odaenathus of Palmyra, yet also received the title Galliena from Emperor Gallienus. Records then become scarce. The Notitia Dignitatum still lists it guarding the Euphrates at Melitene at the beginning of the 5th century.
lex-hortensia: In the annalistic tradition a plebeian named Hortensius was appointed dictator around 287 BCE to deal with a civil uprising, which led to the secession of the plebs to the Janiculum hill; they returned only after the law had been passed in the Centuriate Assembly. The annals put the uprising down to debt, with a call to arms against the Lucanians as the immediate occasion, since the patricians needed plebeian manpower for the war.

There is considerable reason to doubt this account, which Livy attributes to an urban rabble in the forum. Large masses of urban poor did not really exist in the middle Republic, and rural landowners controlled 29 of the voting blocs of the Plebeian Council, which never numbered more than 35. The more likely cause is the wish of rural plebeians to control the distribution of the public lands won in the Third Samnite War, though the extreme measures of the consuls suggest considerable unrest in the city as well. An organised movement was needed to pass such a law, and it was probably coordinated by the plebeian tribunes.

In the early Republic the resolutions of the Plebeian Council, the plebiscita, bound only plebeians, because only plebeians voted there. The lex Valeria-Horatia of 449 BCE allowed them to bind all Romans if the Senate ratified them, and the lex Publilia of 339 BCE moved the Senate's approval to before the vote. The Hortensian law removed the requirement altogether. A plebiscitum remained distinct in name from a lex but was now treated as if it were one; later all binding laws came to be called leges.

The law also restricted when votes could be held. They were no longer allowed on market days, when they could have interfered with business, which hindered rural plebeians from taking part, since those were the days when they would have been in the city.

The law secured theoretically equal political rights for patricians and plebeians. It established the pre-eminence of the Tribal Assembly and the Plebeian Council in legislation, so that in the late Republic the other assemblies passed mainly minor and procedural laws, and it made the plebeians and their tribunes important political players, which the earlier laws had failed to do.
lex-manilia: The war against Mithridates, commonly called the Third Mithridatic War, had been conducted by Lucius Licinius Lucullus. By the winter of 68–67 BCE he had driven Mithridates out of Pontus and invaded the Armenian empire of his ally Tigranes the Great. His advance stopped when his discontented troops mutinied under the leadership of Publius Clodius Pulcher; many of these Fimbrian legions had been in the East since the command of Gaius Flavius Fimbria in 86 BCE.

Mithridates and Tigranes took their chance. Mithridates invaded Pontus and Tigranes Cappadocia, and in the summer of 67 BCE Mithridates inflicted a crushing defeat on Roman forces under Lucullus's legate Triarius at the Battle of Zela. Lucullus was superseded by the consul of 67 BCE, Manius Acilius Glabrio, who, seeing the difficulty of the situation, lingered in Bithynia. By the end of that year Mithridates had recovered the whole of his former kingdom.

The law recalled the three commanders then in the East, Lucullus in Pontus, Glabrio in Bithynia and Quintus Marcius Rex in Cilicia, and transferred all their legions and the entire conduct of the eastern war to Pompey. He was already in the East, completing the command against the pirates given him by the lex Gabinia of 67 BCE.

That earlier law had been opposed by almost the whole Senate. The proposal of Manilius, by contrast, had the support of many senators and of several eminent former consuls, among them Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus, Gaius Scribonius Curio, Gaius Cassius Longinus Varus and Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus. Cicero was serving as praetor when he delivered his speech for it, which survives. Opposition was largely confined to Quintus Hortensius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus, whose arguments against giving Pompey the command Cicero answers at length.

The law was passed in the Comitia Tributa without the violence that had attended the proposal of Gabinius the year before. Pompey soon moved against Mithridates and Tigranes and had defeated both by the end of 65 BCE, though Mithridates was not killed until 63 BCE. Manilius himself was prosecuted twice after leaving office in December 66 BCE. On the first occasion Cicero defended him against a charge of extortion, and the case was dropped in January 65 BCE amid disturbances and violence. On the second he was condemned on a charge of maiestas and went into exile.
lon-nol: Lon Nol was born in Prey Veng Province on 13 November 1913 to a family of mixed Khmer and Chinese descent. He was educated at the Lycée Chasseloup-Laubat in Saigon and at the Cambodian Royal Military Academy. He entered the French colonial civil service in 1937 as a magistrate and by 1946 was governor of Kratie Province. He joined the army in 1952 and fought the Viet Minh. After independence his nationalist Khmer Renovation party became part of the core of the Sangkum, the movement set up by Norodom Sihanouk for the elections of 1955.

He was appointed army chief of staff in 1955, commander-in-chief in 1960 and deputy prime minister in 1963. He became prime minister after the elections of 1966, and the following year troops savagely repressed the Samlaut Uprising in Battambang Province. Injured in a car crash in 1967, he withdrew for a time, then returned as prime minister in 1969 with Prince Sisowath Sirik Matak as his deputy.

On 12 March 1970 the two men closed the port of Sihanoukville to the North Vietnamese and demanded that all North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces leave Cambodia within 72 hours. Lon Nol at first refused to see Sihanouk deposed; on the night of 17 March Sirik Matak, with three army officers, compelled him at gunpoint to sign the necessary documents. Pro-Sihanouk demonstrations on 28 and 29 March were suppressed with several hundred deaths. The republic was declared on 9 October 1970. Sihanouk later claimed that the CIA had planned the coup, but there is no concrete evidence of its involvement.

The regime carried out mass killings of Vietnamese Cambodians. After a stroke in February 1971 Lon Nol's rule grew erratic and authoritarian: he made himself Marshal in April and suspended the National Assembly in October. By 1975 his government held little more than Phnom Penh and the temple of Preah Vihear.

He resigned on 1 April 1975, his name being first on a list of people the Khmer Rouge had vowed to execute, and went to Indonesia and then to Hawaii. In 1979 he settled in Fullerton, California, where he died of a heart condition on 17 November 1985. His brother Lon Non, a minister of the republic, was executed by the Khmer Rouge after the fall of Phnom Penh. Lon Nol called his ideology, a blend of nationalism and mysticism, Neo-Khmerism, and hoped to unite the Khmers of Cambodia with those of the Mekong Delta and Thailand.
lyuh-woon-hyung: Lyuh Woon-hyung, known by the art name Mongyang, was born on 25 May 1886 in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province, into the Hamyang Yeo clan. In 1907 he joined the National Debt Repayment Movement, and around then he became a Protestant and an associate of the American missionary Charles Allen Clark. In 1910 he broke with tradition by freeing the slaves of his household. He entered the Pyongyang Presbyterian Theological Seminary in 1911, and in 1914 went to China, where he studied English literature at a university in Nanjing before moving to Shanghai in 1917.

In Shanghai he founded in 1918 what became the Shanghai Korean People's Association and led the New Korean Youth League. In 1919 he took part in drawing up the February 8 Declaration of Independence in Tokyo, a precursor of the declaration that opened the March First Movement, and in efforts to send Korean delegates to the Paris Peace Conference. In April 1919 he was among the founders of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea.

In 1920 he joined the Korean Communist Party. In 1922 he attended the Congress of the Peoples of the East in Moscow, where he met Vladimir Lenin and Leon Trotsky. The Japanese authorities arrested him in Shanghai in 1929 and he served three years in prison. From 1933 he headed the newspaper Chosŏn Chungang Ilbo, and was forced out in 1936 after Korean newspapers erased the Japanese flag from pictures of the Olympic gold medallist Sohn Kee-chung. In 1944, expecting Japan's defeat, he organised a secret committee that spread across Korea.

Just before the surrender the Japanese official Endo Ryusaku made contact with him and agreed to release prisoners. The preparatory committee he founded on 17 August 1945 set up over 140 branches in north and south within the month. In October, under pressure from the United States Military Government, he stepped down from the People's Republic and formed the People's Party of Korea. When a movement to unite left and right arose in May 1946 he represented the centre-left, and was attacked from both extremes.

On 19 July 1947 he was killed in Seoul by Han Chi-geun, a 19-year-old who had fled from North Korea and belonged to the White Shirts Society, a right-wing terrorist group. His death was widely mourned. He is one of the few modern Korean politicians revered in both South and North Korea, and on 21 February 2008 South Korea awarded him the Order of Merit for National Foundation posthumously.
maeotians: The name comes from the sea: Maeotian was at first a label for the tribes living around the Maeotis, above all on its eastern coast. In sources of the 4th century BCE it has three senses: a broad term for the peoples around the sea, the name of the coastal tribes later listed by Strabo, and, in the usage of the Bosporan chancery, the lesser tribes of the Kuban region as distinct from the Sindi.

Their language, and even its family, is uncertain; the place names of their country suggest that they were not of Iranian stock. The Cambridge Ancient History reports two main views, that they were of Cimmerian ancestry, akin to the Thracians, or that they were Caucasian natives under Iranian overlordship. Soviet scholars concluded that they were among the ancestors of the Circassian, or Adyghe, people.

Strabo names among them the Sindi, Dandarii, Toreatae, Agri, Arrechi, Tarpetes, Obidiaceni, Sittaceni and Dosci, and adds that there were many others. Which peoples counted as Maeotian was disputed already in antiquity: Hellanicus of Lesbos and Pseudo-Scylax set the Sindi apart, while Pseudo-Scymnus and Strabo include them. The Sindi are the best attested and were probably the dominant people of the region.

The Maeotians lived in earthworks and open settlements on the Taman Peninsula and along the middle Kuban. According to Strabo they were as warlike as their nomadic neighbours, paid tribute at times to the rulers of Tanais and at times to the Bosporans, and rose in revolt from time to time. In the Kuban region they lived under successive steppe overlords. The graves show it: the ruling Scythians, and in Sindica the Sindian elite, were buried in richly furnished kurgans, while the Maeotian population used poorly equipped flat cemeteries.

In the early 4th century BCE Maeotian tribes fought a major war against the Bosporan Kingdom and its Sindian subjects. When the Sindian king Hecataeus repudiated his Maeotian wife Tirgatao, she roused her people, the Ixomatae, and other tribes to a destructive war on both kingdoms, which ended only under Gorgippus through supplication and gifts.

After Leucon I annexed Sindica, probably in the 380s BCE, the tribes of the Kuban were brought into the Bosporan state by stages. Leucon ruled the Toretae, Dandarii and Psessi as king, and under Paerisades I the royal style became king of the Sindi and all the Maeotians. Under Aspurgus, in the early 1st century CE, the royal titles still listed the Sindi and Maeotians, now with the Tarpetes and the people of Tanais.
mahapadma-nanda: What is told of Mahapadma comes from the Puranas, which make him the first Nanda king and the son of Mahanandin, the last king of the preceding Shaishunaga line, by a Shudra woman. His name, also given as Mahapadma-pati, means lord of the great lotus. Other traditions about the founder of the dynasty do not use this name at all.

Buddhist texts call the first Nanda king Ugrasena and describe him as of unknown lineage. According to the Mahavamsa-tika he came from the frontier region, was captured by a gang of robbers and later became their leader. One theory holds that Ugrasena was probably another name for Mahapadma. Jain texts such as the Parishishtaparvan and the Avashyaka sutra say that the Nanda king was the son of a courtesan by a barber and that he succeeded Udayin, with Kalpaka, a Jain, as his chief minister.

The Puranas describe him as ekarat, sole sovereign, and as sarva-kshatrantaka, destroyer of all the Kshatriyas, the warriors and rulers. The lines he is said to have exterminated include the Maithalas, Kasheyas, Ikshvakus, Panchalas, Shurasenas, Kurus, Haihayas, Vitihotras, Kalingas and Ashmakas.

The length of his reign is uncertain. The Matsya Purana assigns him 88 years, the Vayu Purana only 28. Modern estimates of his coronation also differ: the Indologist F. E. Pargiter put it in 382 BCE, the historian R. K. Mukherjee in 364 BCE and the historian H. C. Raychaudhuri about 345 BCE, and the beginning of Nanda rule has been placed as early as the 5th century BCE.

According to the Puranas, eight sons of Mahapadma ruled in succession after him for twelve years in all; only one, Sukalpa, is named. The Buddhist texts instead make the next eight kings brothers of the first, give the dynasty 22 years in total and name the last of them as Dhana Nanda.

Greek and Roman writers call the Nanda king of the time of Alexander's invasion Agrammes, possibly a corruption of the Sanskrit Augraseniya, son or descendant of Ugrasena. They suggest that the founder was a barber who took the throne from the last king of the earlier dynasty. The Roman historian Curtius, of the 1st century CE, reports on the authority of Porus that this barber became the queen's lover, murdered the king, seized power while pretending to act as guardian of the princes and later killed them, and that the king reigning in Alexander's day was his son.
majeerteen: The Majeerteen, also known as Mohammed Harti, belong to the Harti branch of the Darod. They traditionally inhabit the Bari, Nugaal and Mudug regions, from Bosaso to Garacad, between the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and are most numerous in the regional capitals of Bosaso, Garowe and Galkacyo. Migrations that began in the 19th century took some to Kismayo in the south, and some live in the Dollo Zone of the Somali Region of Ethiopia. Historically the clan formed part of a coastal trading network around the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.

The first recorded mention of the clan in English is by Henry Salt, who described them as living on the coast of Hafun under a Sultan Hassan. Salt relates that the Imam of Muscat had sent gifts and asked leave to build a small fort there, and that both the request and the gifts were refused. In the 19th century Majeerteen merchants were active across the Red Sea. One of them, Ahmed Muhammad, was granted the island of Baka by the Damoheita Afar, and his family ruled it as sultans into the period of Italian rule in Eritrea.

The Majeerteen Sultanate was founded in the 15th or 16th century and rose to prominence in the 19th under Boqor Osman Mahamuud. It was nearly destroyed by his struggle with his cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid, who was forced into exile in Yemen, returned with a band of Hadhrami musketeers, overpowered the local Hawiye clans and founded the Sultanate of Hobyo in 1878.

Kenadid signed a protectorate treaty with Italy, and Boqor Osman followed in late 1889. Each hoped to use Italian support against the other and to avoid direct occupation. When Kenadid refused to let British troops land in his territory to fight the Dervish forces of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, the Italians exiled him to Aden and then to Eritrea. After two years of resistance by Boqor Osman and Majeerteen rebels, which Italian forces put down with long coastal bombardments of towns and naval blockades, the territory came under the full authority of Rome by late 1927.

Osman Yusuf Kenadid, a son of the first sultan of Hobyo, devised the Osmanya script for the Somali language in the 1920s. Members of the clan held many government posts in the 1960s and 1970s, among them Abdirashid Shermarke, the first prime minister and second president of Somalia. In the 1980s and 1990s the Somali Salvation Democratic Front was a predominantly Majeerteen political group.
manas-river: The Manas, known in Bhutan as the Drangme Chhu, is the largest of Bhutan's four major river systems. It drains 41,350 square kilometres of eastern Bhutan and northeast India through three main branches, the Drangme Chhu, the Mangde Chhu and the Bumthang or Chamkhar Chhu. Part of its main stem rises in southern Tibet at about 4,500 metres and enters India in the Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh before crossing into Bhutan near Trashigang. The Lhobrak or Kuri Chhu, its main central tributary, is the only one that rises north of the Great Himalayas.

In Bhutan the river runs southwest through V-shaped gorges between two ranges of the Lower Himalayas. In the foothills the valley widens into swamps and marshes. The Aie River joins it in Assam, and it then meanders for about 75 kilometres to the Brahmaputra near Jogighopa. It is the largest tributary on the Brahmaputra's north bank and contributes 5.48 per cent of its average volume. From May to October the southwest monsoon brings more than 4,000 millimetres of rain to the southern part of the basin; the flow in the monsoon is said to be as much as 20 times that of the dry season.

The core of the present Manas Wildlife Sanctuary in Assam was designated a sanctuary in 1928 and declared a tiger reserve in 1978; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in December 1985. A dam proposed in the 1970s would have sent a canal 100 kilometres long through the tiger reserve to the Sankosh River. India's Ministry of Environment and Forests objected, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO supported the objection, and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi discontinued the project. Two dams proposed on the Bhutanese side were dropped in 1986. In February 1989 members of the All Bodo Students Union entered the park and killed several wardens and guards.

The lowlands north of the confluence, the Duars, are very fertile and have been made into tea estates and paddy fields. Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan, raised to a national park in 1993, is 92 per cent forested, and five thousand people live in villages inside it. The two reserves shelter the Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, greater one-horned rhinoceros, wild water buffalo, pygmy hog, hispid hare and golden langur, and the Ganges river dolphin lives in the river.
manghud: The Manghud belonged to the Urud-Manghud federation of the Mongolian plateau, and ancient sources derive them from the Kiyat Mongols. The Persian historian Rashid-al-Din Hamadani, who chronicled the Mongols, claimed that many old Mongol clans, the Manghud among them, were founded by members of the Borjigin.

Some Manghud warriors supported Genghis Khan, while a body of them resisted his rise to power. As the Mongol Empire expanded, the Manghud were carried westward with many other Mongol tribes. The clan name was also used for Mongol vanguard troops, though sources differ widely on the military units called mangudai.
