In the Golden Horde the Manghud supported Nogai, who died in 1299, and formed a horde of their own, semi-independent of the khans at Sarai. After Nogai's death most of their warriors entered the service of Tokhta Khan. Edigu, who lived from 1352 to 1419 and was the son of the noble Kutlukiya, led the eastern begs and by the end of the 14th century dominated the Golden Horde.

The Nogais guarded the northern borders of the Astrakhan and Crimean khanates and by organised raids into the northern steppes prevented Russian and Lithuanian settlement. Many entered the service of the Crimean khan and contributed to the formation of the Crimean Tatars. About 1630 the Kalmyks, migrating from southern Siberia to the lower Volga, drove the Nogais out; they fled to the plains of the northern Caucasus and to the Crimea, and a small part joined the Kazakh Khanate.

Other Manghits had been settled by Genghis Khan around the city of Qarshi, which remained their base under the Khanate of Bukhara. Their power there grew in the early 18th century through the office of ataliq to the khan. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi had the ruling Abu al-Fayz Khan and his young son killed. The family ruled behind the scenes until the 1780s, when the emir Shah Murad declared himself ruler openly. Not being descendants of Genghis Khan, the Manghits took the Islamic title of emir, not khan, and based their legitimacy on Islam.

The last emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, was ousted by the Soviet Red Army in September 1920 and fled to Afghanistan. Whether his dynasty was of Mongol or of plain Uzbek origin is disputed. The Nogai and Karakalpak peoples are counted among the descendants of the Manghud, and Manghits are found among the Tatars of Russia, the Bashkirs and the Kazakhs, as well as among the Khalkha Mongols of Mongolia.
mattavilasa-prahasana: The play opens with two drunken Kapalikas, the mendicant Satyasoma and his partner Devasoma, stumbling from tavern to tavern in search of more liquor. The Kapalikas are presented as followers of a heretical Saivite sect whose rites included drinking, wild dancing and singing, and ritual intercourse. Asking for alms, Satyasoma finds that his skull-bowl is gone. It is not at the tavern they last visited, and he suspects that either a dog or a Buddhist monk has taken it.

A Buddhist monk named Nagasena then enters, and Satyasoma accuses him of the theft. He charges the monk with stealing, lying and desiring liquor, meat and women although his religion forbids them, and accuses Buddhism itself of stealing ideas from the Mahabharata and the Vedanta. The monk denies everything and the quarrel becomes a brawl, which a Pasupata acquaintance of Satyasoma tries to mediate. In despair the monk hands over his own begging bowl. At last a Madman comes on stage carrying the real skull-bowl, which he has recovered from a dog; it is returned to its owner and all leave on friendly terms.

The play was written during a strong revival of Hinduism in southern India, which Mahendravarman I supported; he had temples cut into the rock, most of them dedicated to Siva. It is widely held to be a satire on sects that seemed degenerate or peculiar in his day. The Kapalikas stood for Tantrism, in which enlightenment was sought through unorthodox rituals involving liquor and ritual intercourse; the monk, in turn, wonders why Buddhism forbids liquor and women, and both Kapalikas call the Jains heretics.

The text also gives a view of life in seventh-century Kanchipuram, with references to the sound of drums, flower shops, festive taverns, temple towers and courts whose officials were sometimes bribed. English translations include those of Michael Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat, of 1981, and David Lorenzen, of 2001. A dance-theatre adaptation directed by Stella Uppal-Subbiah, which gave prominence to bharatanatyam, toured the United Kingdom in 2003 and 2004.
may-coup-poland: Józef Piłsudski had largely controlled the politics of the re-established Polish state but lost that advantage after the failed Kiev offensive of spring 1920, while keeping the esteem of parts of the armed forces. In November 1925 the cabinet of Władysław Grabski gave way to that of Aleksander Skrzyński, backed by the National Democrats and the Polish Socialist Party; when the socialists withdrew, it fell in turn and was replaced by a government under Wincenty Witos, formed by the Polish People's Party "Piast" and the Christian Union of National Unity. It had even less popular support than its predecessors.

Piłsudski regarded the constant shifts of power in the Sejm, the Polish parliament, as chaotic and damaging. He also saw threats to Poland's independence in the Locarno Treaties of 1925, by which the western but not the eastern borders of Germany were guaranteed, and in the Treaty of Berlin concluded by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1926.

On 10 May 1926, the day the Witos government was formed, Piłsudski told the newspaper Kurier Poranny that he was ready to fight the evil of sejmocracy, a contemptuous word for rule by parliament, and promised a sanation, or restoration to health, of political life. The edition was confiscated. In the night of 11–12 May units of the Warsaw garrison marched to Rembertów and pledged him their support; on 12 May they moved on Warsaw and took the bridges over the Vistula River.

At about 17:00 Piłsudski met President Stanisław Wojciechowski on the Poniatowski Bridge. He demanded the resignation of the cabinet; the president demanded that his forces capitulate. Fighting began at about 19:00. On 14 May the Polish Socialist Party declared for the rebels and called a general strike, and striking railwaymen kept government reinforcements from reaching Warsaw. To prevent a nationwide civil war, Wojciechowski and Witos resigned. In all 215 soldiers and 164 civilians were killed and some 900 people wounded.

Kazimierz Bartel formed a new government with Piłsudski as minister of military affairs. On 31 May the National Assembly nominated Piłsudski as president, but he declined, and Ignacy Mościcki took the office. Piłsudski held the posts of defence minister and inspector general of the armed forces in every government until his death, and headed two of them himself, in 1926–1928 and 1930. In 1935 his supporters replaced the democratic March Constitution with the April Constitution, which provided for a strong presidency but came too late for him to assume it.
megali-idea: The expression first appeared in the debates between Prime Minister Ioannis Kolettis and King Otto that preceded the constitution of 1844, but the hope behind it was older. Greeks had long looked for liberation from Ottoman rule and a restoration of the Byzantine Empire; folklore told that the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, had been turned to marble and lay beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople awaiting the call to reconquer the city. The state created in 1830 was designed by the Great Powers, and most ethnic Greeks still lived outside it, within the Ottoman Empire.

The new state was imagined as the Greece of Two Continents and Five Seas, reaching from the Ionian Sea to Anatolia and the Black Sea and from Thrace, Macedonia and Epirus to Crete and Cyprus. When the Danish prince Wilhelm Georg was elected king in 1863 he was styled King of the Hellenes rather than King of Greece, implying a king of all Greeks wherever they lived.

The Ionian Islands were acquired in 1864. In 1897, with violence growing in Crete, a Greek force of 1,500 men under Colonel Timoleon Vassos landed at Kolymbari on 1 February and proclaimed the island's union with Greece. Irregulars then raided Turkish outposts in Thessaly without orders, and the Ottoman Empire declared war. The Greek army fell back, an armistice was signed in May, and Greece lost small border territories and paid reparations; Crete became an autonomous state with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner.

Eleftherios Venizelos, a Cretan who became prime minister after the Goudi coup of 1909, was a major proponent of the idea, and under him Greek territory doubled in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13. Greece joined the Allies in 1917 and afterwards gained a protectorate over Smyrna and its hinterland, where a referendum was to follow five years of Greek administration, and a frontier in Thrace a few miles from the walls of Constantinople.

Turkish revolutionaries defeated the Greek army and expelled the Greeks from Anatolia. By the Treaty of Lausanne, Greece ceded Eastern Thrace, Imbros, Tenedos and Smyrna. During the conflict 151,892 Greeks had already fled Asia Minor; the treaty moved 1,104,216 Greeks from Turkey, while 380,000 Turks left Greece. The League of Nations arranged a loan of 150 million francs to help settle the refugees. In 1930 Venizelos paid an official visit to Turkey, where he proposed Mustafa Kemal for the Nobel Peace Prize. The Dodecanese were acquired after the Second World War, in 1947.
micaela-bastidas: Micaela Bastidas was born on 23 June 1744, the natural daughter of Josefa Puyucahua Sisa and Manuel Bastidas, who died in 1746. Virtually nothing is known of her father, who was perhaps a priest or of African descent; some documents call her a zamba, the colonial term for a person of mixed African and indigenous ancestry, while her marriage certificate lists both parents as Spaniards, a label that may have been a sign of respectability. As an illegitimate child she was marginalised in the overwhelmingly indigenous highlands. She spoke Quechua better than Spanish, was a devout Catholic and had little formal schooling.

She married on 25 May 1760, before her sixteenth birthday, in the church of Our Lady of Purification in Surimana. Her husband, a descendant of the Inca Túpac Amaru I, was named cacique of Pampamarca, Tungasuca and Surimana in 1764 and traded across a wide network with 350 mules. They lived in Tinta and had three sons, Hipólito, Mariano and Fernando. Letters exchanged early in the rebellion show endearments and concern for each other's safety.

The rebellion opened on 4 November 1780, when the local Spanish commander Antonio de Arriaga was taken prisoner; he was later hanged. The rebels made their headquarters at Tungasuca and defeated the Spanish at Sangarará on 18 November. Because indigenous people were forbidden firearms, obtaining weapons was among the hardest of her tasks. She also issued safe-conducts, took charge of the rearguard, guarded against espionage and organised a service of mounted chasquis that carried messages across rebel territory.

Local rulers called her Señora Gobernadora, La Coya or La Reina, and one description calls her a superior strategist to her husband and certainly more daring. He held off from Cuzco, which allowed the Spaniards to bring in reinforcements. By March 1781 the rebel army numbered seven thousand men and women.

On 18 May 1781 the prisoners were taken to be executed. Hipólito had his tongue cut out and was hanged. Micaela Bastidas fought her executioners until they subdued her and cut off her tongue. A hand-cranked garrote made for the occasion could not be used because her neck was so slender, and she was strangled with a rope, beaten with a club and kicked to death, in front of her husband, who was then killed. Their bodies were dismembered and the parts sent to towns of the region for display. The involvement of women in such risings shocked the Spanish authorities, who gave them the same penalties as men.
mir-osman-ali-khan: Mir Osman Ali Khan was born on 5 or 6 April 1886 at Purani Haveli, the second son of Mahboob Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI, and Amat-uz-Zahra Begum. He was educated privately and reportedly became fluent in Urdu, Persian, Arabic and English; from early 1899 Brian Egerton served for two years as his English tutor. His father died on 29 August 1911, and he was proclaimed Nizam the same day; the coronation was held at the Chowmahalla Palace on 18 September 1911. He lived at King Kothi Palace from the age of 13 until his death.

Hyderabad was the largest of the princely states of colonial India, and its ruler was one of only five princes entitled to a 21-gun salute. For his financial contribution to the British war effort in the First World War, amounting to nearly £25 million, King George V raised his style in 1918 to His Exalted Highness, and he was named Faithful Ally of the British Government. After the Great Musi Flood of 1908 he had two reservoirs, Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar, built on the advice of Sir M. Visvesvaraya. In 1919 he formed an Executive Council, and in 1941 the Hyderabad State Bank, which managed the state's own currency.

When the British withdrew in 1947 the Nizam ruled more than 16 million people. He refused to sign the instrument of accession, preferring a separate kingdom within the British Commonwealth, and signed a one-year standstill agreement instead. He negotiated openly with India and covertly with Pakistan, while his power was weakened by the Telangana Rebellion and by the Razakars, a Muslim militia he could not put down. In 1948 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Polo, under Major General Jayanto Nath Chaudhuri, and the annexation was over in 109 hours. The Nizam kept his personal wealth and title.

He served as Rajpramukh of Hyderabad State from 26 January 1950 to 31 October 1956, after which the state was partitioned. He gave 14,000 acres of his estate to the Bhoodan movement of Vinoba Bhave for distribution among landless farmers. He died on 24 February 1967 and was buried the next day, as his will asked, in the Masjid-e Judi, where his mother lay; the chief curator of the Nizam's Museum, D. Bhaskara Rao, put the funeral procession at an estimated one million people. His grandson Mukarram Jah succeeded him as titular Nizam.
moamoria-rebellion: The followers of the Mayamara Satra were predominantly Morans, the mainstay of the Ahom militia, joined by Sonowal Kacharis, Chutias, professional castes such as potters, weavers and fishermen, and some Ahom nobles and officers. The Ahom state rested on the Paik system, under which any able-bodied man who was not a Brahmin or a noble could be called up for labour, service or the army. The satras gave refuge to those seeking to escape it, and the loss of manpower brought them into growing conflict with the kingdom. The Mayamara Satra belonged to the non-conformist Kala-samhati sect, which competed with the royalist satras.

On 15 September 1769 Raghav Moran, a leading disciple of the satra, was flogged by Ahom officials for not supplying the required number of elephants. The Morans gathered an army of about seven thousand, and on 21 November 1769 they occupied the capital, imprisoned King Sunyeophaa and placed Ramakanta, son of the rebel leader Naharkhora, on the throne. After four months, when the peasant soldiers had gone home for the spring festival, nobles in disguise killed Raghav Moran on 14 April 1770 and retook the capital.

In April 1782 the Moamorias attacked the convoy of the newly crowned King Suhitpangphaa and briefly held Rangpur; the royalists who drove them out killed several thousand people. A third rising began in 1786. The rebels surrounded Rangpur in January 1788, the king left for Guwahati, and the continuous fighting in Upper Assam brought a famine described as the severest in the history of Assam. The rebels struck coins in the names of their leaders Bharat and Sarbananda but set up no central administration. A British contingent under Captain Welsh captured Rangpur in March 1794, but it was recalled and the rebels took the city again.

After the king's death Purnananda Burhagohain became the effective ruler and raised a standing army of paid sepoys in place of the paik militia. In 1805 his forces fought those of Sarbananda in the Bengmara region. Both sides recognised a stalemate, and Sarbananda accepted peace: he received the title of Barsenapati and autonomous command of the region, which came to be called the Matak rajya and paid annual tribute to the Ahom kingdom.

The population fell to about half of what it had been and economic life was disrupted. The paik and khel systems broke down, compelling the state to move towards a money economy. The weakened kingdom later fell to a Burmese invasion, which ultimately led to British colonisation.
mohamed-amin-didi: Mohamed Amin Didi was born on 20 July 1910, the son of Athireegey Ahmed Dhoshimeynaa Kilegefaan and Roanugey Aishath Didi, and through his father a descendant of the Huraa dynasty. In 1920 he was sent to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to study at Saint Joseph's College in Colombo, and in 1928 he went to India for further studies at Aligarh Muslim University, returning to the Maldives a year later. He married Fathimath Saeed; their only child was a daughter, Annabeela Ameena Mohamed Amin.

In 1931 he was appointed to the Constituent Assembly convened by Sultan Muhammad Shamsuddeen III to draft the country's first written constitution. He went on to hold many posts: chief officer of customs, head of the post office, minister of trade, minister of education from 1933 to 1936 and from 1944 to 1952, minister of finance from 1942 to 1952 and minister of foreign affairs from 1944 to 1953. He sat in the first Maldivian parliament and was principal of Majeedhiyya School from 1946 to 1953.

He was appointed prime minister on 1 January 1947, at a time when the country was suffering widespread famine and exhausted resources after the Second World War. He led the first political party in the Maldives, the Rayyithunge Muthagaddim Party. His programme included the advancement of women and a ban on tobacco smoking. As prime minister he also wrote a booklet for foreigners, Ladies and Gentlemen: The Maldive Islands, on the life, culture and economy of the country.

According to a report in the newspaper Mihaaru, the revolt of 1953 was staged by Ibrahim Zaki, Mohamed Zaki and Ibrahim Nasir, who invited the vice-president, Ibrahim Muhammad Didi, to join; he agreed out of distaste for Amin's handling of state funds. A special assembly passed a vote of no confidence that handed all powers temporarily to Ibrahim Didi. Amin, in Sri Lanka, learned of events by letter but not of his removal. He returned by way of RAF Gan to Malé, was taken to Dhoonidhoo, where he was beaten by the army, and was then banished to Vihamanaafushi, where he died of health complications on 19 January 1954.

In September 2021 a member of parliament, Ibrahim Rasheed, lodged a case with the Office of the Ombudsperson for Transitional Justice seeking justice for his death and the overturning of his conviction as a traitor. The office's mandate expired on 19 November 2023.
moskva-river: The river rises about 140 kilometres west of Moscow, crosses Smolensk and Moscow Oblasts and reaches the Oka about 110 kilometres south-east of the capital. Its length is given as 473 kilometres, or by another measure 502, its basin covers 17,600 square kilometres, and it falls 155 metres along its course. An estimated 61 per cent of its water comes from thaw, 12 per cent from rain and 27 per cent from underground sources. It normally freezes around November or December and begins to thaw in late March. On its banks, besides Moscow, stand Mozhaysk, Zvenigorod, Zhukovsky, Bronnitsy and Voskresensk.

Recent studies suggest that the river has occupied its present bed for about 12,000 years. Finnic peoples lived along it, as did Slavic tribes such as the Vyatichi. The name of the city is thought to come from that of the river. The most widely accepted explanation derives it from a Proto-Balto-Slavic root connected with wetness, so that it may have meant a river in a marsh or wetland. One Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, black river. To tell the two apart, Russians usually call the river Moskva-reka.

The first stone bridge across it, the Bolshoy Kamenny Bridge, was built in 1692. The Vodootvodny Canal, dug in the 1780s, created the island opposite the Kremlin that Muscovites informally call Bolotny Ostrov, Bog Island. Dams built in 1785, 1836 and 1878 failed to keep the river navigable through summer droughts. The highest recorded water level in central Moscow, 127.25 metres above sea level against a usual 120, was reached in the flood of 1908.

Since the Moscow Canal was completed, in 1932–1937, the river has also carried a share of water from the upper Volga, which has made commercial shipping reliable. The average discharge, Volga water included, rises from 38 cubic metres a second near Zvenigorod to 250 at the mouth. As of 2007 there were 49 bridges over the river and its canals within the city, where it is 120 to 200 metres wide and narrowest under the Kremlin walls. Moscow draws its drinking water from five stations on the river and from the upper Volga reservoirs. The stretch within the city freezes only occasionally, on account of contamination.
muhammad-al-amin-bey: Born on 4 September 1881, he married Lalla Jeneïna Beya, the daughter of a Tripolitanian merchant of Tunis, in 1902. On 25 June 1942 Moncef Bey named him Bey al-Mahalla, the heir apparent. A month later he warned Moncef that the court counsellor General M'hammed Belkhodja was urging the French Resident General Jean-Pierre Esteva to depose him.

In May 1943 General Alphonse Juin came to Tunis with orders to remove Moncef Bey for alleged attempts to collaborate with the Axis forces. Juin found no grounds for condemning him. Lamine at first refused to promise that he would accept the throne and agreed largely because of the benefits to his family. Juin installed him at the Bardo palace on 15 May 1943. Moncef abdicated only on 6 July.

For most Tunisians he remained a usurper, the Bey of the French. The other Husainid princes boycotted him. The death of Moncef Bey in exile on 1 September 1948 removed the possibility of a restoration, and his subjects began to regard him as their legitimate ruler.

He then worked clandestinely with Habib Bourguiba and Salah Ben Youssef for self-government. In 1952 the Resident General Jean de Hauteclocque imprisoned Bourguiba and had the Bey's ministers arrested; the Bey refused to sign decrees, bringing government to a standstill, and gave way after the trade union leader Farhat Hached was assassinated in December 1952. In 1954 he accepted a reform package negotiated by Muhammad Salah Mzali while Bourguiba was still confined. After the French Prime Minister Pierre Mendès France announced internal autonomy on 31 July 1954, France dealt with the Neo Destour alone.

As king he signed without protest the decree of 31 May 1956 that abolished the privileges of the ruling family. On 15 July 1957 the Tunisian army replaced the Royal Guard around the palace, and on 25 July the Constituent Assembly voted by a show of hands to abolish the monarchy.

He was taken with members of his family to an abandoned palace in Manouba without water or electricity; two of his sons and his son-in-law were imprisoned. In October 1958 he and his wife were moved to a small villa in La Soukra, still under house arrest. She died two days after three days of interrogation about the family jewels, and his confinement was then lifted. He died in Tunis on 30 September 1962 and was buried beside her in the cemetery of Sidi Abdelaziz in La Marsa, not in the dynasty's mausoleum of Tourbet el Bey.
muhammad-shaybani: Muhammad Shaybani was a Shaybanid, a descendant of Shiban, son of Jochi Khan and grandson of Genghis Khan. His father was Budaq Sultan, one of the eleven sons of Abu'l-Khayr Khan, ruler of the Uzbek ulus, and his mother was Aq Quzi Begum. According to the historian Kamal ad-Din Binai, his father nicknamed him Shibägh, wormwood. Budaq Sultan was an educated man who had Persian works translated into Turkic, and Shaybani was fluent in both languages. He was fond of history in his youth, and in 1475 was presented with the Alexander Romance of Nizami Ganjavi.

He first appears leading 3,000 men in the army of the Timurid ruler of Samarkand, Sultan Ahmed Mirza. When Ahmed went to war with Sultan Mahmud Khan of Moghulistan over Tashkent, Shaybani secretly agreed with the Moghul khan to betray and plunder Ahmed's army, which he did at the Battle of the Chirciq River in 1488. Mahmud Khan rewarded him with Turkistan. There he oppressed the local Kazakhs, which led to a war between Moghulistan and the Kazakh Khanate that Moghulistan lost, while Shaybani's standing among the Uzbeks grew.

He ousted the Timurids from Samarkand in 1500, retook it in 1501, conquered Bukhara the same year and founded the Shaybanid dynasty of the Khanate of Bukhara. He fought successfully against Babur, later founder of the Mughal Empire, and married Babur's sister Khanzada Begum; Babur's freedom to leave Samarkand depended on his consent. He aligned himself with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II against the Shia Safavids. He patronised the Yemeni religious figure known as Mir-i Arab and wrote religious and philosophical works in Chagatai, among them the Bahr ul-Khudo of 1508. Raids on Kazakh lands in 1508–09 ended in a major defeat by Kasym Khan in 1510.

In 1510 Ismail I invaded western Khorasan. Shaybani had lost most of his cavalry in a campaign against the Hazaras, so he withdrew behind the walls of Merv. Ismail besieged the city for a month without result and then feigned a retreat. According to some sources the khan's emirs advised waiting for reinforcements, but his wife Aisha Sultan Khanum shamed the council into fighting. His army was surrounded by Ismail's 17,000 men and destroyed, and Shaybani was killed trying to escape, on 2 December 1510. Shaybani was succeeded by an uncle, a cousin and a brother, whose descendants ruled Bukhara until 1598 and Khwarezm until 1687.
mukunda-deva: Mukunda Deva, also called Mukunda Harichandana, traced his descent from the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, and the traditions of Odisha call him Telinga Mukundadeva. His Bhimeswara temple inscription names his father as Saravaraju and his grandfather as Singaraju. He took the throne at Kataka in 1559 after killing Raghuram Raya Chotaraya, the last ruler of the Bhoi dynasty, and is counted as the founder and only monarch of a Chalukya dynasty of Odisha.

As king he tried to revive the power of Odisha. He laid out two streets from the Lion's Gateway to the Gundicha Temple and made the road smooth by filling its pits and holes. On the outer side of the southern walls he raised a swing arch, the Dola Mandap, on which the deities are swung during the Dola festival in the last five days of the month of Falguna. He also built a chain of forts at Raibania, in the present Balasore district.

His foreign relations were shaped by two powers: the Sultan of Bengal, his enemy, and the Mughal emperor Akbar, his ally. In 1560 Sultan Ghiyasuddin Jalal Shah of Bengal invaded and marched as far as Jajpur, and Mukunda Deva defeated him and drove him out.

In 1567, while Akbar was occupied with the invasion of Chittorgarh, the Karrani sultan of Bengal invaded. Mukunda Deva was defeated and took shelter in the fort of Kotsima, and the Bengal army under the general Kalapahada made a devastating attack on the capital, Cuttack. In the king's absence Ramachandra Bhanja, a feudatory of Sarangagarh, declared himself king. Mukunda Deva hurried back and met him in battle at Gohiratikiri, near Jajpur, where Mukunda Deva was killed.

Ramachandra Bhanja was himself later executed by the sultan's forces. Afterwards Ramachandra Deva I of the Bhoi dynasty, son of Danai Vidyadhara, allied himself with Akbar to avoid an Afghan invasion and continued to rule as a subordinate king of Odisha.
norodom-of-cambodia: Norodom was born Ang Voddey on 3 February 1834, the eldest son of King Ang Duong, whom a peace treaty between Siam and Vietnam had recognised as king after decades of war fought largely on Cambodian soil. In 1850 his father sent him and his half-brother Prince Sisowath to study in Bangkok, where they grew up near members of the Siamese royal family. In 1857 he served in the Royal Siamese Army as a military adviser. He was elected to the throne in 1860.

In 1861 another half-brother, Si Votha, rebelled, and Norodom abandoned the capital of Oudong and fled to Bangkok. The Siamese court returned him to Phnom Penh early in 1862. He could not be crowned, because Siam held the royal regalia, which a Khmer monarch needed to be a legitimate ruler. After French military pressure, including a steamboat sent up the Chao Phraya river to Bangkok, the Siamese reluctantly gave the regalia back, and it was the French who crowned him in 1864.

The treaty of 1863 gave France control of Cambodia's foreign relations in exchange for his personal protection against his enemies. On 17 June 1884, with French gunboats anchored outside the Royal Palace, he was forced to sign a treaty giving up control of public revenue, customs taxes and public works. The anger this caused led in 1885 to a revolt against French rule under Si Votha; the French suspected Norodom of supporting it in secret. It ended when he assured Cambodians that the French had offered him concessions, and for a time afterwards the French were less inclined to press him. In October 1887 Cambodia became part of French Indochina.

He reduced the number of provinces to cut administrative costs and, following King Chulalongkorn of Siam, abolished commercial monopolies, slavery and the civil lists of the royal family. Under his supervision Wat Oudong was consecrated on 6 June 1875 and the Silver Pagoda built in 1892. Classical dance recovered prestige at his court, and after a visit to Manila in 1872 he brought Filipino musicians to Cambodia to teach modern music.

Norodom named his son Prince Norodom Yukanthor heir apparent, but Yukanthor fell out with the French and did not succeed. The king died in the palace at Phnom Penh on 24 April 1904 and was cremated in the traditional Buddhist fashion in 1906; his half-brother Sisowath followed him on the throne. His reign of 43 years and 188 days is the longest in Cambodian history that can be dated exactly.
nuno-da-cunha: Born about 1487, Nuno da Cunha was the son of Antónia Pais and of Tristão da Cunha, the navigator, admiral and ambassador to Pope Leo X. He first proved himself in the fighting at Oja and Brava and at the capture of Panane, under the viceroy Francisco de Almeida. King John III of Portugal, to whom he had been close since the king was a prince, named him ninth governor of the Portuguese possessions in India, with orders to end the government of Lopo Vaz de Sampaio and send him to Portugal in chains.

The pirates he subdued at Mombasa on the passage out had been harassing the coast of Portuguese Mozambique, whose watering stations were essential to the route to western India. His brothers Pero Vaz da Cunha and Simão da Cunha were to have served as his second and third in command, as was expected in the Estado da Índia, but both died on the voyage, and during his long rule he had to rely on local networks of clientage in Goa. He took office in April 1529 and held it for nine years, longer than any other governor of Portuguese Asia in the sixteenth century.

In 1529 he sent an expedition that sacked and burned Damão in Gujarat. On 20 January 1533 forces under his control captured Baxay, the later Bassein and present Vasai, from Bahadur Shah. The next year it became the capital of the Portuguese province of the North, and its citadel of black basalt was begun; the citadel was completed in 1548 and still stands. In 1538 an army of the Sultanate of Gujarat under Khadjar Safar, aided by Ottoman forces, besieged the Portuguese in Diu.

Court intrigues forced his return to Portugal. He was shipwrecked at the Cape of Good Hope on the way and drowned; his death is dated 5 March 1539. He had married first Maria da Cunha and then Isabel da Silveira. The main source for his career is the history of the Portuguese in the East by João de Barros, who lived from 1496 to 1570.
oda-clan: Oda Nobunaga first claimed that the family descended from the Fujiwara clan and later from Taira no Sukemori of the Taira clan. According to the clan's official genealogy, after Sukemori was killed at the Battle of Dannoura in 1185, his son Taira no Chikazane was entrusted to a Shinto priest at a shrine in Otanosho in Echizen Province and became the founder of the Oda.

Modern scholars find no evidence for the Taira descent. One theory holds that the family came from the Inbe clan, Shinto priests in Otanosho. Another suggests that Nobunaga claimed Taira ancestry to justify his seizure of power, drawing on a belief of the time that the Minamoto and Taira clans were destined to alternate in rule, though it has been questioned whether people then really held this belief.

In the middle of the Muromachi period the Oda served the Shiba clan, military governors of Echizen. When Shiba Yoshishige was appointed governor of Owari Province the Oda followed him there, and Oda Jōshō became deputy governor. After the Ōnin War the Shiba split into two warring factions, and from around 1466 the Oda did the same, with Iwakura Castle and Kiyosu Castle as the strongholds of the two sides.

As the Shiba declined, Oda Tatsusada rebelled against them in 1513, failed and was killed. Oda Nobutomo then made the Shiba his puppets. During the Tenbun period Oda Nobuhide overtook the main family, captured Nagoya Castle in 1538 and became the strongest lord in Owari. Oda Nobunaga, operating from Nagoya Castle, besieged and killed Nobutomo, his uncle, in 1555, and his branch then brought the whole province under its control before turning on the Imagawa, Saitō, Azai, Asakura and Takeda clans. Nobunaga was forced to suicide by his vassal Akechi Mitsuhide in the Incident at Honnō-ji in 1582.

The Oda did not disappear after Nobunaga. One branch became hatamoto, direct retainers of the Tokugawa shogun, and others ruled as minor daimyo. At the end of the Edo period these were the domains of Tendō in Dewa Province and Kaibara in Tanba Province, each rated at 20,000 koku, and Yanagimoto and Kaiju in Yamato Province, each at 10,000 koku. Under the daimyo Oda Nobutoshi the Oda of Tendō signed the pact that created the Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei.

When the feudal domains were abolished in 1871, after the Meiji Restoration, the heads of all four houses were made viscounts in the new hereditary peerage. Descendants of the clan live throughout Japan today, mainly in the south and south-west.
onake-obavva: Obavva belonged to the Holaya community. Her husband, Kahale Mudda Hanuma, was the guard of a watchtower in the rocky fort of Chitradurga, which the troops of Hyder Ali besieged during the reign of Madakari Nayaka. As the story is told, a chance sighting of a man entering the fort through a hole in the rocks gave Hyder Ali the plan of sending his soldiers in by the same way.

The guard on duty near the hole had gone home for his meal. When he wanted water, Obavva went to fetch it in a pot from a pond near the hole, halfway up the hill, and there saw the soldiers trying to enter. She struck each on the head with the pestle as he came through and quietly moved the body aside, so that those behind suspected nothing. Mudda Hanuma returned to find her standing with the bloodstained pestle among the enemy dead.

She was found dead later the same day, either from shock or killed by enemy soldiers. Her act saved the fort on that occasion, but Madakari Nayaka could not withstand Hyder Ali's attack in 1779, when Chitradurga was lost to him.

In Karnataka she is honoured beside Abbakka Rani, Keladi Chennamma and Kittur Chennamma as one of the foremost women warriors of the state. Since 2021 the Government of Karnataka has celebrated 11 November as Onake Obavva Jayanti. A sports stadium in Chitradurga bears her name, and a statue of her by the sculptor Ashok Gudigar stands in front of the District Commissioner's office there. Her deed is shown in a song sequence of the film Nagarahavu, directed by Puttanna Kanagal, in which the actress Jayanthi played her, and in the 2019 Kannada film Chitradurgada Onake Obavva, with the actress Tara in the role.
ottonian-dynasty: The family's earliest known member is the Saxon count Liudolf (d. 866), who held large estates on the Leine river west of the Harz and in the Eichsfeld of Thuringia. About 852 he and his wife Oda, with Bishop Altfrid of Hildesheim, founded Brunshausen Abbey, which after its move to Gandersheim became the family monastery and burial ground. In 869 his daughter Liutgard married Louis the Younger, son of the Carolingian king Louis the German.

Liudolf's son Otto the Illustrious was, according to the Saxon chronicler Widukind of Corvey, already a candidate for the East Frankish crown in 911, when it passed instead to the Franconian duke Conrad I. Otto died in 912, and his son Henry the Fowler succeeded him as Duke of Saxony.

Elected king in May 919, Henry won the support of the Franconian, Bavarian, Swabian and Lotharingian dukes and in 933 defeated the Hungarians at the Battle of Riade. Otto I put down revolts by his brother Duke Henry I of Bavaria and his son Duke Liudolf of Swabia, reducing the dukes to royal subjects, and made the Church in Germany a base of royal power. He was crowned emperor by Pope John XII, married his heir to Theophanu, niece of the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes, and in 968 established the Archbishopric of Magdeburg.

Otto II was defeated by the Saracens at the Battle of Stilo in 982, faced the Great Slav Rising in 983 and died that year aged 28, leaving a three-year-old son for whom Empress Theophanu acted as regent. Otto III installed his confidants Bruno of Carinthia and Gerbert of Aurillac as popes and in 1000 travelled to the Congress of Gniezno; expelled from Rome in 1001, he died the next year aged 21. Henry II, of the Bavarian line, was crowned king on 7 June 1002 and emperor by Pope Benedict VIII on 14 February 1014, and founded the Bishopric of Bamberg in 1007.

Henry II's marriage to Cunigunde of Luxembourg was childless, and with his death in 1024 the dynasty became extinct. The crown passed to Conrad II of the Salian dynasty, a great-grandson of Liutgarde, daughter of Otto I; the Salians held the imperial throne until 1125. Pope Eugene III canonized Henry II in 1146. Historians disagree about how the Ottonians governed: those following Karl Leyser stress oral and ritual means, while others, such as David Bachrach, argue for the continued use of writing in administration.
ovra: After the young Anteo Zamboni tried to assassinate Benito Mussolini in Bologna on 31 October 1926, the Italian government quickly passed repressive laws. All parties and associations opposed to the regime were dissolved. On 25 November 1926 the State Defence Law set up a Special Court to try those accused of being enemies of the state and restored the death penalty. The public security code enacted in 1926 specified a department of political police as a special division of the force. Its existence stayed secret until December 1930, when the official press agency Agenzia Stefani named the OVRA as a special section of the police.

Arturo Bocchini appointed the inspector Francesco Nudi as head of the OVRA; he was later replaced by Guido Leto. The organisation compiled files on around 130,000 potential subversives with the aid of approximately 100,000 informants, and by 1930 it was organising around 20,000 raids each week. About 6,000 of those it arrested, mainly communists and members of Giustizia e Libertà, are believed to have been tried by the Special Court or exiled to remote Mediterranean islands, where conditions were extremely poor. It also kept the Casellario Politico Centrale, an archive of personal profiles of known subversives.

The OVRA spied on Pope Pius XI, blackmailing priests into informing; the historian David Kertzer described its network in the Vatican as robust. Heinrich Himmler met Bocchini repeatedly, and the two police forces signed a secret protocol of cooperation on 2 April 1936. During the Second World War the OVRA was used against resistance groups in the Balkans, and in 1943 it tried to infiltrate the British Special Operations Executive with double agents. Many agents followed Mussolini to the Italian Social Republic, where they were favoured targets of communist partisans.

The OVRA was officially disbanded after the war, but a decree of 26 April 1945 ordered that the central political archive be maintained. A new police division, the Servizio Informazioni Speciali, took over its management, and many former OVRA officers were reinstated in it; its head, Inspector General Santoro, had been one of Leto's deputies. Most of the public security laws of 1931 were kept in force by the Italian Republic, and Leto himself was later reinstated as a police officer and put in charge of supervising the police academies.
palk-strait: The strait stretches for about 137 km and is between 64 and 137 km wide. Its waters are shallow: around the shoals of Ram Setu they are typically only 1 to 3 metres deep, the central part is typically around 20 metres deep, and the greatest depth is 35 metres. To the north, in the Bay of Bengal, the waves are mostly swells, while in Palk Bay to the south they are mostly smaller wind waves. In the Hindu epic Ramayana the shoals are part of a bridge built by the vanara army of Rama to rescue his wife Sita from the Asura king Ravana.

During the Last Glacial Period, when sea levels fell to as much as 120 metres below their present values, the whole of the shallow strait was dry land. It was submerged again as the sea rose during the Holocene, by around 7,000 years ago.

The construction of a shipping channel through the strait was first proposed to the British government of India in 1860. Pamban Island was linked to the Indian mainland by the Pamban Bridge, opened for traffic on 24 February 1914. Trains ran from Madras to Dhanushkodi at the southern tip of the island, where a ferry crossed to Talaimannar on Mannar Island and another train carried passengers on to Colombo. The railway line to Dhanushkodi was destroyed in the 1964 Dhanushkodi cyclone together with a passenger train, killing around 200 people. A ferry between Rameswaram and Talaimannar continued into the 1970s and was discontinued by the Indian government in 1984.

The shallows, small islands and reefs make the strait difficult for large ships, though fishing boats and small craft navigate it. The Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project, commissioned by the Government of India in 2005 to dredge a channel, met opposition on religious grounds. A road bridge beside the Pamban Bridge was opened in 1988, and a new railway bridge was completed in 2024 after rail traffic on the old bridge was suspended permanently in February 2023 over concerns about its stability. A combined undersea tunnel and bridge linking India and Sri Lanka, the Palk Strait Bridge, was first discussed in 2002 and has been examined several times since.
pandara-vanniyan: Kulasegaram Vairamuthu Pandara Vanniyan was a native of the Vanni and is said to have reigned there from 1785. Much about his family is unclear, but reports give him a sister, Nallanachal Vanniyan, and two younger brothers who served as his minister and his commander. He married into the family of Kumarasinghe Maha Vanniya of Nuwara Wewa, and so gained political power in the southern Vanni as well as the north. He is said to have lived at Kumulamunai, in the present Mullaitivu District.

The Vanni served as a buffer zone between the north and south of Sri Lanka. After the Portuguese captured the Jaffna Kingdom in 1621 the region was under their nominal control, and around 1782 the Dutch defeated the Vanniar chieftains.

Pandara Vanniyan is said to have defeated the Dutch officer Lieutenant von Driberg several times. Against the British, the Vanniars carried on a predatory warfare in Mannar and Trincomalee and reached the Jaffna Peninsula, and the British built forts to keep them at bay. In alliance with the Kandy Kingdom he rose to expel the British from his district. On 25 August 1803 he attacked the Government House at Mullaitivu, drove out the garrison under Captain Edward Mudge of the 19th Regiment and seized the fort and its cannons. He then overran the northern districts as far as Elephant Pass.

He turned from conventional warfare to guerrilla tactics, but the British organised a three-pronged attack from Jaffna, Mannar and Trincomalee. Von Driberg, who had stayed on after the British ousted the Dutch, defeated him on 31 October 1803 at Katsilaimadu, capturing a cannon given to him by the Kandyan king Sri Wickrema Rajasinghe. His houses were burned and his people dispersed into the jungle and out of the Vanni.

No longer a ruler, Pandara Vanniyan withdrew to areas near the Kandy Kingdom. Accounts of his end differ: by one he died fighting the British, by another he remained there until September 1810, when British forces ambushed him, and later died of his injuries. Von Driberg set up a granite monument at Katsilaimadu recording the defeat; in 2010 it was found broken. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa declared him a national hero in 1982, and a statue stands in Vavuniya. Tamil nationalists honour him as an epic hero, and he is the subject of a novel by M. Karunanidhi and of a play by Mullaimani Ve Cuppiramaniyam that won a prize from the Ceylon Art Council in 1964.
pataliputra: Pataliputra stood where the Ganges, the Gandhaka and the Son rivers met, a position that made it a water fort, or jaldurga, and let it dominate the river trade of the Indo-Gangetic Plain. One traditional etymology derives the name from the pāṭalī tree; another makes it the son of Pāṭali, daughter of a Raja Sudarsan. The city was also called Kusumapura, city of flowers. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, who lived there under the Maurya Empire and called it Palibothra, described a city in the shape of a parallelogram, surrounded by a ditch and a wall with 570 towers and 64 gates. Strabo adds that the walls were of wood.

The place began as a village, Pataligrama, fortified by the Magadha ruler Ajatashatru; the date given is 490 BCE. Jain and Hindu sources name his son Udayabhadra as the king who moved the capital there from Rajgriha. Archaeological evidence shows urban growth no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE. Under Ashoka it was one of the world's largest cities, with an estimated population of 150,000 to 400,000, and early Buddhist texts record the Third Buddhist council there.

Faxian, visiting about 400, found the people rich and described hospitals where the poor were treated without charge. Xuanzang in 637 found the old city in ruins, with a small walled town of about 1,000 people by the river. Suggested causes of the decline are a shift in the course of the Ganges, a flood on the Son recorded in a later Jain work and placed in the late 500s, and destruction by Hunas in the early 500s. An inscription of the Pala king Dharmapala from the early 800s describes it as a river port and royal camp. Sher Shah Suri later made it his capital under the name Patna.

Much of the ancient city lies buried under modern Patna. Its site was first identified in modern times by Laurence Waddell in 1892, and excavations have been made at Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan. They have found stretches of the wooden palisade over several kilometres, but no stone fortifications. At Kumhrar the remains thin out from the 300s and stop about 600, and a thick layer of ash in the hall of 80 pillars suggests that it was burnt.
paul-doumer: Joseph Athanase Doumer, commonly known as Paul, was born on 22 March 1857 at Aurillac in the Cantal department into a family of modest means. A former student of the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, he became a professor of mathematics at Mende in 1877 and taught at Remiremont from 1879 to 1883, leaving on health grounds to become chief editor of a regional newspaper, the Courrier de l'Aisne. In 1878 he married Blanche Richel. They had eight children, four of whom were killed in the First World War. He was initiated into Freemasonry in 1879 and became Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient de France in 1892.

Doumer entered politics in 1885 as chef de cabinet to Charles Floquet, president of the Chamber of Deputies, and was elected Radical deputy for the Aisne in 1888. Defeated in 1889, he was returned in 1890 by the arrondissement of Auxerre. As minister of finance in 1895–1896 he tried without success to introduce an income tax.

When he arrived in Indochina the colonies were losing millions of francs a year, and his taxes were meant to put them on a paying basis. Vietnamese, Cambodians and Laotians who could not or would not pay lost their houses and land and often became day labourers. He made Indochina a market for French products and a field for French investment. In 1898 he persuaded the French government to approve the railway to Yunnan, with a view to annexing the south of that province.

Back in France he was elected deputy for Laon, refused to support the ministry of Émile Combes and led a group of dissident Radicals that eventually helped bring it down. He was president of the Chamber from 1902 to 1905, minister of finance again in 1925 and president of the Senate from 1927. On 13 May 1931 he was elected president of the Republic, defeating the better-known Aristide Briand.

On 6 May 1932, at the opening of a book fair at the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild in Paris, Doumer was shot by Paul Gorguloff, a Russian émigré, while talking to the author Claude Farrère. He died in hospital at 04:37 on 7 May, the second French president to be assassinated and the first to be shot. Gorguloff wrote that the act was a protest on behalf of exiled White Russians and against France's relations with the Soviet Union; he was guillotined four months later. Doumer wrote L'Indo-Chine française (1904) and Le Livre de mes fils (1906).
peter-tordenskjold: Peter Jansen Wessel was the tenth child of the Trondheim alderman Jan Wessel. An unruly boy, he stowed away on a ship to Copenhagen in 1704 and tried without success to become a naval cadet. The king's chaplain, Peder Jespersen, sent him on a voyage to the West Indies and at last found him a cadetship. After voyages to the East Indies he was made second lieutenant on 7 July 1711. The Norwegian admiral Waldemar Løvendal gave him the four-gun sloop Ormen and in June 1712 the 18-gun Løvendals Galej, against the advice of the Danish admiralty, which thought him unreliable.

He took part in the destruction of Swedish transports at Rügen on 29 September 1712. On 26 and 27 July 1714, off Lindesnes, he fought the 28-gun Swedish privateer Olbing Galley until both ships were badly damaged, then sent to thank her crew and to ask for more ammunition so as to go on. King Frederick IV had him court-martialled for disclosing his lack of ammunition and for risking his ship against a stronger one; he was acquitted on 15 December and made captain on 28 December.

At Kolberg on 24 April 1715 he captured the Swedish Rear-Admiral Hans Wachtmeister and the frigate Hvita Örn, which became his flagship. At Dynekilen on 8 July 1716, with two frigates and five smaller ships, he took or destroyed around 30 Swedish vessels. A failure against the Gothenburg squadron in 1717 brought a second court-martial in 1718, which was quashed after Ulrik Christian Gyldenløve intervened. He became rear-admiral in December 1718 and vice-admiral after partly destroying and partly capturing the Gothenburg squadron on 26 September 1719.

On 12 November 1720, aged 30, he was killed by the sword of the Livonian colonel Jakob Axel Staël von Holstein in a duel at Gleidingen near Hildesheim. The quarrel arose at a dinner where Tordenskiold spoke of a friend cheated at gambling. As duelling was against Danish law, his body was brought to Holmen Church without much ceremony. He is named in the Danish anthem Kong Christian stod ved højen mast of 1778 and the Norwegian anthem Ja, vi elsker dette landet of 1864. A story that at Marstrand his men moved from post to post to seem more numerous gave Danish and Norwegian the phrase Tordenskjold's soldiers.
prince-vijaya: The Mahavamsa gives Vijaya a marvellous ancestry. His grandmother Suppadevi, daughter of the king of Vanga and a princess of Kalinga, was carried off by Sinha, the lion, whom some modern interpreters take to have been an outlaw living in the forest. Their son Sinhabahu escaped with his mother and sister, killed his father, founded the city of Sinhapura in the Lala country and married his sister Sinhasivali. Vijaya was the eldest of their thirty-two sons. Where Sinhapura lay is uncertain: it has been placed in Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, among other places.

Made prince regent by his father, Vijaya became notorious with his followers for violent deeds, and prominent citizens demanded his death. Sinhabahu instead expelled them: their heads were half shaved and they were put on a ship, their wives and children being sent off on separate ships.

In the Mahavamsa's telling the kingdom was named Tambapanni, copper-red hands, because the red soil coloured the hands of Vijaya's men, and his people were called Sinhala after Sinhabahu. His ministers founded villages, among them Upatissagama. To be crowned he needed a queen of noble house, and the Pandya king of Madhura, identified with Madurai, sent his daughter with a hundred noble maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of eighteen guilds, who landed at the port of Mahatittha.

Vijaya then sent Kuveni away, since his people feared supernatural beings. She went with their two children, Jivahatta and Disala, to the Yakkha city of Lankapura, where she was killed as a traitor. The children fled to Sumanakuta, and from them the chronicle derives the Pulinda, identified with the Vedda people. Vijaya, crowned, is said to have given up his evil ways and ruled in peace and justice.

Having no heir, Vijaya in old age sent for his twin brother Sumitta, but died before a reply came. His ministers governed for a year until Panduvasudeva, Sumitta's youngest son, arrived from Sinhapura to rule. The older Dipavamsa tells a similar story without Kuveni or the South Indian princess, and two other versions of the legend, one recorded by Xuanzang and one a Jataka painted at Ajanta, give the founding prince other names.

There is no archaeological evidence for the story. In Sri Lanka it is often treated as history and used in political argument: Sinhalese scholars such as K. M. de Silva have cited it for the Indo-Aryan origins of the Sinhalese, while Tamil authors such as Satchi Ponnambalam have dismissed it as fiction serving Sinhalese territorial claims.
punctation-of-olmutz: The German Confederation, dominated by Austria, had been dissolved in the Revolutions of 1848 and partially succeeded by the Frankfurt Assembly. After the assembly failed, Prussia took the initiative in early 1850 with the Erfurt Union, a federation of most of the German states under its own lead. The two powers were thus in conflict over the leadership of Germany.

A dispute between the Elector of Hesse and his subjects gave the Austrian chancellor Felix zu Schwarzenberg the occasion to isolate Prussia further. Austrian and allied armies advanced into the Electorate of Hesse, and on 8 November 1850 the Prussian army came close to war with Bavaria, an ally of Austria, near Fulda-Bronnzell. In the Warsaw negotiations of October 1850 Tsar Nicholas I of Russia had already taken Austria's side, which was part of the reason why Prussia decided to give in.

The agreement, also called the Agreement of Olmütz, came out of a conference held in the town, now Olomouc in the Czech Republic, and closed the Autumn Crisis of 1850. Prussia gave up its claim to lead the German states and submitted to Austrian leadership of the restored confederation. It agreed to demobilise, to take part in the intervention of the German Diet in Hesse and in Holstein, and renounced any resumption of the Erfurt Union. Austria for its part agreed to call a conference of ministers to discuss a reform of the confederation.

The ministerial conference that Austria had promised met in Dresden the following year and ended without result, so that the confederation continued unreformed under Austrian leadership. The name of humiliation was given to the treaty because many saw in it a capitulation of the Prussians to the Austrians.
purandar-singha: Purandar Singha was born in 1807 at Silmari in British-ruled Bengal, a great-great-grandson of the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha. His grandfather and his father Brajanath Gohain had conspired against reigning kings and lived there as exiled princes in poverty. In 1818 Ruchinath Burhagohain, who held King Chandrakanta Singha responsible for bringing in the Burmese, invited Brajanath to claim the throne, and their force entered the capital Jorhat on 17 February 1818. Brajanath had coins struck in his own name, but the mutilation of one of his ears barred him from kingship, since an Ahom king had to be without blemish. His son, then ten years old, was acclaimed instead.

Real authority lay with Brajanath and Ruchinath, who removed the officers suspected of loyalty to Chandrakanta. A Burmese army of 30,000 sent by King Bodawpaya defeated the Assamese on 17 February 1819; Purandar, his father and Ruchinath fled to Guwahati with the valuables of the royal treasury, worth 3.5 million rupees. After a second defeat on 11 June 1819 they escaped to Bengal. The Governor-General Lord Hastings refused to help. They recruited soldiers in Goalpara, Bengal and Bhutan, armed with the aid of a British trader, Robert Bruce, and fought both Chandrakanta and the Burmese before withdrawing in 1822.

After the Treaty of Yandabo of 24 February 1826 the British held the Brahmaputra valley. Sensing discontent, they considered in 1832 restoring Upper Assam as a tributary princedom and chose Purandar over Chandrakanta; some historians think they expected a long-exiled prince to be the more grateful and submissive. From April 1833 he ruled from Jorhat, without Sadiya and Matak, for a tribute of 50,000 rupees. Within three years he fell behind in his payments and asked for a reduction. An enquiry by Captain Francis Jenkins found corruption and oppression, and the king himself amassing a personal fortune.

The kingdom was placed under direct British control in September 1838. Purandar stayed in Jorhat and refused the pension of 1,000 rupees a month granted in October 1838, hoping that a petition to the Governor-General would restore his state; it was turned down. When officials and adventurers dug into the royal tombs, the maidams, at Charaideo in search of treasure, he first protested and then opened many tombs himself. He died on 1 October 1846 and was entombed at Jorhat, at the place now called Raja Maidam.
qizilbash: The name comes from Turkish and means red head, after a crimson cap of twelve gores which marked adherence to the Twelve Imams and to Shaykh Haydar, head of the Safavid order. It began as a pejorative used by their Sunni Ottoman enemies and was taken up as a mark of pride. In the 15th century Haydar organised his followers into militant troops. They were at first drawn from seven Turkish-speaking tribes: the Rumlu, Shamlu, Ustajlu, Afshar, Qajar, Tekelu and Zulkadar. Their beliefs were heterodox: they regarded their Safavid leader as a manifestation of the divine, and orthodox Twelver Shia classed them as ghulat, extremists.

By the summer of 1500 about 7,000 supporters had rallied to the young Ismail at Erzincan. They overcame a force of 30,000 Aq Qoyunlu and took Tabriz. In 1510 the Qizilbash defeated the Uzbeks at Marv, but in 1512 an army was destroyed at the Battle of Ghazdewan after Turcoman Qizilbash mutinied against their Persian commander, Najm-e Thani. On 20 August 1514 the Ottoman sultan Selim I, whose army had firearms and cannon and was reported to outnumber them as much as three to one, defeated them badly at Chaldiran. The defeat destroyed Ismail's belief in his own invincibility and changed his relation to his followers.

For almost ten years afterwards rival Qizilbash factions fought for control of the kingdom, and the ten-year-old Tahmasp I, who succeeded in 1524, was at first the ward of the Qizilbash amir Ali Beg Rumlu. Tahmasp reasserted his authority, and the Qizilbash defended the kingdom against Uzbeks and Ottomans until the Peace of Amasya in 1555. Abbas I, who came to power in 1588, built a standing army and administration from Circassian, Georgian and Armenian ghulams and ended the independent rule of Turcoman chiefs in the provinces. By the end of his reign a fifth of the high-ranking amirs were ghulams.

The Qizilbash remained part of the Safavid army and administration, and the Afshar and Qajar rulers who followed the Safavids came from a Qizilbash background. By the 18th century the name was applied broadly to anyone in the service of the Safavid state. Many Qizilbash were settled in Kabul and Kandahar during the conquests of Nader Shah, and others joined the Mughal court. In Afghanistan the Qizilbash live mainly in cities such as Kabul, Kandahar and Herat; estimates of their number range from 30,000 to 200,000.
ranoji-scindia: Ranoji Scindia, also known as Ranoji Sendrak, was born about 1700 into a Maratha family. His father, Jankoji Rao I, was hereditary patil, or village head, of Kanherkhed, a village in the present Satara district of Maharashtra. In earlier centuries his forefathers had served as shiledars, cavalrymen, under the Bahmani Sultanate, and had held jagirs. As a young man he entered the service of Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath. Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar, one of the Peshwa's diplomats, recognised his talents and had him made personal bodyguard to the Peshwa's son, Baji Rao I.

When Baji Rao was appointed Peshwa at the age of twenty by Chhatrapati Shahu, the appointment aroused the jealousy of senior officials at the Maratha court. He therefore promoted talented young men, barely out of their teens, to command his troops, among them Ranoji Scindia, Malhar Rao Holkar, the Pawar brothers, Pilaji Jadhav and Fateh Singh Bhosle. None of them came from families that had held hereditary deshmukhi rights under earlier rulers such as the Deccan Sultanates.

Ranoji was in charge of the Maratha campaign that Baji Rao began in Malwa in 1726, and after it he established his capital at Ujjain in 1731. He appointed Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar as his dewan, or administrator, and Yashaji Rambhaji as commander of his army, and himself spent most of his life on campaign. Some historians credit him with bringing the Kumbh Mela to Ujjain in 1732.

Ranoji died on 3 July 1745. He had five sons: Jayappa Rao, Jyotiba Rao, Dattaji Rao, Tukoji Rao and Mahadji. The four eldest died in battles in northern India between 1750 and 1761. The dynasty went on to dominate central and northern India in the later 18th century through its presence at Delhi, its collection of chauth from neighbouring rulers and a modernised army, and his descendants ruled the princely state of Gwalior under the British.
rashid-ali-al-gaylani: Rashid Ali was the son of Sayyid Abd al-Wahhab al-Gailani and belonged to a prominent Baghdad family whose name points to an origin in Gilan in Iran and which traces its ancestry to the Prophet Muhammad; he also descended from Circassian governors of the Ottoman period. He studied at the law school in Baghdad and practised as a lawyer before entering politics.

In 1924 Yasin al-Hashimi made him minister of justice in his first government, and he was elected president of the Chamber of Deputies in 1925 and 1926. Both men were nationalists opposed to any British part in Iraq's internal politics. They rejected the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty signed by the government of Nuri as-Said in 1930 and formed the Party of National Brotherhood. Gaylani was prime minister for the first time from March to November 1933.

He returned to the premiership on 31 March 1940, after the early death of King Ghazi, when Emir Abdul-Illah was regent for the four-year-old Faisal II. Gaylani refused Allied troops passage through Iraq, rejected calls to break with Fascist Italy and sent his justice minister, Naji Shawkat, to Ankara, where on 5 July 1940 he met the German ambassador, Franz von Papen. Britain imposed economic sanctions, and under pressure from the regent he resigned on 31 January 1941.

With the Golden Square he then planned to assassinate the regent, who discovered the plot on 31 March and fled. The coup followed on 1 April, and on 3 April a National Defence Government took office under Gaylani. He sent artillery against the RAF base at Habbaniya. On 2 May the base's commander struck first at the Iraqi positions; within a week the Iraqis left the escarpment, and British forces advanced through Fallujah on Baghdad. Gaylani fled to Iran on 30 May. An armistice was signed the next day, and the regent returned on 1 June. Immediately afterwards the Farhud, a violent pogrom against Jews, took place in Baghdad.

After British and Soviet forces invaded Iran on 25 August 1941 he went on to Italy and then Berlin, where Adolf Hitler received him and he was recognised as leader of an Iraqi government in exile. On Germany's defeat he found refuge in Saudi Arabia. He returned to Iraq only after the revolution of 1958 that overthrew the monarchy, plotted a revolt against the government of Abdul Karim Kassem and was sentenced to death. Pardoned in July 1961, he lived in Lebanon, where he died on 28 August 1965 at the age of 72.
republic-of-serbian-krajina: The name Krajina, meaning frontier, came from the Military Frontier that the Habsburg monarchy carved out of Croatia and Slavonia between 1553 and 1578 against the Ottoman Empire. In the 1991 census Serbs made up about 12.2 per cent of the population of Croatia. After Franjo Tuđman was elected president of Croatia in April 1990, the Serb Democratic Party of Jovan Rašković broke with the Croatian parliament. In August 1990 Serbs blocked roads with logs in what became known as the Log Revolution, cutting Dalmatia off from the rest of the country, and a referendum confined to Serbs backed Serb sovereignty and autonomy by 99.7 per cent.

The Croatian constitution of December 1990 reduced the Serbs from a constituent people to a national minority. On 21 December 1990 the administration of Milan Babić announced a Serbian Autonomous Oblast of Krajina, which on 1 April 1991 declared that it would secede from Croatia.

Wider war began in August 1991. Between August and December approximately 80,000 Croats were expelled and some were killed; estimates of all exiled Croats and other non-Serbs range from 170,000, the figure of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, to a quarter of a million, that of Human Rights Watch. On 19 December 1991 the autonomous oblasts of Krajina and Western Slavonia proclaimed the republic, and that of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia was added on 26 February 1992.

The Vance plan and the Sarajevo Agreement of January 1992 established four United Nations Protected Areas and froze the front lines for three years. Refugees were not allowed to return. Babić, who opposed the plan, was replaced as president on 26 February 1992 by Goran Hadžić; Milan Martić won the presidency in January 1994. The economy depended wholly on the rump Yugoslavia: by 1994 only 36,000 of 430,000 citizens were employed. Croatian forces took Western Slavonia in Operation Flash in May 1995.

In Operation Storm between 150,000 and 200,000 Serbs fled, and only 5,000 to 6,000, mostly elderly, remained; some who refused to leave were murdered, tortured or expelled by the Croatian army and police. The remaining territory in eastern Slavonia was placed under a United Nations transitional authority by the Erdut Agreement and returned to Croatia in 1998.

The tribunal sentenced Babić, who pleaded guilty, to 13 years in 2004 and Milan Martić to 35 years in 2007. The Croatian generals Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač were convicted in April 2011 of crimes during Operation Storm and acquitted on appeal in November 2012.
ronnie-brunswijk: Ronnie Brunswijk was born on 7 March 1961; his birth village was Moiwana. He joined the Suriname National Army at the age of 18, was considered a good soldier and was sent to Cuba for commando training, after which he was appointed a personal bodyguard of Desi Bouterse. In 1984 he asked for a raise; instead he was discharged on 16 April and refused his back pay. He then sought recognition and rights for the Maroons of the interior, descendants of Africans who had escaped slavery and founded independent communities in the 17th and 18th centuries.

The Surinamese Interior War began at Stolkertsijver on 22 July 1986, when the Jungle Commando captured twelve soldiers guarding a checkpoint. During the war the group received arms and funding from the Netherlands. On 29 November 1986 the Surinamese army attacked Moiwana, murdered at least 39 villagers, mostly women and children, and burned Brunswijk's house; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights later ordered the government to compensate the survivors. The war caused hundreds of deaths and drove more than 10,000 refugees into French Guiana. A ceasefire was negotiated at Kourou on 21 July 1989, and a final peace treaty was signed on 8 August 1992.

A Dutch court in Haarlem convicted Brunswijk in absentia of cocaine smuggling and sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment, reduced to six years on appeal in 2000; he contested the evidence. He chairs the General Liberation and Development Party and has sat in the National Assembly. He owned a gold-mining company, Robruns NV, whose concessions he transferred to a foundation in July 2020 in order to qualify for the vice-presidency.

In the 2020 elections Brunswijk was elected to the National Assembly, and on 29 June 2020 he became its chairman. On 13 July he was elected vice-president by acclamation, with Chan Santokhi as president, and was inaugurated on 16 July. He also owns the football club Inter Moengotapoe and in 2002 built a stadium in Moengo. On 21 September 2021 he played 54 minutes for the club in the CONCACAF League against C.D. Olimpia of Honduras, aged 60 years and 198 days. After a video showed him paying Olimpia players, CONCACAF disqualified both clubs and banned him from its competitions for three years.
rurik-dynasty: Modern scholars consider Rurik a legendary and perhaps entirely fictional figure. The Primary Chronicle, of the early twelfth century, tells of the Calling of the Varangians: tribes at war with one another invited three brothers from overseas to rule them, of whom Rurik settled in Novgorod, Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor in Izborsk. No earlier Kievan source knew of Rurik, and genealogies of the princes usually stopped with Igor of Kiev. Even if Rurik existed, scholars have long doubted or rejected that he was Igor's father.

Before the mid-15th century no source claims that Rurik founded a dynasty. The tradition was set out by churchmen in the 16th century, in the Book of Royal Degrees of 1560 by Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow, which traced the ruling house of Moscow to Rurik and to a supposed kinsman of Augustus Caesar named Prus. For this reason some scholars prefer the name Volodimerovichi, descendants of Volodimer I of Kiev.

The house underwent a major schism after the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054, dividing into branches descended from his sons Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod. By the middle of the twelfth century Kievan Rus' had dissolved into independent principalities, each under a different branch. Vsevolod's line, the Monomakhovichi, named after Vladimir II Monomakh, became predominant. The Olgovichi, descended from Sviatoslav, ruled in Chernigov until the early 14th century. The Romanovichi, the line of Roman the Great, were crowned kings of Galicia and Volhynia and ruled until 1323.

In the north-east the Yurievichi descended from Yuri Dolgorukiy, the founder of Moscow. His great-grandson was Alexander Nevsky, whose son Daniel of Moscow founded the ruling house of Moscow, the Daniilovichi. In all, the house ruled for 21 generations in the male line, a period of more than 700 years. It was briefly revived in Vasili IV of Russia, of the Shuyskiy line, who died without issue. The Time of Troubles lasted until 1613, when Mikhail I founded the Romanov dynasty; his father was descended from the Rurikids through the female line.

Russian and Ukrainian historians have long debated the inheritance of Kievan Rus'. The Russian view treats the Principality of Moscow as its sole heir, resting largely on religious and historical claims. The Ukrainian view of succession, summarised most clearly by Mykhailo Hrushevsky in his History of Ukraine-Rus', is based on continuity through the Kingdom of Ruthenia, Lithuania-Ruthenia and the Cossack Hetmanate. Several branches of the family survive, among them the houses of Shakhovskoy, Gagarin and Lobanov-Rostovsky.
sadashivrao-bhau: Sadashivrao Bhau was born on 4 August 1730 at Satara into a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family, the son of Chimaji Appa, younger brother of Peshwa Baji Rao I, and Rakhmabai of the Pethe family. His mother died when he was about a month old and his father when he was ten, and he was raised by his grandmother Radhabai and his aunt Kashibai. He served as a finance minister during the reign of the Maratha ruler Rajaram II.

His first campaign was in Karnataka in 1746. He won his first battle at Ajra, south of Kolhapur, and took thirty-six parganas. In a later Carnatic campaign he conquered territory from the Nawab of Savanur and put down the revolt of Yamaji Shivdev.

Having seen the effect of artillery and light guns in British hands, he built similar units for the Maratha army. In 1760 he engaged Ibrahim Khan Gardi, a former officer of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who brought 2,500 trained soldiers and fifteen cannons. Within two years the infantry and artillery division had grown to 10,000 men and 56 guns.

Appointed to lead the army to Delhi against Ahmad Shah Abdali, he set out from Patdur on 14 March 1760 with about 55,000 men and roughly 200,000 non-combatants, including families and pilgrims. Unlike Malharrao Holkar and Raghunathrao he did not know the politics of the north. He disregarded the advice of Suraj Mal, the Jat ruler of Bharatpur, to leave the civilians at Agra. The army took Delhi on 2 August 1760 and then stormed the fort of Kunjpura, killing its entire garrison.

Abdali crossed the swollen Yamuna at Baghpat between 23 and 25 October 1760, surprised the Marathas and cut their supply lines. A two-month blockade near Panipat brought famine to the camp, where many civilians and animals died. On 14 January 1761 the Marathas tried to break out. After his nephew Vishwasrao, the Peshwa's heir, was killed around 2 p.m., Sadashivrao reportedly left his elephant and charged on horseback; the empty howdah led some troops to think him dead. He died fighting, and the remaining civilians were massacred. Some records say his headless body was recovered three days later, others that it was never found.

His widow Parvatibai, who had accompanied the campaign, refused the conventional life of widowhood. Around 1770 a man appeared in Pune claiming to be Sadashivrao; he was exposed and became known as Totayaa, the impostor. The Sadashiv Peth quarter of Pune is named after him.
samnite-wars: The Samnites were a confederation of four tribes living in the mountains east of Campania. Rome and the Samnites made a treaty in 354 BCE whose terms are not recorded; modern historians have proposed that it made the River Liris the boundary between their spheres. Livy, the only continuous source for the first war, says it began when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini and then the Campanians, and Capua surrendered itself to Rome. Modern historians doubt his three Roman victories of 343 BCE. The war ended in 341 BCE in a negotiated peace: Rome accepted that the Sidicini lay in the Samnite sphere but kept its alliance with the Campanians.

The second war grew out of Roman moves in Campania: a colony founded at Fregellae in 328 BCE and the taking of Naples in 326 BCE. In 321 BCE the consuls Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius Albinus were trapped by the Samnite commander Gaius Pontius in the Caudine Forks and surrendered; their soldiers passed unarmed under the yoke and six hundred equites were given as hostages. Livy says Rome rejected the agreement and avenged it, a claim some modern scholars doubt. Fighting resumed in 316 BCE, and in 304 BCE, after the fall of Bovianum, the Samnites sought peace; Livy says the old treaty was restored.

The third war began in 298 BCE, when the Lucanians asked for Roman protection against Samnite invasion. In 295 BCE Rome faced a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senone Gauls. At Sentinum the consul Publius Decius Mus devoted himself, charging into the enemy line to his death, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus won the battle; Livy gives 8,700 Roman dead and 20,000 of the enemy. Livy's surviving narrative ends in 293 BCE, and the last campaigns to 290 BCE are known only in outline.

The Samnites were forced to become allies of Rome, on terms that must have been unequal, and a colony was planted at Venusia in south-eastern Samnia. Gaius Pontius was captured, paraded in a triumph and beheaded. Around Samnia Rome had already bound the Marsi, Marrucini, Paeligni and Frentani by alliance in 304 BCE and the Vestini in 302 BCE, and it annexed the Hernici and the Sabines by giving them citizenship without the vote. The allies supplied soldiers at their own expense and shared the spoils, which greatly enlarged the manpower Rome could call on.
sandzak: Sandžak covers around 8,500 square kilometres between the south-eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the borders with Kosovo and Albania. Six of its municipalities are in Serbia (Novi Pazar, Sjenica, Tutin, Prijepolje, Nova Varoš and Priboj) and seven in Montenegro (Pljevlja, Bijelo Polje, Berane, Petnjica, Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav). The name is the Serbo-Croatian form of the Ottoman Turkish sancak, a province; Serbs have historically known the region as Raška, of which it was part in the 12th century.

The Ottoman Empire invaded the Serbian Despotate in 1455. The spread of Islam in Sandžak had several causes: Muslims did not pay the jizya tax or the child levy and were privileged over Christians in administration and the courts; after the Great Turkish War (1683–1699) part of the Orthodox population was driven north and the land was settled by people who were or became Muslim; and the region was a centre of trade. Until 1790 it belonged to the Sanjak of Bosnia, which is why its Muslims identify with the Slavic Muslims of Bosnia.

When Serbian and Montenegrin troops seized the region in October 1912, many Slavic Muslims and Albanians left for Ottoman Turkey. In 1919 an Albanian revolt in the Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav districts against inclusion in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was put down; seven hundred Albanians were killed in Rožaje and about 450 civilians in Plav and Gusinje.

In 1941 the region was partitioned between Italian-held Montenegro, the Italian protectorate of Albania and German-occupied Serbia, and Muslim militias, Chetniks and Partisans fought there. On 2 March 1942 the Jews of Novi Pazar were rounded up and killed in camps.
