In May 1943 Chetnik forces under Pavle Đurišić massacred an estimated 5,400 Albanian men, women and children in Bihor, and an estimated 9,000 Muslims in all were killed by Chetniks and affiliated groups during the war. A Partisan council for Sandžak, founded at Pljevlja on 20 November 1943, accepted on 29 March 1945 the division of the region along the line of 1912.

The municipalities of Sandžak have around 361,656 inhabitants. Bosniaks form 54.8 per cent, Serbs 30 per cent, Montenegrins 5 per cent, people who declare themselves Muslims by ethnicity 3.4 per cent and Albanians 1 per cent. Novi Pazar is the economic and cultural centre. A referendum on autonomy organised by the Muslim National Council of Sandžak between 25 and 27 October 1991 was declared illegal by Serbia. The region remains underdeveloped, and census data show emigration by all its peoples.
sarissa: A sarissa had two main parts, a long wooden shaft and a metal tip; some may also have had a metal butt at the other end, with which the weapon could be stood in the ground without damage to the shaft. Ash, which is long, flexible and light, and cornel wood, which is shorter but stronger, are the likeliest woods. It replaced the considerably shorter dory.

Ancient writers agree that its length set it apart, but not on the figure: Theophrastus, a contemporary of Alexander the Great, puts the longest at 12 cubits, and Polybius gives 16 cubits in the original design, reduced in practice to 14. In modern units this suggests about 5.8 m in Alexander's time and perhaps 6.3 m later.

The weapon needed both hands, so the phalangite carried only a smaller shield, the pelta, perhaps hung from a neck strap. On the march the sarissas were held upright; levelled for battle, fully five rows of points projected in front of the first rank, while the rear ranks held theirs angled upward, which also deflected arrows. A phalanx so formed was considered practically invulnerable from the front, but it turned with difficulty, and a soldier out of formation had to fall back on a sword or dagger.

Sarissa-armed phalanxes were vital in the early battles of Alexander, including the Battle of Gaugamela, though in his later campaigns he gradually reduced their importance. The surest way to beat such a phalanx was to break its formation or outflank it, as the Romans did at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. A light cavalry unit of Alexander's army, the sarissophoroi, carried somewhat shorter versions; Nicholas Victor Sekunda argues that the Macedonian cavalry spear is better classed as a xyston.

A leaf-shaped spearhead 51 cm long, found by Manolis Andronikos in a Macedonian tomb at Vergina, shaped much scholarship between 1970 and 2000, but more recent work doubts that it belonged to a sarissa; Sekunda favours a small diamond-shaped iron tip of about 13.5 cm. Earlier estimates put the weight at 5.5 to 6.5 kg, yet Peter Connolly reconstructed a pike 5.8 m long in cherry wood that weighed only 4.05 kg. Scholars also draw on later pikemen, such as the Swiss and the German Landsknecht: preserved English pikes are 5.6 to 5.9 m long, which suggests that the lengths reported for the Macedonian weapon were workable.
schmalkaldic-league: The League was officially established on 27 February 1531 as a defensive religious alliance: its members pledged to defend each other if Emperor Charles V attacked their territories. At the insistence of the Elector of Saxony, membership was conditional on agreement to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession. Unlike earlier alliances such as the League of Torgau it had a substantial military, the members agreeing to provide 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry for their mutual protection.

Its formation, together with the advance of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1532, led Ferdinand of Austria to grant a religious peace, concluded at Nuremberg on 23 July 1532. Supporters of the Reformation obtained religious liberty until the meeting of a council.

In December 1535 the League opened itself to anyone who subscribed to the Augsburg Confession, and Anhalt, Württemberg, Pomerania and the cities of Augsburg, Frankfurt am Main and Kempten joined. It allied with Denmark-Norway in 1538 and gained the Electoral Palatinate in 1545. The members rarely provoked Charles directly, but they confiscated church land, expelled bishops and Catholic princes and helped spread Lutheranism through northern Germany. Martin Luther attended the meeting of 1537, for which he prepared the Smalcald Articles; they were not formally adopted then but entered the Book of Concord in 1580.

For fifteen years the League met no opposition, because Charles was at war with France and the Ottoman Empire. Francis I of France, though he persecuted Protestants at home, supported the princes from 1535 until the Treaty of Crépy in 1544. Once at peace, Charles turned on the League. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 its leaders could not agree on a plan of battle; on 24 April 1547 the imperial forces routed them at the Battle of Mühlberg, and Philip of Hesse surrendered in May. Reformers such as Martin Bucer fled to England.

In 1548 Charles forced the League to accept the Augsburg Interim. A Protestant victory in the Second Schmalkaldic War in 1552 made him flee across the Alps, and Ferdinand signed the Peace of Passau, which granted some freedoms to Protestants. Three years later the Peace of Augsburg gave Lutheranism official status in the Holy Roman Empire and let princes choose the religion of their domains, by the principle of cuius regio, eius religio.
scholar-officials: The Chinese term, shi dafu, joins two ranks that were once distinct. In the order ascribed to the Duke of Zhou under the Western Zhou dynasty, the dafu were aristocrats who served as officers, and the shi stood between them and the ordinary people and could hold only low offices. During the Warring States period, as states annexed one another and bureaucracies grew, talented shi gave valuable service to their lords and gained influence, while dafu became an office and ceased to be a hereditary rank. The two merged. In the scheme of the Four Occupations the scholar-officials stood first, above farmers, artisans and merchants.

From the Han dynasty to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, officials were chosen through the recommendatory and nine-rank systems, and came mostly from prominent clans such as the Wang clan of Langya and the Cui clan of Qinghe, which supplied officials for generations and intermarried with one another and with the imperial family. The civil service examination was officially established in 587 under the Sui dynasty. In the early Tang dynasty Empress Wu Zetian reformed it by instituting a metropolitan examination, whose graduates were called jinshi; candidates were tested on poems and essays.

The Song dynasty is described as the golden age of the class. Examination had become the main path to office and the bureaucracy replaced the aristocracy. The Song was also the only dynasty to grant scholar-officials a judicial privilege: one who committed a crime faced internal impeachment in place of the ordinary courts, and for a lesser offence only a reprimand. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties the fixed form of the eight-legged essay dominated the examinations, and the political climate left officials less free to speak and write. The Qing government abolished the examinations in 1905, and the class gradually disappeared.

Only a few degree-holders became court or local officials. Most stayed in their villages and towns as social leaders: they taught in private schools, organised welfare, helped settle minor disputes, supervised community projects, kept local order, conducted Confucian ceremonies and assisted in collecting taxes. The district magistrate, who was barred from serving in his home district, depended on them for advice, which gave them power to benefit themselves and their clients. In Confucian theory ministers were not mere subordinates and might oppose an unfit ruler. The system offered a path of upward mobility but had no formal safeguard against corruption beyond the moral teaching it examined.
sextus-pompey: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius was the son of Pompey by his third wife, Mucia Tertia, with an elder brother, Gnaeus Pompeius, and a sister, Pompeia. When Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, Gnaeus followed their father to the East while Sextus stayed in Rome in the care of his stepmother, Cornelia Metella. After the defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE the two met Pompey on Lesbos and fled with him to Egypt, where Sextus watched his father killed by treachery on 29 September of that year.

He then joined the resistance to Caesar in the African provinces alongside Metellus Scipio, Cato the Younger and his brother. Caesar defeated the Pompeius brothers at the Battle of Munda in Hispania in 45 BCE. Gnaeus died soon afterwards in a last stand at Lauro; Sextus escaped and raised another army in Spain.

After Caesar's death Mark Antony moved that Sextus be recalled, paid 50 million Attic drachmas for his father's confiscated property and given command of the whole Roman navy. He accepted, but went no further than Massilia before returning to Sicily. When the Second Triumvirate began its proscriptions, many of the proscribed fled to him, and after the battles of Philippi in 42 BCE survivors of the party of Brutus and Cassius did the same. With the whole island as his base he built an army and a strong navy.

In 40 BCE his admiral, the freedman Menas, seized Sardinia from Octavian's governor Marcus Lurius. By the Pact of Misenum in 39 BCE the triumvirs recognised his control of Sicily and Sardinia in exchange for keeping the grain supply to Rome open and his pirates in check. The peace was short. Each side accused the other of breaking it, and Menas betrayed Sardinia to Octavian. Sextus defeated Octavian at sea off Messina in 37 BCE.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa spent a winter building and training a fleet near Lake Avernus. He fought Sextus at Mylae in August 36 BCE, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Titus Statilius Taurus invaded Sicily, and after Naulochus Sextus fled to Asia Minor. Captured in 35 BCE, he was put to death without trial at Miletus by Marcus Titius, whom he had once spared, either on Titius's own initiative or possibly on the orders of Antony or Plancus. Plutarch gives him a minor role in the fall of the Republic; Appian treats him as a central figure who might even have emerged as the final victor.
shaduf: One theory holds that the shadoof was invented in Mesopotamia as early as the time of Sargon of Akkad, around the 24th and 23rd centuries BCE. The Minoans are believed to have adopted it next, with evidence of its use from around 2100–1600 BCE. Its appearance in Upper Egypt is placed most likely in the 18th Dynasty. Some historians believe instead that the Egyptians invented it along the Nile, citing tomb drawings of shadoofs at Thebes from 1250 BCE. A third theory places its origin in India at about the same time as in Mesopotamia, because it was so widespread there, but little other evidence supports it.

The pole is hung on its frame about one-fifth of its length from one end. The vessel on the long arm may be a bucket, a skin bag or a reed basket coated with bitumen, and some have an uneven base or a tie at the top so that the water runs out at once. The operator pushes the vessel down with his own weight, and the counterweight raises it full without effort. The water is emptied into runnels that carry it along irrigation ditches. The frame may be one post or a pair, and the vessel may hang from a rope or from a thinner stick.

The device lifts water from 1 to 6 metres, and its efficiency has been calculated at 60 per cent. A study in Nigeria, which measured effort by heart rate, found that suitable adjustments reduced the energy the operator spent from about 109 to 71 watts.

In ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia shadoofs set in tiers, one above another, raised water to higher levels by the work of several people. In Egypt under the Middle and New Kingdoms, pleasure gardens watered by shadoof became a mark of luxury residences and a symbol of status. Women have often worked it, since it is easy to use.

The name comes from the Arabic šādūf; in English it is also called a well sweep or swape. The ancient Greeks knew it as the kēlōn or kēlōneion, the Chinese call it jiégāo, and its Hungarian name, gémeskút, means heron well. Today it is very common in rural India and Pakistan, and in Europe in Ukraine, Belarus, Poland and Germany. On the Great Hungarian Plain it is considered a symbol of the region.
siege-engine: Siege engines ranged from the size of a small house to that of a large building. Some were built in place to attack from a distance, while others stood on wheels so that they could be advanced to the walls. From antiquity until the development of gunpowder they were made largely of wood, bound with rope or leather and possibly strengthened with a few pieces of metal at points of stress. Those that threw projectiles built up force by tension, by torsion or, in the trebuchet, by human power or a counterweight.

The earliest siege engines appear to be simple movable roofed towers, used with scaling ladders, depicted during the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. The Assyrians used battering rams, and in Kush siege towers and rams were built from the 8th century BCE. The Carthaginians used towers and rams against the Greek colonies of Sicily, which influenced Dionysius I of Syracuse, who developed a catapult in 399 BCE. Philip II of Macedonia and Alexander the Great were the first rulers to use siege engines to a large extent. The Helepolis of Demetrius Poliorcetes, of 304 BCE, was nine stories high, plated with iron, 40 metres tall and weighed 180 tonnes.

The Romans preferred to build earthen ramps or simply to scale the walls, their soldiers working under shelters called vineae. Roman legions first used siege towers around 200 BCE, and the onager was the main Roman invention in the field. In China the earliest documented siege artillery, a levered traction catapult and a large siege crossbow, is described in the Mozi, a Mohist text of about the 4th to 3rd century BCE.

Medieval armies used catapults such as the mangonel, the ballista, the traction trebuchet, first designed in China in the 3rd century BCE, and the counterweight trebuchet, first described by Mardi bin Ali al-Tarsusi in the 12th century though of unknown origin. Besiegers could also starve a castle out, set fires against its walls, dig mines under the foundations or throw diseased animals and human corpses over the walls to spread disease.

With gunpowder came the cannon, the petard and the mortar, which proved so effective that fortifications had to be built low and thick, as in the designs of Vauban. Specialised siege artillery culminated in the two world wars, with guns such as Big Bertha and the German Schwerer Gustav, a railway gun of 80 cm calibre. Such guns took so long to move and deploy that they were vulnerable to air attack and unsuited to rapid warfare.
socialist-party-of-albania: The Party of Labour of Albania, founded by Enver Hoxha, had ruled the country for over four decades. Hoxha's successor, Ramiz Alia, was forced to introduce limited reforms in the late 1980s, and on 11 December 1990 he announced that the party had given up its monopoly of power. It won the Constitutional Assembly election of 1991, the first free elections held in Albania in almost 80 years, by which time it was no longer a Marxist-Leninist party. At an extraordinary congress held from 10 to 13 June 1991 it reorganised itself as the Socialist Party in order to survive in the new system.

Fatos Nano, a man from the intelligentsia, was elected the first chairman. He helped to reform the old communist party and brought it into the Socialist International. In 2004 a faction led by Ilir Meta broke away and formed the Socialist Movement for Integration. On 10 October 2005, after losing the parliamentary election of that year, Nano resigned and was succeeded by Edi Rama.

Under Rama the party formed the Alliance for a European Albania, which united several parties and won the parliamentary election of 2013, returning the Socialists to government after eight years. Running alone, the party won the elections of 2017 and 2021 with 74 seats in each, enough to govern by itself, though it has had the outside support of the Social Democratic Party in parliament.

The party is described as social-democratic. Its platform of 2013 pledged to replace the flat tax with a progressive tax and supported universal health care. It is pro-European, supports Albania's accession to the European Union and its membership of NATO, and regards Kosovo as the country's main strategic partner and ally. It is an associate of the Party of European Socialists. Its emblem is based on the fist and rose designed by José María Cruz Novillo for the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party in 1977, used without that party's official consent.
sonderbund-war: In the early 1840s the radical Free Democratic Party of Switzerland, strong in the largely Protestant cantons and among the urban bourgeoisie, won a majority in the Federal Diet, the Tagsatzung, and proposed a new constitution that would draw the cantons closer together. The Diet had also acted against the Catholic Church, closing the monasteries and convents of Aargau in 1841 and seizing their property. When Lucerne recalled the Jesuits to head its education, bands of armed radicals known as Freischärler invaded the canton.

In 1845 Lucerne, Fribourg, Valais, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, all predominantly Catholic and under conservative governments, formed the Sonderbund, or separate alliance. Ticino and Solothurn, Catholic but liberal, stayed out. On 21 October 1847 the Diet ordered the league dissolved as a breach of the Federal Treaty of 1815, which forbade such alliances. Austria sent the Sonderbund some money and munitions, but the great powers could not agree on intervention, which Lord Palmerston of Britain refused to support.

The Sonderbund's commander was Jean-Ulrich de Salis-Soglio of Grisons, himself a Protestant. The Diet's choice, Guillaume Henri Dufour of Geneva, was sworn in on 25 October after first declining the office. Neuchâtel and Appenzell Innerrhoden declared themselves neutral and sent no troops. The Sonderbund moved first: troops from Uri seized the St. Gotthard Pass in early November, and the first deaths came on 4 November.

Dufour turned first on isolated Fribourg, which surrendered on 14 November; its act of surrender became the template for the other cantons. Zug's parliament voted to give up on 21 November. On 23 November the federal divisions converged on Lucerne. At Gisikon a third assault, led in person by Colonel Eduard Ziegler, carried the Sonderbund position after two hours; thirty-seven men were killed and about 100 wounded. Federal troops entered Lucerne unopposed the next morning. Unterwalden, Schwyz and Uri yielded between 25 and 27 November, and Valais on 29 November.

The federal army reported 78 killed and 260 wounded; later research arrived at 60 dead and 386 wounded on the federal side and 33 killed and 124 wounded among the Sonderbund. Dufour had ordered his troops to care for the injured and declined to use Congreve rockets, so as not to give the war a violent character. The Sonderbund governments were forced to resign, and Liberals took power in Fribourg, Lucerne and Valais. Federal troops left the occupied cantons by February 1848. The constitution of that year banished the Jesuits from Switzerland, a provision lifted by a vote on 20 May 1973.
state-protection-authority: The force began in 1945 as the Budapest Department of State Political Police. In 1946 it became the State Defence Department of the Hungarian State Police, the ÁVO, and in 1950 the State Protection Authority. Gábor Péter headed it from 1945 to 1952. László Rajk, the Communist minister of the interior, played a crucial part in organising it, and in 1949 became one of its victims: he was arrested, tried for nationalism and Titoism and executed. On 1 January 1950 the authority was removed from the Ministry of the Interior, made independent and given the Border Guard.

The authority served the Hungarian Working People's Party directly, with little reference to the norms of government, and its actions were not subject to judicial review until the early years after Stalin. It gathered intelligence through a vast network of informants. Secret arrests were followed by periods of torture lasting from 3 to 18 months, after which the public prosecutors and courts were called in to pass sentence.

Prisons and internment camps were placed under its supervision, the most notorious at Recsk, Kistarcsa, Tiszalök and Kazincbarcika. Before 1953 some camps aimed at the eventual death of their inmates through overwork and maltreatment. The first government of Imre Nagy, from 1953 to 1955, greatly improved conditions in the camps and ended these efforts.

In 1953 the authority prepared a show trial meant to prove that Raoul Wallenberg had not been taken to the Soviet Union in 1945 but had been killed by Zionists in Budapest. Leaders of the Jewish community, among them Miksa Domonkos and Lajos Stöckler, and two intended witnesses were seized and tortured. After the death of Stalin the preparations were stopped and the prisoners released in the autumn of 1953. Domonkos died shortly afterwards, mainly from the torture.

On 29 October 1956, during the revolution, the militia of József Dudás stormed the secret police headquarters and massacred the officers inside, and the crowd lynched others. The students' and workers' councils then set up armed patrols to detain members of the authority for their own safety and for later trial. When Soviet forces intervened, its officers carried out brutal reprisals against revolutionaries.

The government of János Kádár, who had himself been tortured by the authority, did not revive it under its old name. Its work passed to a department of the Ministry of the Interior, known as III, which operated with considerably more restraint. Its former headquarters at 60 Andrássy Avenue in Budapest is now a museum, the House of Terror.
stuart-restoration: Richard Cromwell, Lord Protector from 1658 to 1659, ceded power to the Rump Parliament, and for a year government was dominated by the army leaders Charles Fleetwood and John Lambert. On 20 October 1659 George Monck, governor of Scotland under the Cromwells, marched south to oppose them. Lambert's army melted away and Monck reached London unopposed. The Presbyterian members excluded in Pride's Purge of 1648 were recalled, and on 24 December the Long Parliament was restored.

On 4 April 1660 Charles issued the Declaration of Breda, setting out his promises on recovering the crown. Monck organised the Convention Parliament, which first met on 25 April and on 8 May proclaimed that Charles II had been lawful king since the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649. Charles left The Hague on 23 May, landed at Dover on 25 May and entered London on 29 May, his thirtieth birthday, a date kept afterwards as the holiday of Oak Apple Day. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1661.

The Indemnity and Oblivion Act, law from 29 August 1660, pardoned past treason but excluded those involved in the trial and execution of Charles I. In October 1660 ten men were hanged, drawn and quartered in London, among them Thomas Harrison and the preacher Hugh Peters; three more followed on 19 April 1662, and a further 19 were imprisoned for life. In January 1661 the corpses of Oliver Cromwell, Henry Ireton and John Bradshaw were exhumed and hanged in chains at Tyburn.

The Cavalier Parliament, overwhelmingly royalist, met on 8 May 1661 and sat until 24 January 1679. The leading minister of the first years was Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon, and the Church of England was restored as the national church, backed by the Clarendon Code and the Act of Uniformity 1662. In Scotland the Rescissory Act 1661 annulled all legislation back to 1633; in Ireland the union of the Commonwealth years was treated as void, and James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, returned as Lord Lieutenant in 1662.

The colonies followed at different speeds. Barbados declared for the king in July 1660, Rhode Island in October 1660 and Massachusetts last, in August 1661; New Haven, which sheltered three regicides, was merged into Connecticut in 1662. The period is commonly taken to end with the Glorious Revolution of 1688, when William of Orange landed on 5 November and James II fled to France, and with the Bill of Rights 1689.
suniti-devi: Suniti Devi was born on 30 September 1864, a daughter of Keshub Chandra Sen of Calcutta and Jagonmohini Sen. She was fourteen when she married. For two years afterwards she stayed in her father's house, since her husband left for London for higher studies immediately after the wedding. She had four sons and three daughters. Two of her sons, Rajendra Narayan and Jitendra Narayan, later became Maharajas of Cooch Behar. Her daughters Sudhira and Pratibha married the brothers Alan and Miles Mander of Wightwick Manor in England, and Sukriti married Jyotsna Nath Ghoshal, a nephew of Rabindranath Tagore.

In 1887, when she attended the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria with her husband, she was made a Companion of the Order of the Crown of India, the first Indian woman to receive the honour. She was also present at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

The girls' school that her husband set up in her name in 1881, later called Suniti Academy, was her idea. She gave it annual grants, exempted the pupils from tuition fees and rewarded those who did well. She arranged for palace cars to carry the girls between home and school and, to avoid controversy, ordered the car windows to be curtained. With her sister Sucharu Devi, Maharani of Mayurbhanj, she financed the foundation of the Maharani Girls' High School in Darjeeling in 1908. She was President of the State Council and in 1932 the first President of the All Bengal Women's Union.

She was also an author. Bengal Dacoits and Tigers, a collection of short stories, was published in Calcutta in 1916. The Beautiful Mogul Princesses, published in London in 1918, tells the lives of Mumtaz Mahal, Zebunissa, Nur Jahan and another princess. The Autobiography of an Indian Princess appeared in London in 1921, and her last book, The Life of Princess Yashodara: Wife and Disciple of the Lord Buddha, in 1929. She died suddenly at Ranchi on 10 November 1932. In Cooch Behar the school, Sunity Road and a tank known as the Sunity Tank or Bairagi Dighi are named after her.
treaty-of-ghilajharighat: The Treaty of Asurar Ali of 1639 fixed the limit between Ahom and Mughal interests at the Barnadi river on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and the Asurar Ali on the south. During the Mughal war of succession of 1658–1659 Pran Narayan, king of Koch Bihar, attacked the Mughal faujdar at Guwahati. The Ahoms refused a Koch offer to partition Kamrup, drove the Koches out and took the whole valley up to the Sankosh River.

Aurangzeb made Mir Jumla II subahdar of Bengal. He annexed Koch Bihar in December 1661, recovered Guwahati on 5 February 1662 and occupied Garhgaon on 17 March. The rains from April turned the country to marsh and brought food shortage and cholera to the camps, while the Ahoms waged the guerrilla warfare devised by Atan Burhagohain. When the rains ended the Mughals recovered and the king withdrew to Namrup. The Ahom commander-in-chief, Baduli Phukan, defected at the end of November, and Mir Jumla, by then ill, reached Tipam by 18 December with a worn-out army eager to go home.

Atan Burhagohain persuaded the king that further fighting was futile and sent four emissaries offering tribute if the Mughals left Assam. Mir Jumla, who had refused everything short of unconditional surrender, took the opening and left the bargaining to Dilir Khan. The terms are pieced together from Persian and Assamese sources that do not fully agree.

The king accepted Mughal vassalage; his daughter Ramani Gabharu went to the imperial harem with a dowry of 20,000 tolas of gold and 120,000 of silver. The indemnity was 300,000 tolas of silver within a year and 90 elephants in instalments, the annual tribute 20 elephants. Four sons of leading nobles were to be hostages. The ceded land ran from Guwahati to the Bharali River on the north bank and to the Kolong River on the south.

The princess left on 5 January 1663 with the gold, silver and part of the elephants, and Mir Jumla ordered the retreat from Tipam on 10 January. He died on board on 31 March 1663. Jayadhwaj Singha founded a new capital at Bakata and died in November 1663; his cousin succeeded as Chakradhar Singha. Neither king could accept tributary status, and the terms were only partly fulfilled. The treaty was the root of the later conflicts, which ended with the Mughal defeat at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671 and, after the Battle of Itakhuli in 1682, the end of Mughal interests in the Brahmaputra valley.
tukoji-rao-holkar-iii: Tukoji was born on 26 November 1890, the son of Shivajirao Holkar, Maharaja of Indore, and Maharani Sita Bai. His father abdicated on 31 January 1903, and as the new maharaja was only thirteen a council of regency governed until he came of age. He was educated at the Daly College in Indore and at Dehradun. On 6 November 1911 he was invested with ruling powers, and in the same year he attended the coronation of King George V in London.

As ruler he founded two orders, the Order of Merit of Holkar in February 1914 and the Order of Ahilyabai Holkar on 22 November 1920. In the New Year Honours of 1918 he was made a Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Star of India.

In January 1925 Mumtaz Begum, a courtesan and one of his mistresses, left his harem after what she described as repressive conditions and the death of her daughter, which she blamed on palace nurses. While performing in Bombay she met Abdul Bawla, a 25-year-old Memon businessman, who was threatened several times and told to send her back, and refused. On 12 January a group of assassins attacked the couple at Malabar Hill. Bawla was shot in the head and killed; Mumtaz Begum survived with a wound to the face after British officers who were nearby intervened.

She testified against nine accused, among them men of the maharaja's household. The court sentenced three men to death and three to life imprisonment. One of the latter, General Anandrao Gangram Phanse of the Indore army, escaped the death penalty after being represented by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The court did not formally hold Tukoji responsible, but under British pressure he abdicated on 26 February 1926 and left Indore.

After his abdication he lived mainly in France. He had married three times. His senior wife, Chandravati Gawade, whom he married on 16 March 1895 when both were small children, stayed in Indore and brought up their son, the new maharaja. His second wife, Indira Talcherkar, married in 1913, also remained there and became a patron of historical research bodies such as the Rajwade Historical Research Institute.

In 1928 he married Nancy Anne Miller, who before the wedding embraced Hinduism, was received into the Dhangar community and took the name Sharmista Devi Holkar; they had four daughters. The Bawla case inspired a film of 1925, Kulin Kanta, and two books. Tukoji died in Paris on 21 May 1978, leaving one son and six daughters.
ulises-heureaux: Ulises Hilarión Heureaux Leibert, nicknamed Lilís, was born in Puerto Plata on 21 October 1845. His father, José D'Assás Heureaux Fortune, was born in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, the son of a judge of the civil court there and a member of his household staff; his mother, Josefa Leibert, was born on the island of Saint Thomas. He spoke French and English fluently as well as Spanish. In the rebellion that followed the Spanish annexation of 1861 he became the principal lieutenant of Gregorio Luperón. In 1876 he organised an uprising that seized Puerto Plata and led to the election of Ulises Espaillat.

When Luperón became president in 1879 and stayed in Puerto Plata, he delegated authority in Santo Domingo to Heureaux. Under the priest Fernando Meriño, president from September 1880, Heureaux was interior minister, and Meriño handed the government to him on 1 September 1882. In 1884 Luperón backed General Segundo Imbert as successor; Heureaux promised to respect the result but had ballot boxes stuffed for General Francisco Gregorio Billini. Billini was driven to resign on 16 May 1885. In the 1886 election the fraud committed by Heureaux was so blatant that supporters of his opponent, Casimiro de Moya, rose in the Cibao Valley, and he suppressed the rising brutally.

In 1888 he exiled Luperón, and the next year he forced Congress to abolish the bar on presidential re-election and to end direct elections. He brought members of both rival factions, the Rojos and the Azules, into his government, and kept an extensive network of secret police and informants, assassinating or exiling the politicians he could not co-opt. Cuban planters who arrived after the Ten Years' War received large tracts of the southeastern coastal plain and built the country's first mechanised sugar mills. His government electrified Santo Domingo, bridged the Ozama River and began a railway from Santiago to Puerto Plata.

In 1888 he borrowed three-quarters of a million pounds sterling from the Amsterdam house of Westendorp, which went bankrupt in 1892. The San Domingo Improvement Co. of New York bought out its claims. In 1897, with the country near bankruptcy, he printed five million dollars of unsecured paper money, the papeletas de Lilís, which ruined many merchants and helped to provoke a revolt among the tobacco planters and merchants of the Cibao. He was killed by Ramón Cáceres on 26 July 1899. The national debt then exceeded 35 million dollars, fifteen times the annual budget; the government declared bankruptcy, and the American military intervened.
ulugh-khan: Ulugh Khan was originally named Almas Beg. His father, Shihabuddin Mas'ud, was the elder brother of Sultan Jalaluddin, founder of the Khalji dynasty, and both Almas Beg and his elder brother Alauddin married daughters of Jalaluddin. Under Jalaluddin he held the post of Akhur-beg, equivalent to master of the horse. In 1296, after Alauddin had raided Devagiri and kept the loot, Almas Beg assured the sultan of his brother's loyalty and persuaded him to visit Kara, where Alauddin killed him on 20 July 1296. The new sultan made his brother barbeg with the title Ulugh Khan, meaning Great Khan. He also held the iqta' of Bayana.

In November 1296 Alauddin sent him and Zafar Khan with an army of 30,000 to 40,000 against Multan, held by Jalaluddin's son Arkali Khan. After two months of siege the leaders of the defence went over to Delhi. Ulugh Khan promised Arkali Khan and his brother Ruknuddin Ibrahim that they would not be harmed, but imprisoned them once the city was occupied; they were later blinded or killed by Nusrat Khan on Alauddin's orders. According to the courtier Amir Khusrau, he reached the Sutlej River on 6 February 1298 and defeated the Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate there, with 20,000 Mongol dead.

On the way back from Gujarat in 1299, near Jalore, he and Nusrat Khan punished soldiers for withholding the khums, the fifth of the loot due to the treasury. Recently converted Mongol soldiers mutinied; some 2,000 to 3,000 attacked his camp and killed a nephew of Alauddin whom they took for him. Against Hammira of Ranthambore in 1301 he defeated and killed the general Bhimasimha at the Banas River, but after Nusrat Khan was killed in the siege he was forced back to Jhain, and Alauddin came in person and took the fort in July 1301.

Ordered to prepare a march on the Kakatiya capital Warangal, he assembled a large army but died a few months later. The chronicler Ziauddin Barani writes that Alauddin was greatly depressed and gave much in charity for his brother's soul. Barani's contemporary Isami claims instead that Alauddin had him poisoned, suspecting that he had been ready to take the throne when the sultan was wrongly reported dead; later chroniclers repeat this. The historian Banarsi Prasad Saksena dismisses Isami's account as false, while Kishori Saran Lal thinks it not impossible. Claims that he led the invasion of Gujarat in 1304, or governed it for 20 years, are of doubtful accuracy.
umar-marvi: The tale is said to date back to the 14th century and probably originated in the Soomra period, between 1050 and 1350. It was first written down in the 16th century by Shah Abdul Karim of Bulri, the great-great-grandfather of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, in his Bayan ul Arifeen, known to Sindhis as Karim Jo Risalo. It also appears in two chronicles, the Tarikh-i Tahiri, compiled in 1621, and the Tuhfat-al-Kiram of 1766–67.

In the story as it is told, Marvi is a young Khaskheli girl of the Panhwar tribe, and her captor is Umar Soomro, then ruler of Umerkot, who wanted to marry her for her beauty. When she refused him she was held for several years in Umarkot Fort. She resists both the ruler's overtures and the temptation to live in the palace as a queen, preferring a simple rural life among her own village people.

In the Shah Jo Risalo the tale stands among seven popular tragic romances of Sindh, with Sassui Punnhun, Sohni Mehar, Lilan Chanesar, Noori Jam Tamachi, Sorath Rai Diyach and Momal Rano. Their heroines are commonly known as the Seven Queens of Sindh, or the seven heroines of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. Marvi is regarded, for her courage, as a symbol of love for one's soil.

The story has been retold in modern forms. A film, Umar Marvi, directed by Shaikh Hassan and produced by Syed Hussain Ali Shah Fazlani, who also acted in it, was released on 12 March 1956 as the first Sindhi-language feature film made in Pakistan. The Pakistan Television Corporation broadcast a serial, Marvi, in 1993, which set the story in modern times. The Indian writer Ram Panjwani wrote a Sindhi play, Umar Marui, and a Sindhi song of Coke Studio's fifteenth season, Aayi Aayi, was inspired by the tale.
verica: Verica's coinage presents him as a son of Commius and king of the Atrebates, a tribe that was probably Belgic. His predecessors are likely to have influenced a wide area covering Berkshire, Surrey, western Kent, Sussex, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The distribution of his own coins shows a much smaller kingdom, limited to modern Sussex and east Hampshire, with its capital in or near the later Roman town of Noviomagus Reginorum, the modern Chichester. He succeeded his elder brother Eppillus in about 15 CE.

He may also have ruled the northern Atrebatic kingdom at Calleva Atrebatum, the modern Silchester. Rome recognised him as rex, and he appears to have had friendly trading and diplomatic links with the empire, perhaps in an attempt to restore the kingdom to its former strength. Unlike those of nearby areas, the hillforts in the core of his kingdom show no sign of refortification, which implies that its inhabitants were well disposed to Rome.

The Catuvellauni pressed on his territory from the east. Epaticcus, brother of Cunobelinus, conquered Calleva in about 25 CE. After the death of Epaticcus about 35 CE Verica regained some territory, but Caratacus, the son of Cunobelinus, conquered the entire kingdom some time after 40 CE. By the time of his expulsion the kingdom had been reduced to a core around Chichester and the Manhood Peninsula.

Dio Cassius records that a Berikos, widely taken to be Verica, fled to the emperor Claudius because of a revolt, and Suetonius mentions British demands that Rome return certain deserters. His ties with Rome have been used to argue that the invasion landed on the south coast and not at the traditional site of Richborough in Kent. He may have been restored afterwards, but this is not attested, and a new ruler of the region, Cogidubnus, soon appeared; he may have been Verica's heir.

Most scholars take Verica to have been a man. The archaeologist Miles Russell has argued that Verica was a woman, citing the ending of the name and the horsewomen on the coinage. Roger Tomlin disputes this, since no female client ruler is known to have used the title rex, and Daphne Nash notes that some coins show Verica with an Adam's apple and in male priestly dress.
vikramaditya-i: Vikramaditya was one of several sons of Pulakeshin II; the later Chalukyas of Kalyani made him a son of Pulakeshin's son Adityavarman, a statement that can be dismissed as inaccurate. Pulakeshin was defeated and probably killed when the Pallavas invaded Vatapi around 642, and the history of the next decade is unclear. The throne may have passed to Adityavarman, his son Abhinavaditya and then another brother, Chandraditya, whose widow Vijaya-Bhattarika appears to have acted as regent for their minor son.

During that regency Vikramaditya seems to have risen as supreme commander of the army and ruler in practice. His inscriptions say that he recovered the regal fortune of his father, which had been concealed by three kings. The historian K. A. Nilakanta Sastri took these to include his brothers and supposed a partition of the kingdom, but there is no evidence of one; D. C. Sircar and others hold that he fought the Pallavas as a subordinate of his brothers and took the throne only after their deaths. His Gadval inscription of about 674, dated to his twelfth regnal year, places his accession about 655.

With the help of his maternal grandfather, a king of the Western Ganga dynasty, Vikramaditya ended a Pallava occupation that had lasted thirteen years. He gave his loyal younger brother Jayasimhavarma the viceroyalty of Lata in southern Gujarat. Against the Pallava kings Mahendravarman II and Paramesvaravarman I he allied himself with the Pandyas, and by 670 he had a military camp at Malliyur, west of Kanchipuram. Chalukya records claim that he defeated Paramesvaravarman I and took Kanchi but did not destroy it; the writer Anirudh Kanisetti holds that the city was sacked.

Chalukya records place him in camp at Uragapura on the south bank of the Kaveri river on 25 April 674. At Peruvalanallur he met Paramesvaravarman I and a Pandya king, and Pallava and Pandya records alike claim that the Chalukyas were defeated there. Pallava inscriptions also speak of the destruction of the city of Ranarasika, an epithet of Vikramaditya, but several historians question whether Vatapi was sacked a second time; Chalukya records credit his son Vinayaditya and grandson Vijayaditya with defeating the invaders.

Vikramaditya bore titles that advertised his military power, among them Rana-rasika, lover of war, Anivarita, unopposed, and Raja-malla, royal wrestler. He was married to the Western Ganga princess Gangamahadevi. Under him the Chalukya kingdom recovered most of the territory it had controlled under Pulakeshin II. He died in 680 and was succeeded by his son Vinayaditya.
warli: Until the 1870s the Warli were the primary owners of all land in the Umbergaon, Dhanu and Palghar talukas of the Thane district. In that decade the British colonial administration brought their territories under direct control, and outsiders, among them Mahajans and petty officers, used the Warlis' illiteracy to take their lands. The Warli became labourers on land they had owned. Under the begar system they cultivated the landlords' holdings without pay; as sharecroppers on small plots of inferior land they surrendered at least half the produce. Records of the period document public whippings, torture and the sexual oppression of Warli women.

In 1939 an inquiry by the British magistrate David Symington found that their living conditions had reached an abysmal depth. Organised resistance followed, led by Shamrao and Godavari Parulekar. In May 1945 about 5,000 Warlis gathered at Zari and pledged to end the begar system. In October 1945 police fired on a rally of 7,000 people at Talwada, killing five activists, among them the leader Jethya Gangad. The begar system was abolished and minimum wages were established, and by the early 1950s most of the feudal exactions had ended.

The Warli speak Varli, an unwritten language of the southern zone of the Indo-Aryan languages. They have animistic beliefs of their own and have also adopted many Hindu beliefs. Traditionally semi-nomadic, living in small groups led by a headman, they are today mainly agriculturists who grow rice and wheat among other crops. Married women wear toe rings and necklaces, and some Warli practise polygyny.

Their ritual paintings are made inside the huts, for occasions such as weddings and harvests, in white rice paste on walls of branches, earth and cow dung, with a bamboo stick chewed at the end as a brush. At the centre stands a square, the chauk, which in one type encloses the mother goddess Palaghata, symbol of fertility; around it are scenes of hunting, fishing, farming and dancing. Human and animal bodies are drawn as two triangles joined at the tip.

Painting was the preserve of Warli women until the late 1970s. In that decade Jivya Soma Mashe and his son Balu Mashe began to paint outside any ritual, as an artistic pursuit of their own. The writer Yashodhara Dalmia, in The Painted World of the Warlis, claimed that the tradition reaches back to 2500 or 3000 BCE.
yashwant-rao-holkar: Yashwant Rao was the third son of Tukoji Rao Holkar. He was educated in accountancy and could read Persian, Marathi and Urdu. On 29 January 1797 Tukoji named his eldest son, Kashi Rao, as his successor. The second son, Malhar Rao, rebelled and Yashwant Rao joined him; on 14 September the army of Daulat Rao Scindia surprised their camp, Malhar Rao was killed and Yashwant Rao fled wounded. He gathered a following that included Pindharis and Afghans under Mir Khan. Claiming to act for his infant nephew Khande Rao, he declared himself head of the Holkars in January 1799, and by April had defeated Kashi Rao's commander, the Chevalier Dudrenec.

In 1799 the widows of Mahadaji Scindia asked his help to recover Ujjain and promised him four lakh rupees; he accepted five lakh from Ambaji Ingle to betray them, and looted the city. His victory over Scindia and the Peshwa on 25 October 1802, the day of Diwali, was won at Hadapsar near Pune. The Peshwa fled to Sinhagad, and Holkar took over the administration at Pune and appointed Amrutrao as Peshwa. The British, fearing for their own territories and those of their ally the Nizam of Hyderabad, decided to restore the Peshwa under their protection.

On 8 October 1804 he marched on Delhi to gain control of the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and besieged it for more than a week, but could not overcome the defence under Colonel Ochterlony. The emperor nevertheless gave him the title Maharajadhiraja Raj Rajeshwar Alija Bahadur. He appealed to other Indian rulers to join him against the British, but Daulat Rao Scindia would not fight and others gave no direct help. He fled to the Sikh Empire, where Ranjit Singh refused a British request to arrest him.

By the treaty signed at Rajghat on 24 December 1805 the British returned his territory, accepted his dominion over Jaipur, Udaipur, Kota and Bundi and undertook not to interfere in Holkar affairs; he gave up his claims to Bundelkhand and the lands north of the Chambal. He thus avoided the subsidiary alliance imposed on other Maratha chiefs. Lord Lake resigned in protest at the abandonment of the Company's Indian allies. In a letter of 15 February 1806 Holkar wrote that he had concluded the war when he found himself abandoned on all sides. He died on 28 October 1811.
yury-of-moscow: Yury Danilovich was the eldest son of Daniel of Moscow, the first prince of Moscow. His first military action was the defence of Pereslavl-Zalessky against Andrey of Gorodets, grand prince of Vladimir. Because Daniel had never held the grand princely title, his descendants had no legitimate claim to Vladimir under the traditional rules of succession. When Andrey died on 27 July 1304, Tokhta, khan of the Golden Horde, therefore gave the title to Yury's uncle, Mikhail of Tver. Yury rebelled, and two campaigns by Mikhail against Moscow, in 1305 and 1308, forced him to accept the khan's decision.

Yury meanwhile arranged the murder of Prince Konstantin of Ryazan, whom his father had captured in 1302 and held in Moscow, and annexed the Ryazan fortress of Kolomna. He also took Mozhaisk, which had belonged to the princes of Smolensk. By 1314 he had the backing of Metropolitan Peter and a military alliance with Novgorod against Tver.

In 1315 he went to the Horde, where he spent two years. His bride Konchaka converted to Orthodox Christianity and was baptised Agafiia. Returning with a large force of Tatars, he approached Tver, but his army was defeated and his wife and his brother Boris were captured; he fled to Novgorod and sued for peace. When his wife died unexpectedly as a hostage in Tver, he told the khan that Mikhail had ordered her poisoned. Both princes were summoned to Sarai, and after a trial Mikhail was executed on 22 November 1318.

As grand prince from 1318 to 1322 Yury was resisted by other princes and by the people, who thought his appointment illegitimate. He was charged with gathering the tribute for the Horde, and in his last two years in the office the khan sent no fewer than four punitive expeditions to the northeastern principalities to enforce it.

In 1322 Dmitry of Tver persuaded the khan at Sarai that Yury had kept a large part of the tribute, and received the patent for Vladimir himself. Yury then led the army of Novgorod against the Swedes, founded a fort at the mouth of the Neva River, signed the Treaty of Orekhovo in 1323 and conquered Velikiy Ustyug the same year. Summoned to the Horde for trial, he was killed by Dmitry on 21 November 1325 before any formal investigation. Dmitry was executed at the Horde eight months later. Early in 1326 Yury's remains were brought to Moscow and buried by the bishops under Metropolitan Peter.
yusuf-adil-shah: Yusuf was born in 1450, and accounts of his origin differ. He may have been a Georgian slave purchased by Mahmud Gawan, the Bahmani prime minister; other historians call him Persian or Turkmen, and one theory makes him a Turkman of the Aq-Quyunlu. The historian Firishta presents him as a son of the Ottoman sultan Murad II, a story that modern historians consider unfounded. The Portuguese knew him as Hidalcão.

He rose quickly in the Bahmani sultan's favour and was made governor of Daulatabad; Mahmood Shah Bahmani II gave him the title Adil Khan. He led the foreigners, the Afaqis, in their conflict with the local nobility, the Deccanis, a struggle in which Mahmud Gawan was put to death in 1481. Yusuf then left Daulatabad to seize Gawan's former territories of Bijapur and Belgaum, and soon came into conflict with Malik Naib, leader of the Deccani party.

He and his son Ismail did not place the title Shah before their names but kept Adil Khan, out of respect for the Bahmanis; Ibrahim Adil Shah I formally claimed independence in 1538 and was the first of the line to use it. At Bijapur Yusuf built the citadel, the Arkilla, and the palace called the Faroukh Mahal. He invited poets and artisans from Persia, Turkey and Rome to his court and was himself an accomplished musician and scholar.

He was killed in the Battle of Koilkonda against Vijayanagara on 5 December 1510, a few days after the loss of Goa. His son Ismail Adil Shah, a minor, succeeded him, aided in his rule by a certain Kamal Khan. Yusuf had married Punji, sister of the Maratha lord Mukundrao Kadam, who was renamed Bubuji Khanum; their daughters married the sultans of Ahmednagar and Berar and a Bahmani prince. The sultanate he founded lasted for close to two centuries, until Aurangzeb ended it in 1686.
zhang-jinghui: Zhang Jinghui was born on 21 June 1871 in Tai'an, south-west of Mukden in Liaoning Province, an area that became a battlefield in the First Sino-Japanese War. At an early age he joined the Honghuzi irregular cavalry of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin, forces that the Japanese recruited as mercenaries during the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905. When Yuan Shikai died in 1916 the Beiyang Army split into mutually hostile factions.

Zhang Jinghui deserted Zhang Zuolin for the Zhili clique of Wu Peifu, but later rejoined him. He served as minister of war in the Beiyang Government from May 1926 to June 1927 and as minister of industry in the National Pacification Army Government from June 1927 to June 1928, and was then appointed governor of the Harbin and China Eastern Railway Special District in northern Manchuria. After Zhang Zuolin was killed in the Huanggutun Incident on 4 June 1928, his relations with the son and successor, Zhang Xueliang, deteriorated.

Following the Mukden Incident and the invasion of Manchuria by the Japanese Kwantung Army in 1931, Zhang called a conference on 27 September to form an emergency committee aiming at the secession of Manchuria from China. He proclaimed his territory self-governing and was inaugurated as governor on 7 January 1932. He then came to terms with Japan and accepted the governorship of Heilongjiang Province in Manchukuo. His refusal to leave Harbin for Qiqihar caused friction with the Kwantung Army, and he was set aside when General Ma Zhanshan accepted the post on 14 February 1932. Ma revolted in April, and Zhang replaced him as minister of defence.

His appointment as prime minister on 21 May 1935 was made at the instigation of the Kwantung Army and over the objections of Emperor Puyi. He is said to have spent his days copying Buddhist sutras and was nicknamed the Tofu Prime Minister in his own lifetime. He is recorded as speaking out against the Japanese administration only once, to criticise the forced sale of land to Japanese colonists. In 1943 he represented Manchukuo at the Greater East Asia Conference in Tokyo; in the same year Time magazine published a false report that he had killed his family and his Japanese adviser and then himself.

After the war the Soviet Union held him in Siberia until 1950, when he was extradited to the People's Republic of China and imprisoned at the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre. He died there of heart failure on 11 January 1959.
zhu-wen: Zhu Wen was born on 5 December 852, the youngest of three sons of Zhu Cheng, an instructor in the Five Classics in Dangshan County. His father died while he was a boy, and his mother took her sons to the household of Liu Chong of Xiao County. He formed a bandit gang and in about 877 joined the rebel army of Huang Chao. After Huang Chao took the capital Chang'an in January 881, Zhu received a separate command and captured Tong Prefecture.

By 882 Huang Chao was effectively surrounded. Zhu surrendered to the Tang governor Wang Chongrong. Emperor Xizong of Tang rewarded him with a command and a new name, Quanzhong, wholeheartedly loyal. On 3 May 883 he was appointed military governor of Xuanwu Circuit at Bian Prefecture, the modern Kaifeng. In spring 884 he and Li Keyong, chief of the Shatuo Turks, routed Huang Chao's generals. On the night of 11 June 884 Zhu tried to have Li Keyong assassinated, which began a struggle of forty years between their houses.

He destroyed rival warlords such as Qin Zongquan, Shi Pu, Zhu Xuan and Zhu Jin. In 902 he besieged Li Maozhen at Fengxiang, where Emperor Zhaozong of Tang was held, and in 903 Li Maozhen handed the emperor over; all the palace eunuchs were then slaughtered. In spring 904 Zhu forced the emperor, his household and the people of Chang'an to move to Luoyang. That autumn he had Emperor Zhaozong murdered and a child, Emperor Ai of Tang, enthroned. Nine of the dead emperor's sons were killed, and some 30 senior officials of aristocratic family were forced to commit suicide at Baima and their bodies thrown into the Yellow River.

The deposed Emperor Ai was made Prince of Jiyin and poisoned in 908. Most circuits submitted to the new emperor, but the realms of Li Keyong, Li Maozhen, Yang Wo and Wang Jian did not. A siege of the Jin city of Lu was broken in 908 by Li Keyong's son Li Cunxu, and in spring 911 the Later Liang army was crushed at Boxiang.

The histories describe him as violent towards his subordinates and say that he raped the wives of his officers and of his own sons. In summer 912, gravely ill, he meant to leave the throne to his adoptive son Zhu Youwen and ordered another son, Zhu Yougui, away from the capital. Fearing execution, Zhu Yougui led imperial guards into the palace and killed him on 18 July 912.
ziusudra: One version of the Sumerian King List, the recension known as WB-62 or the Weld-Blundell prism, names Ziusudra of Shuruppak as the last king of Sumer before the flood. It makes him the son of Ubara-Tutu, from whom he inherited the rule, and says that he reigned as both king and gudug priest for ten sars, periods of 3,600 years, a figure that is probably a copyist's error for ten years.

Sediment layers at Shuruppak, the modern Tell Fara, and at Uruk, Kish and other sites attest a river flood radiocarbon-dated to about 2900 BCE, and Kish flourished soon after it. On this ground Max Mallowan held that there were good reasons to believe Ziusudra was a prehistoric ruler of a historic city.

The Sumerian tale survives on a single fragmentary tablet, dated by its script to the 17th century BCE and published in 1914 by Arno Poebel. Its first part tells of the creation of humans and animals and the founding of the first cities, Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar and Shuruppak. The passages in which the gods decide on the flood and in which the boat is described are lost. Where the text resumes, a storm rages for seven days. The sun god Utu then appears, and Ziusudra opens a window, prostrates himself and sacrifices an ox and a sheep.

After another gap he bows before the gods An and Enlil, who give him breath eternal. The rest of the poem is lost. The word used for his new home in Dilmun, kur, is ambiguous. Samuel Noah Kramer explained that its first meaning is mountain, from which came the senses of foreign land and of land in general.

Ziusudra is one of several heroes of Near Eastern flood stories, with Atrahasis, Utnapishtim and the biblical Noah, and many elements are shared among the versions. The eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh calls Utnapishtim man of Shuruppak. Ziusudra is also named in The Death of Gilgamesh, The Poem of Early Rulers and a late version of the Instructions of Shuruppak, a text Kramer dated to about 2600 BCE.

In Greek he became Xisuthros, known from the writings of Berossus, a priest of Bel in Babylon. In that version the god Enki is identified with the Greek Cronus, Xisuthros is the son of one Ardates and reigns 18 saroi, reckoned as 64,800 years, and his reed boat is said to have survived until Berossus's own day in the Corcyrean Mountains of Armenia.
zulfiqar-khan: Zulfiqar Khan was born Muhammad Ismail, in 1649 according to the historian Satish Chandra or in 1657 according to William Irvine. His father, Asad Khan, became the long-serving wazir of Emperor Aurangzeb, and his mother, Mehrunissa Begum, was a daughter of Asaf Khan, wazir under Shah Jahan. The family was Iranian on the father's side: his grandfather had moved to India after his great-grandfather, the governor of Safavid Shirvan, was executed around 1600 by Shah Abbas I. In 1677 he married a daughter of the noble Shaista Khan and received the title Itiqad Khan.

In 1689 he captured the Maratha fort of Raigad. The Maratha king Rajaram Bhonsle escaped to Jinji, but the family of his predecessor Sambhaji, including the young Shahu, was taken, and Muhammad Ismail was given the title Zulfiqar Khan. Assigned in 1690 to the Siege of Jinji, he made slow progress against a strong fort and disrupted supply lines, and the length of the siege led contemporaries to accuse him of collusion with the enemy. In 1693 he and his father arrested Prince Kam Bakhsh for negotiating with Rajaram against orders. He became mir bakhshi, or paymaster general, in 1702.

In the war of succession of 1707 he reluctantly sided with Prince Azam Shah but deserted him at the Battle of Jajau. The victor, Bahadur Shah I, reconciled him, confirmed him as mir bakhshi and in 1709 made him governor of the Deccan. When Bahadur Shah lay dying in 1712, Zulfiqar Khan allied three of his sons against the strongest, Azim-us-Shan, and then helped Jahandar Shah, the weakest, to kill the others. For this the historian Munis Faruqui calls him the first kingmaker in Mughal history. As wazir he held effective power, abolished the jizya and continued to conciliate the Marathas.

Farrukhsiyar, a son of Azim-us-Shan, rebelled with the support of the Sayyid brothers and defeated Jahandar Shah at Agra in January 1713. The emperor sought shelter in Delhi at the house of Asad Khan, but father and son handed him over in the hope of winning the victor's favour. Despite assurances, Zulfiqar Khan was executed on 11 February 1713, and his body and that of Jahandar Shah were paraded on elephants and left before the Delhi Gate. According to Richard Eaton, his kingmaking set the precedent for power brokers raising puppet emperors to the Mughal throne.
zuo-zhuan: Little is known of how the work came into being. Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, of the 1st century BCE, calls it Master Zuo's Spring and Autumn Annals and says that Zuo compiled it from the scribal records of Confucius to preserve the true teachings. The identification of this Zuo with the Zuo Qiuming praised in the Analects rests on no specific evidence and was challenged as early as the 8th century. Excavated manuscripts and analysis of its language suggest that its composition was largely complete by 300 BCE.

In the early 19th century Liu Fenglu argued that the text was not originally a commentary on the Annals, a view now generally accepted. Kang Youwei went further and held that the Han scholar Liu Xin had forged it; that theory is now considered discredited. The present arrangement, in which each entry of the Annals is followed by the matching narrative, was made by Du Yu in the 3rd century CE.

The work has 30 chapters and tells its events from the perspective of the State of Lu. Each year opens with the terse entry of the Annals, followed by narratives that are often long and detailed: battles, assassinations, intrigue, oppression and uprisings, ghosts and portents. Because the order is strictly chronological, connected episodes may be separated by the events of intervening years. Its account of the Battle of Chengpu in 632 BCE, in which the State of Jin under Chong'er defeated the State of Chu, is typical in giving more space to preparations, omens and the division of spoils than to the fighting.

The narration stays in the third person and conveys its lessons through speech and action: the haughty and wicked generally bring disaster on themselves, and ritual propriety governs all conduct, including war, though the good are also shown suffering senseless violence. Many anecdotes end with a brief verdict attributed to Confucius or to an unnamed gentleman; these were added later by Confucian scholars.

The work was canonised as one of the Chinese classics in the 1st century CE and remained a cornerstone of education in China, Japan and Korea until modern times. It is the source of more chengyu, or set idioms, than any other work, and the Qing anthology Guwen Guanzhi took 34 passages from it, more than from any other source. The oldest surviving manuscripts are six fragments found among the Dunhuang manuscripts by Paul Pelliot, dating from the 3rd to the 7th century.
